Ya'qub reassures his sons that his prayer will be effective because Allah is characterized by these very attributes. This part of the verse also serves as a general reminder to all believers about God's willingness to forgive those who sincerely seek repentance. It teaches that even after committing grievous sins, hope remains in God's infinite compassion and capacity to forgive.  The emphasis on both 'Forgiving' (الغفور) and 'Merciful' (الرحيم) highlights a dual aspect: God not only covers our sins but also showers us with His mercy after that covering.
orig: قال سوف أستغفر لكم ربي إنه هو الغفور الرحيم

translation: So when they entered upon Joseph, he took his parents to himself and said, "Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security."
interpretation:
This verse describes the moment when Joseph's brothers, along with his parents Jacob and Leah (or Rachel according to some traditions), finally arrived in Egypt and were reunited with him. The key aspects of the verse and its significance are as follows: 

*   **"فلما دخلوا على يوسف" (So when they entered upon Joseph):** This marks the culmination of the long and arduous journey of Jacob and his family to Egypt, driven by famine and also as fulfilment of Joseph's childhood dream. It highlights the long-awaited reunion. The phrase emphasizes their entering his presence, indicating that he was in a position of power and authority. 

*   **"آوى إليه أبويه" (he took his parents to himself):** This portrays Joseph's deep love and respect for his parents. The term "آوى" (awaa) suggests that he welcomed them warmly and closely, providing them with shelter and protection. It signifies his desire to have them near and to care for them after many years of separation.

*   **"وقال ادخلوا مصر إن شاء الله آمنين" (and said, 'Enter Egypt, if Allah wills, in security'):** This is a welcoming statement from Joseph to his family. It is a proclamation of safety and security they would experience in Egypt, under his protection. Joseph’s reference to "إن شاء الله" (if Allah wills) indicates that even with his power, ultimate control and safety lies with Allah. It also conveys a sense of humility and reliance on God's will in everything. "آمنين" (secure) is a vital assurance, contrasting with the fear and hardship they had faced during their travels and with the family troubles that plagued them in Canaan. 

Overall, this verse encapsulates the themes of family reunion, divine providence, and Joseph's rise to power. It shows how Allah's plan unfolds, despite the difficulties, leading to security and comfort for those who believe in Him. Joseph, as a person of great power, recognizes that his position is ultimately a result of Allah's will, and he attributes all outcomes to divine control. His kindness and devotion towards his parents demonstrate his noble character. The verse provides comfort to believers that even in difficult times, the will of God will prevail and there is always hope and the possibility for a brighter future under God's grace.
orig: فلما دخلوا على يوسف آوى إليه أبويه وقال ادخلوا مصر إن شاء الله آمنين

translation: And he raised his parents upon the throne, and they fell down to him in prostration. And he said, "O my father, this is the explanation of my vision of before. My Lord has made it truth. And He was surely good to me when He took me out of prison and brought you from the desert after Satan had caused conflict between me and my brothers. Indeed, my Lord is subtle in what He wills. Indeed, He is the Knowing, the Wise."
interpretation:
This verse recounts a pivotal moment in the story of Prophet Joseph (Yusuf) in the Quran. After years of trials and tribulations, including being thrown into a well, sold into slavery, falsely accused, and imprisoned, Joseph is finally reunited with his family. The verse describes Joseph welcoming his parents, Jacob (Ya'qub) and his mother (or stepmother, depending on interpretations), to his seat of power in Egypt. Their prostration was not an act of worship to Joseph, but rather a profound expression of respect, gratitude, and recognition of the divine power that had elevated him. This was an established custom at the time. The prostration is often interpreted in this context as a cultural or honorific gesture. Joseph then acknowledges that his dream from long ago, which foretold his prominence, has come to pass through God's will ('My Lord has made it truth'). 

He then expresses gratitude to Allah for His blessings, not just for his freedom from prison, but also for bringing his family together after a long separation. He also reflects on the past discord instigated by Satan between him and his brothers, recognizing that divine intervention brought about their reconciliation. The closing statement, 'Indeed, my Lord is subtle in what He wills. Indeed, He is the Knowing, the Wise', underscores the theme of divine providence and wisdom. It emphasizes that God's plans, often mysterious and seemingly difficult, are ultimately for the best and are executed with infinite knowledge and wisdom. The verse highlights that despite the trials he endured, Joseph acknowledged that everything was part of God’s greater plan and was done with purpose. It serves as a reminder of God’s ability to transform hardship into blessings and emphasizes the importance of faith and trust in God's will.
orig: ورفع أبويه على العرش وخروا له سجدا وقال يا أبت هذا تأويل رؤياي من قبل قد جعلها ربي حقا وقد أحسن بي إذ أخرجني من السجن وجاء بكم من البدو من بعد أن نزغ الشيطان بيني وبين إخوتي إن ربي لطيف لما يشاء إنه هو العليم الحكيم

translation: My Lord, You have given me dominion and taught me the interpretation of narratives. Creator of the heavens and earth, You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter. Cause me to die as one who has submitted [to You] and join me with the righteous.
interpretation:
This verse (12:101) from Surah Yusuf (Joseph) is a supplication made by Prophet Yusuf (Joseph) after God granted him power and knowledge. It beautifully encapsulates his gratitude, reliance on God, and his yearning for a righteous end. Here's a breakdown:

*   **"My Lord, You have given me dominion (آتيتني من الملك)..."**: Yusuf acknowledges that his position of power in Egypt (both politically and in terms of influence) is not due to his own merit, but is a gift from God. He recognizes that all authority originates from God.

*  **"...and taught me the interpretation of narratives (وعلمتني من تأويل الأحاديث)."**: This refers to the divine gift of understanding dreams and visions. This ability was key to his survival and eventual rise to power. It also highlights that religious and spiritual knowledge, particularly the capacity to understand divine messages, is a favor from God.

*   **"Creator of the heavens and earth (فاطر السماوات والأرض)..."**: This phrase emphasizes God's absolute power and authority as the sole creator and sustainer of all things. By recognizing God's creative power, Yusuf establishes a basis for his complete trust and reliance upon Him.

*   **"You are my protector in this world and the Hereafter (أنت وليي في الدنيا والآخرة)."**: This declaration signifies the Prophet's complete submission and dependence on God as his sole protector in this life and in the life to come. The concept of 'wali' signifies a guardian, protector, and helper, which is here applied solely to God.

*   **"Cause me to die as one who has submitted [to You] (توفني مسلما)..."**: This is a crucial supplication, demonstrating Yusuf's greatest desire: to die in a state of complete submission (Islam) to God. It is a plea for a righteous end, free from any deviation from God’s path. He wishes to maintain his submission until his final breath.

*   **"...and join me with the righteous (وألحقني بالصالحين)."**: This concludes the supplication, demonstrating Yusuf's wish to be counted among the righteous people in the Hereafter. He desires to be in the company of the virtuous, both in this life and the next. 

In essence, the verse is a profound expression of a Prophet’s deep faith, gratitude, dependence on God, and yearning for a blessed end. It highlights the importance of recognizing God's blessings, maintaining complete submission to His will, and aspiring to join the company of the righteous. It serves as a powerful reminder for believers to seek guidance and protection from God and to strive for a righteous life and death.
orig: رب قد آتيتني من الملك وعلمتني من تأويل الأحاديث فاطر السماوات والأرض أنت وليي في الدنيا والآخرة توفني مسلما وألحقني بالصالحين

translation: That is from the news of the unseen which We reveal to you, [O Muhammad]. And you were not with them when they decided upon their plan and they were devising a scheme.
interpretation: This verse, revealed to Prophet Muhammad, is speaking about a past event, likely a story from the scriptures that was known to the Jews and Christians, but unknown to the Arabs. It highlights the divine source of the Prophet's knowledge, asserting that the details he conveys are not from his own experience or learning, but rather directly revealed by Allah. The phrase 'That is from the news of the unseen' (ذَلِكَ مِنْ أَنبَاءِ الْغَيْبِ) emphasizes that this information is not accessible through ordinary means and is beyond human observation. The statement 'And you were not with them when they decided upon their plan and they were devising a scheme' (وَمَا كُنتَ لَدَيْهِمْ إِذْ أَجْمَعُوا أَمْرَهُمْ وَهُمْ يَمْكُرُونَ) further emphasizes the divine nature of the revelation. It clarifies that the Prophet wasn't present during the historical event that the verse alludes to, underscoring that his knowledge of it is solely from Allah. The final part mentioning 'their plan' and 'devising a scheme' suggests that the story involves a plot or conspiracy, indicating a situation where people tried to conceal their actions or deceive others. Therefore, this verse serves to authenticate the Prophet's message by highlighting his access to knowledge that would be impossible through ordinary means, as well as pointing to a past plot or scheme that the Prophet had knowledge of through Divine revelation. This strengthens the idea that his message is divine in origin, as he is privy to information beyond the human scope, particularly things which occurred before he was born and events which were done privately by others.
orig: ذلك من أنباء الغيب نوحيه إليك وما كنت لديهم إذ أجمعوا أمرهم وهم يمكرون

translation: And most of the people, even if you strive eagerly, will not be believers.
interpretation: This verse highlights a profound reality about human nature and the limits of even the Prophet's (peace be upon him) efforts in guiding people to faith. It indicates that belief is ultimately a matter of divine guidance and individual choice. Despite the Prophet's sincere and tireless efforts, a large portion of humanity will choose not to believe. The phrase 'even if you strive eagerly' emphasizes the Prophet's dedication and the extent of his efforts, underscoring that the lack of faith in many is not due to any deficiency in the message or its delivery, but rather, is attributed to the predispositions and choices of individuals. The verse serves as both a consolation to the Prophet and his followers, reminding them not to be overly disheartened by the rejection of their message, and a call for believers to acknowledge that faith is a gift and a responsibility, not something to be taken for granted. It also serves as a reminder that success in conveying the message is not measured by the number of converts, but by the sincerity of the effort and the clarity of the presentation.
orig: وما أكثر الناس ولو حرصت بمؤمنين

translation: And you do not ask them for any payment for it. It is not but a reminder for the worlds.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the selfless nature of the Prophet Muhammad's mission and, by extension, the message of the Quran itself.  The phrase 'And you do not ask them for any payment for it' highlights that the Prophet's delivery of the message is not motivated by worldly gain, profit, or compensation. He is not seeking any personal reward for his efforts in conveying the divine revelation. This underscores the purity of his intentions and the sincerity of his prophethood. The following statement, 'It is not but a reminder for the worlds,' clarifies the purpose of the Quran and the Prophet's mission: to serve as a reminder for all of humankind. The word 'worlds' (al-'alameen) denotes the universality of the message; it is not limited to a particular group, time, or place. The Quran is a divine guidance and reminder of God's oneness, His commandments, and the ultimate purpose of life. The emphasis on 'reminder' also implies that the knowledge of God and guidance is inherent within the human soul, and the Quran serves to awaken this innate understanding. Therefore, the verse serves as a dual testament: first, to the Prophet's selflessness in his divine duty and, second, to the Quran's status as a universal reminder for all humanity to attain spiritual and moral well-being.
orig: وما تسألهم عليه من أجر إن هو إلا ذكر للعالمين

translation: And how many a sign within the heavens and the earth do they pass by, while they are turning away from them!
interpretation: This verse is a powerful reminder of the pervasive nature of God's signs (ayat) in the universe. It highlights the human tendency to become oblivious or indifferent to these signs, despite their abundance and clarity. The phrase "how many a sign" (وكأين من آية) indicates a vast number and variety of these signs, encompassing both the celestial realm and the earthly sphere. These signs can refer to natural phenomena, the intricate workings of creation, or even historical events. The phrase "they pass by" (يمرون عليها) suggests that these signs are not hidden or obscure, but rather readily accessible and observable. The key issue, however, is that people "turn away from them" (وهم عنها معرضون), indicating a deliberate act of disregard or avoidance. This implies a lack of reflection, contemplation, and a failure to recognize the divine wisdom and power manifested through these signs. The verse serves as a rebuke to those who fail to recognize God's presence in His creation and a call for deeper observation and reflection, urging individuals to move beyond superficial perception and engage with the deeper spiritual realities that these signs point towards. It emphasizes that the problem is not a lack of signs but rather a deficiency in people's receptiveness and their inclination to ignore the messages conveyed through them.
orig: وكأين من آية في السماوات والأرض يمرون عليها وهم عنها معرضون

translation: And most of them do not believe in God except while they associate others with Him.
interpretation: This verse highlights a critical and paradoxical reality: many people, despite acknowledging the existence of God (Allah), fall into the trap of Shirk (associating partners with God). Their belief is flawed because it's not a pure and exclusive devotion to the One God. They might outwardly profess belief in God, but simultaneously harbor beliefs or engage in practices that attribute divine qualities or powers to other beings, objects, or ideas. This can manifest in various forms, such as: placing excessive reliance on created beings (like saints or idols), seeking help from intermediaries, or holding superstitions that contradict God's absolute power and control. The verse doesn't suggest that the majority are outright atheists, but rather that their belief is compromised by forms of idolatry that often creep into their hearts and actions, often subtly. This verse serves as a strong reminder for Muslims to purify their belief (Tawhid) and avoid any actions or beliefs that could lead to Shirk, emphasizing the importance of understanding and internalizing the true meaning of La ilaha illallah (There is no god but Allah).
orig: وما يؤمن أكثرهم بالله إلا وهم مشركون

translation: Do they then feel secure that a covering punishment from Allah should come upon them or that the Hour should come upon them suddenly while they do not perceive?
interpretation: This verse is a powerful rhetorical question posed to those who reject the divine message and persist in their disbelief and wrongdoings. It challenges their complacency and their false sense of security. The verse implies that their current state of comfort and ease should not lead them to believe they are safe from Allah's punishment. It presents two possibilities: either a 'covering punishment' (ghashiyah min 'adhab Allah), which is a kind of overwhelming calamity or affliction sent by God, or the sudden and unexpected arrival of the Hour (the Day of Judgment). The phrase 'while they do not perceive' highlights the state of heedlessness that many people are in, oblivious to the signs of God and the consequences of their actions. They are so engrossed in their worldly pursuits and desires that they fail to see the imminent possibility of divine retribution or the accountability that awaits them. The verse serves as a warning and a reminder to take heed, to reflect on the signs of God, and to turn back to Him before it is too late. It urges people to break free from their complacency and to seek refuge in God's mercy and guidance.
orig: أفأمنوا أن تأتيهم غاشية من عذاب الله أو تأتيهم الساعة بغتة وهم لا يشعرون

translation: Say, "This is my way; I invite to Allah with insight, I and those who follow me. And exalted is Allah; and I am not of those who associate others with Him."
interpretation:
This verse is a powerful declaration of the Prophet Muhammad's mission and the core principles of Islam. It outlines the methodology of inviting people to the path of Allah (God). Let's break it down:

*   **"Say, 'This is my way...'"**: This is a command to the Prophet, and by extension, to all Muslims. It emphasizes the clarity and definiteness of the path being presented. This isn't a vague or ambiguous teaching, but a clear direction.

*   **"...I invite to Allah with insight..."**: The invitation is not blind or based on hearsay, but founded on 'basirah' which means 'insight, clear vision, and knowledge.' This signifies that the invitation to Islam should be based on sound reasoning, understanding of the divine message, and the evidence it provides. It highlights the importance of intellectual engagement in faith.

*   **"...I and those who follow me."**: This links the Prophet's way to his followers. It means that every Muslim should also be a 'dai' or inviter to Islam, following the same methodology of using sound knowledge and clear evidence. It emphasizes the collective responsibility of Muslims to spread the message of Islam.

*   **"And exalted is Allah..."**: This part emphasizes the transcendence and perfection of Allah. It signifies that the whole invitation is for His sake and glorification, and to establish the Oneness of Allah.

*   **"...and I am not of those who associate others with Him."**: This is a firm declaration of the Prophet's absolute commitment to monotheism and rejection of idolatry or any form of associating partners with God (shirk). It is a clear statement that this message is free from any form of paganism or polytheism. This serves as a stark reminder to all Muslims not to fall into shirk in any of its forms, whether overt or subtle.

In summary, this verse is a foundational statement on the nature of the Prophet's mission and the responsibility of his followers. It emphasizes the importance of clear knowledge, sound reasoning, and absolute monotheism in calling people to Islam. The invitation must come from a place of understanding and with the aim of glorifying Allah alone, and rejecting any form of associating partners with Him. It also stresses the continuity of the prophetic way in the life of his followers.
orig: قل هذه سبيلي أدعو إلى الله على بصيرة أنا ومن اتبعني وسبحان الله وما أنا من المشركين

translation: And We sent not before you [as messengers] except men to whom We revealed from among the people of the cities. So have they not traveled through the earth and observed how was the end of those before them? And the home of the Hereafter is best for those who fear Allah. Then will you not reason?
interpretation: This verse addresses both the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his detractors, emphasizing several key points. Firstly, it clarifies that all messengers before Muhammad were human males, not angels or other beings, and were chosen from established communities within cities, not from isolated or fantastical origins. This grounds the concept of messengership within the realm of human experience and relatable contexts. The verse then poses a rhetorical question, urging the disbelievers to reflect upon the histories of past nations. By traveling the earth and observing the ruins and legacies of those who rejected their messengers, they should be able to see the consequences of their disbelief and rebellion. The phrase 'how was the end of those before them' highlights that their destiny was a direct result of their actions and beliefs. Finally, the verse culminates with the assertion that 'the home of the Hereafter is best for those who fear Allah'. This emphasizes that the true and lasting success lies in acknowledging God and living righteously in accordance with His commands. The phrase 'Then will you not reason?' is a final appeal for rational consideration of the evidence provided by historical examples and the promise of the afterlife. In short, the verse encourages reflection upon the past, discernment of divine patterns, and recognition of the long-term consequences of choices, ultimately calling for faith and God-consciousness.
orig: وما أرسلنا من قبلك إلا رجالا نوحي إليهم من أهل القرى أفلم يسيروا في الأرض فينظروا كيف كان عاقبة الذين من قبلهم ولدار الآخرة خير للذين اتقوا أفلا تعقلون

translation: Until, when the messengers despaired and thought that they had been denied, Our help came to them, and We saved whom We willed. And Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people.
interpretation: This verse describes a critical juncture in the lives of prophets and messengers. It highlights the extreme trials they faced when their calls to guidance were met with resistance, disbelief, and rejection. The phrase 'until when the messengers despaired' illustrates the depth of their struggle. They reached a point of near hopelessness, where they began to question whether their divine mission would ever be successful. The word 'ظنوا' (thought) in 'and thought that they had been denied' is significant. Some interpretations explain that the prophets may have even begun to feel as if they might have been labelled as liars, not by Allah but by the people who rejected them, or even perhaps had a feeling that their message has been rejected. It suggests the immense psychological and emotional pressure they endured. The verse emphasizes that just at their lowest point, when human help seemed impossible, 'Our help came to them'. This divine intervention underscores the power and sovereignty of God, who controls all affairs. 'We saved whom We willed' speaks to God's prerogative to choose who is granted salvation, based on His wisdom. The closing statement, 'And Our punishment is not averted from the criminal people,' serves as a warning. It reaffirms divine justice and clarifies that those who persist in their criminal behaviour will not escape accountability. Thus, the verse provides a profound lesson on patience, perseverance, and faith in divine timing. It highlights that even when faced with extreme hardship and apparent hopelessness, the support of God is always available for those who remain committed to His message and that divine judgement is inevitable for those who persist in their wrongdoing.
orig: حتى إذا استيأس الرسل وظنوا أنهم قد كذبوا جاءهم نصرنا فنجي من نشاء ولا يرد بأسنا عن القوم المجرمين

translation: Indeed, in their stories there is a lesson for those of understanding. It was not a fabricated narration, but a confirmation of what came before it, and a detailed explanation of all things, and guidance and mercy for a people who believe.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound wisdom and purpose behind the narratives presented in the Quran. It emphasizes that these stories are not mere tales for entertainment, but rather contain valuable lessons ('ibrah) for those with intellect and insight ('uli al-albab'). The verse explicitly denies that the Quran is a fabricated work ('ma kana hadithan yuftara'), asserting its divine origin and authenticity. Instead, it affirms that the Quran confirms the truths revealed in previous scriptures ('tasdiq alladhi bayna yadayhi'), thus demonstrating the continuity of divine guidance. Furthermore, the Quran is described as providing a comprehensive explanation of all necessary matters ('tafsil kulli shay'in'), indicating its completeness and sufficiency as a source of guidance. Finally, it is presented as 'huda' (guidance) and 'rahma' (mercy) specifically for those who believe ('li qawmin yu'minun'). This suggests that while the Quran's benefits are universally applicable, they are most fully realized by those who approach it with faith and a desire to learn and follow its teachings. The overall message is to encourage reflection on the Quranic narratives, not as fictional accounts, but as profound sources of wisdom, guidance, and spiritual growth, confirming previous divine revelations and providing a clear path for those who believe.
orig: لقد كان في قصصهم عبرة لأولي الألباب ما كان حديثا يفترى ولكن تصديق الذي بين يديه وتفصيل كل شيء وهدى ورحمة لقوم يؤمنون

translation: Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra. These are the verses of the Book. And what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth, but most people do not believe.
interpretation: This verse begins with the enigmatic 'Alif, Lam, Mim, Ra', which are known as 'Muqatta'at' or disconnected letters. Their precise meaning is not definitively known, and scholars offer various interpretations, often seeing them as a divine secret or a challenge to the reader to contemplate the nature of the Qur'an. The verse then immediately transitions to declare that 'these are the verses of the Book', referring to the Qur'an itself, establishing its divine origin and significance. The following part asserts that 'what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth' - emphasizing that the revelation received by the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) is undoubtedly the absolute truth, emanating directly from God. Finally, the verse concludes with a statement that acknowledges a challenging reality: 'but most people do not believe.' This highlights that the truth of the Qur'an may not be universally accepted, pointing to the human tendency to reject guidance despite its clarity. The verse thus juxtaposes the unequivocal truth of the Qur'an with the stubbornness of human disbelief, urging contemplation, and perhaps subtly encouraging those who do believe to remain steadfast despite the challenges of convincing others.
orig: المر تلك آيات الكتاب والذي أنزل إليك من ربك الحق ولكن أكثر الناس لا يؤمنون

translation: Allah is the one who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see; then He established Himself on the Throne. And He subjected the sun and the moon, each running [its course] for a specified term. He arranges [all] matters; He details the signs that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord.
interpretation: This verse from Surah Ar-Ra'd (13:2) is a powerful declaration of Allah's absolute power and wisdom in creation and governance of the universe. The first part, 'Allah is the one who raised the heavens without pillars that you can see,' emphasizes the miraculous nature of the heavens' existence, challenging any notion of them being supported by physical structures. This highlights Allah's unique ability to create and sustain without any dependency. The phrase 'then He established Himself on the Throne' (istiwa al-al-'arsh) signifies Allah's complete authority and sovereignty over all of creation. It is an assertion of His transcendence and dominion. The subsequent statement, 'And He subjected the sun and the moon, each running [its course] for a specified term,' points towards the precision and order within the cosmos. The celestial bodies are not aimlessly wandering but are governed by divine decree and function within a prescribed timeframe. The phrase 'He arranges [all] matters; He details the signs' indicates Allah's detailed management of all affairs within the universe.  His signs, 'Ayat' - both in creation and revelation, serve as proofs of His existence, power, and wisdom, each detail having a specific meaning and intention.  The final part, 'that you may be certain of the meeting with your Lord,' connects the cosmological evidence with the ultimate purpose of human existence: the accountability and eventual meeting with Allah. Reflecting upon these signs, both in the natural world and the divine scripture, should lead to conviction of the hereafter and the day of judgement.  The verse aims to instill awe and reverence for Allah while fostering a sense of responsibility in this world, preparing humans for their eternal destiny.
orig: الله الذي رفع السماوات بغير عمد ترونها ثم استوى على العرش وسخر الشمس والقمر كل يجري لأجل مسمى يدبر الأمر يفصل الآيات لعلكم بلقاء ربكم توقنون

translation: And it is He who has spread out the earth and placed therein firmly set mountains and rivers; and from all fruits He has made therein two mates. He brings the night as a cover over the day. Indeed in that are signs for a people who give thought.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's power and wisdom through His creation, particularly focusing on the earth and its features. The spreading out of the earth ('mad al-ard') signifies its suitability for habitation, not necessarily its literal shape. The mountains ('rawasi') are anchors that stabilize the earth, and the rivers ('anhar') are vital for life, showcasing God's provision. The pairing of all fruits ('zawjayn ithnayn') indicates a design for reproduction and highlights the concept of duality and balance in creation. Finally, the alternation of night and day ('yaghsha al-layl al-nahar') underscores God's control over time and the cycles of life. The verse concludes by stating that these are signs ('ayat') for those who contemplate and reflect, urging believers to use their intellect to understand the divine presence manifested in the natural world. The verse is not merely a description of natural phenomena, but a call to recognize God’s deliberate design and wisdom, inviting reflection on the patterns and purpose behind His creation.
orig: وهو الذي مد الأرض وجعل فيها رواسي وأنهارا ومن كل الثمرات جعل فيها زوجين اثنين يغشي الليل النهار إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يتفكرون

translation: And in the earth are neighboring tracts, and gardens of vines, and fields of grain, and palm trees, growing from one root and not from one root, watered with one water; and We make some of them excel others in fruit. Indeed in that are signs for a people who reason.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the diversity and interconnectedness of the natural world as signs of God's power and wisdom. It points to several key observations:

1.  **Neighboring Tracts (قطع متجاورات):** The earth is not a uniform, monotonous entity; it is comprised of diverse regions and terrains, placed side by side. This variation in land suggests a purpose and design, rather than random chance.

2.  **Variety of Vegetation (جنات من أعناب وزرع ونخيل):**  The verse specifically mentions vineyards, fields of grains, and palm trees – all essential for human sustenance. The diversity of plant life, and their different requirements, show the comprehensive design of the natural world. This provides a reminder of the abundance of God’s blessings.

3.  **Single Roots and Non-Single Roots (صنوان وغير صنوان):** The phrase “صنوان” (sinwān) refers to palm trees growing from the same root system, which implies clustered growth. While “غير صنوان” (ghayr sinwān) represents those that grow individually. This emphasizes both the unity and diversity in nature's processes, reflecting how God brings forth life both in patterns and variations, using similar underlying principles.

4.  **One Water Source (يسقى بماء واحد):** Despite the differences between lands and plants, they are all watered by the same basic source of water. This indicates that God is the one source of all provision, and all sustenance derives from His power. Despite shared resources, the individual entities remain diverse.

5.  **Superiority in Fruit (ونفضل بعضها على بعض في الأكل):**  Not all fruits or grains are the same; they differ in taste, nutrition, and other characteristics. This shows how God assigns different values and characteristics to things, showing His absolute control and purpose over even similar objects. This highlights that each thing is uniquely crafted with its own purpose and value. It highlights that even while everything is sustained by the same source of life (the water), God gives different levels of favor.

6. **Signs for Those Who Reason (إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يعقلون):** This is a crucial conclusion. The verse suggests that contemplation of nature's diversity, interconnectedness, and patterns leads to recognizing the signs of the Creator. It emphasizes the importance of intellect and observation in understanding the world and, ultimately, in appreciating God’s work and thereby confirming God’s existence, power, and wisdom.

In summary, this verse is not just a description of nature but a call to observe the natural world thoughtfully, discerning within it the signs of God's creation, power, and the meticulous planning behind each individual creation and its role within the whole system. It encourages using one's intellect to grasp the larger purpose of existence and the source of all blessings.
orig: وفي الأرض قطع متجاورات وجنات من أعناب وزرع ونخيل صنوان وغير صنوان يسقى بماء واحد ونفضل بعضها على بعض في الأكل إن في ذلك لآيات لقوم يعقلون

translation: And if you are to be amazed, then amazing is their saying, "When we are dust, will we indeed be in a new creation?" Those are the ones who have disbelieved in their Lord, and those are the ones who will have shackles on their necks, and those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, all believers, highlighting the astonishment and disbelief of those who reject the concept of resurrection. The verse begins by acknowledging that their denial, particularly their question about being resurrected after becoming dust, is indeed something to be amazed by, not in a positive sense, but because it showcases the depth of their misunderstanding and their rejection of God's power. They express disbelief at the possibility of being recreated after death and decomposition, demonstrating a limited understanding of divine power. The verse then immediately condemns them as those who disbelieve in their Lord (God), highlighting that their incredulity about resurrection stems from a fundamental lack of faith.  The 'shackles on their necks' is a metaphorical expression signifying their being bound by their own disbelief and the weight of their sins, leading them inexorably towards punishment. The final statement, 'companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally,' serves as a stark warning about the consequences of disbelief, depicting the eternal nature of hellfire for those who choose to reject faith and the concept of divine justice and resurrection. This verse underscores the importance of belief in the resurrection and provides a counterpoint to the incredulity of those who deny its possibility, making a clear connection between belief and eternal destiny. It's a reminder that the rejection of resurrection is fundamentally a rejection of God’s power and his promise of accountability on the Day of Judgment.
orig: وإن تعجب فعجب قولهم أإذا كنا ترابا أإنا لفي خلق جديد أولئك الذين كفروا بربهم وأولئك الأغلال في أعناقهم وأولئك أصحاب النار هم فيها خالدون

translation: And they impatiently urge you to hasten the evil before the good, while there have already passed before them [many] exemplary punishments. And indeed, your Lord is full of forgiveness for the people despite their wrongdoing, and indeed, your Lord is severe in punishment.
interpretation: This verse describes the behavior of some people who, instead of seeking good or guidance, mockingly challenge the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) by demanding that the promised punishment be brought upon them immediately, showing their arrogance and disbelief. The phrase "before the good" highlights their twisted priorities; they desire suffering rather than the blessings of faith. The verse then reminds them that history is replete with examples of those who were punished for their transgressions (“exemplary punishments” - المثلات) serving as a warning. Despite the wickedness of these people, the verse also emphasizes God's dual nature – He is both "full of forgiveness" (ذو مغفرة) for those who repent from their wrongdoing, and "severe in punishment" (شديد العقاب) for those who persist in their rejection of truth. The verse underscores the balance between divine mercy and justice. It essentially says that God is patient and gives people opportunities to mend their ways, but that ultimate accountability will be meted out to those who continue to oppress others and deny the truth.
orig: ويستعجلونك بالسيئة قبل الحسنة وقد خلت من قبلهم المثلات وإن ربك لذو مغفرة للناس على ظلمهم وإن ربك لشديد العقاب

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" You are only a warner, and for every people is a guide.
interpretation:
This verse highlights a common reaction of disbelief towards prophets and their message. The disbelievers challenge the authenticity of the Prophet Muhammad's prophethood by demanding a miraculous sign ('ayah') from God, seemingly to satisfy their skepticism. They are focusing on tangible, immediate proof as a condition for belief. 

The verse then shifts focus, emphasizing the Prophet's primary role as a 'warner' (mundhir), tasked with conveying God's message and admonishing people against disbelief and its consequences. His responsibility isn't to produce miracles on demand; rather, it's to communicate divine guidance.

The phrase 'and for every people is a guide' (wa li kulli qawmin had) has two layers of meaning. It can refer to every community throughout time having a prophet or a guide from God. It can also refer to the Qur'an itself as a universal guidance for all people. It indicates that God's guidance is not limited to a specific time or people, and that divine guidance has always been available to mankind, thus the Prophet Muhammad is the last prophet who gave people guidance through the Qur'an. Therefore, the verse implicitly addresses the disbelievers' demand for a specific miracle, highlighting that the true sign is the message itself and the guidance that it brings, not merely the production of physical miracles.
orig: ويقول الذين كفروا لولا أنزل عليه آية من ربه إنما أنت منذر ولكل قوم هاد

translation: Allah knows what every female carries and what the wombs lose [of their contents] and what they increase. And with Him, everything is by a measure.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes Allah's absolute knowledge and control over all aspects of creation, particularly concerning the development of life within the womb. The phrase "Allah knows what every female carries" indicates His comprehensive awareness of each pregnancy, from conception to birth, including the sex, health, and characteristics of the unborn child. The subsequent phrase, "and what the wombs lose [of their contents] and what they increase," highlights Allah's knowledge of every detail of the gestational process, including miscarriages, premature births, and any changes in the womb's size or condition. It shows that even seemingly random or natural events are known to Allah with absolute precision. The final part of the verse, "And with Him, everything is by a measure," underscores that all events, including the process of pregnancy and childbirth, are governed by divine decree and occur according to a predetermined plan or measurement. This conveys the idea that Allah's knowledge and power extend to every minute detail of existence and that all things unfold according to His perfect wisdom and preordained plan. The verse ultimately serves as a reminder of Allah's omnipotence, omniscience, and the orderliness of creation.
orig: الله يعلم ما تحمل كل أنثى وما تغيض الأرحام وما تزداد وكل شيء عنده بمقدار

translation: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Grand, the Exalted.
interpretation: This verse describes some of God's attributes and underscores His absolute knowledge and supremacy. "Knower of the unseen (al-Ghayb) and the witnessed (ash-Shahadah)" emphasizes that God's knowledge encompasses all that is hidden and all that is manifest. Nothing escapes His awareness, whether it is in the past, present or future, or in the realm of the seen or unseen. 'Al-Kabeer' (the Grand) denotes His immeasurable greatness and magnificence, highlighting His superior status above all creation. 'Al-Muta'al' (the Exalted) further reinforces His transcendence and supreme position, indicating that He is far above any comparison or limitation. In essence, the verse asserts that God is the all-knowing, the absolutely great and the supreme Being, whose power and knowledge are without bounds. It calls for reverence, awe, and submission to the One who possesses such magnificent qualities.
orig: عالم الغيب والشهادة الكبير المتعال

translation: It is the same [to Him], whether one of you conceals his speech or declares it, and whether one is hidden by night or walks about by day.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the absolute and encompassing knowledge of God. It states that whether a person speaks secretly or openly, whether they act under the cover of night or in the visibility of day, all are equally known to God. The verse conveys that there is no hiding from God's awareness; His knowledge is complete and pervasive, encompassing all actions, thoughts, and circumstances. The phrase 'it is the same' highlights that to God, there is no distinction in terms of awareness between private and public acts, or nocturnal and diurnal activities. This serves as a reminder of God's omniscience and encourages accountability in all aspects of life, as all deeds are known and will be reckoned by God regardless of their perceived secrecy or openness.
orig: سواء منكم من أسر القول ومن جهر به ومن هو مستخف بالليل وسارب بالنهار

translation: For each one are successive angels before and behind him who protect him by the decree of Allah. Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allah intends for a people ill, there is no repelling it, and there is not for them besides Him any patron.
interpretation: This verse highlights several key Islamic concepts: Firstly, it speaks of the presence of guardian angels ('mu'aqqibat') who are assigned to each individual, protecting them according to Allah's command. This underscores the constant divine watchfulness and protection over humanity. However, this protection is not absolute. The verse introduces the concept of 'divine decree' ('amr Allah'), which suggests that while angels guard, events ultimately unfold according to God’s plan. Secondly, the core message of the verse emphasizes the principle of personal responsibility and free will. Allah does not arbitrarily change a people's condition, whether it be prosperity or adversity, until they themselves initiate change within themselves. This change can relate to their faith, values, attitudes, or actions. This highlights that people's choices have real consequences, both individually and collectively, which directly influence their circumstances. It also implies a system of cause and effect. Lastly, the verse affirms Allah's supreme power and the inability of any being to avert His decree when He intends ill for a people, and that ultimately no one can stand as a protector or a patron other than Him. This part serves as a warning, emphasizing that when divine retribution is due, there is no escape and no intercessor. The verse, taken as a whole, establishes a balance between divine power and human responsibility, teaching that positive change requires inward transformation, while also acknowledging that the consequences of one's action are ultimately subject to the decree and will of Allah. It reminds believers that their state is directly related to their deeds and inner disposition, while also reinforcing God’s omnipotence and the limits of worldly power.
orig: له معقبات من بين يديه ومن خلفه يحفظونه من أمر الله إن الله لا يغير ما بقوم حتى يغيروا ما بأنفسهم وإذا أراد الله بقوم سوءا فلا مرد له وما لهم من دونه من وال

translation: He is the One who shows you the lightning, causing fear and hope, and He produces the heavy clouds.
interpretation: This verse highlights God's power and control over natural phenomena, particularly the elements. The lightning, described as a spectacle that inspires both 'fear' (khawfan) and 'hope' (tama'an), embodies this duality. Fear arises from the raw power and potential danger of lightning strikes, while hope comes from the anticipation of rain that often follows, which is crucial for sustenance and life, especially in arid regions. The verse continues by mentioning that He 'produces the heavy clouds' (al-sahab al-thiqal), which further emphasizes God's role in the water cycle, a process vital for life on earth. The verse serves as a reminder of God's signs in the natural world, which are both awe-inspiring and beneficial, encouraging contemplation about His power and providence. It also implicitly points to God's ability to bring about both hardship and relief, highlighting the importance of remaining humble and hopeful in the face of the natural forces He has created.
orig: هو الذي يريكم البرق خوفا وطمعا وينشئ السحاب الثقال

translation: And the thunder exalts [Allah] with His praise, and so do the angels from fear of Him. And He sends the thunderbolts and strikes with them whom He wills, while they dispute about Allah; and He is severe in might.
interpretation: This verse paints a powerful picture of Allah's omnipotence and the awe He inspires in His creation. The thunder ('ar-ra'd'), a dramatic and formidable natural phenomenon, is depicted as actively glorifying Allah through its very existence and sound. This act of glorification ('yusabbihu') is understood not as conscious worship but as a testament to Allah's perfect design and power, where even inanimate objects inherently demonstrate His majesty. Similarly, the angels ('al-mala'ikah'), who are intelligent beings, also glorify Allah, but their glorification stems from a deep-seated fear ('khifat') and reverence for His power. This fear is not a fear of punishment but rather a recognition of their utter dependence on Him and their profound respect for His greatness. Furthermore, the verse speaks of Allah's control over natural forces, specifically the thunderbolts ('as-sawa'iq'), which He sends to strike whom He wills ('man yasha''). This highlights His absolute sovereignty over all creation and His ability to act as He sees fit. The phrase 'while they dispute about Allah' ('wa hum yujadiluna fi Allah') refers to those who deny or question Allah's existence, attributes, or power, even when confronted with undeniable signs of His grandeur. The verse concludes with the affirmation 'He is severe in might' ('wa huwa shadeed al-mihal'), emphasizing Allah's formidable power and the ultimate futility of challenging or disputing Him. The overall message is a reminder of Allah's unmatched power, His deservingness of praise, and the foolishness of those who deny Him despite the overwhelming evidence of His existence and control over all creation. It emphasizes the need for submission and humility in the face of His might.
orig: ويسبح الرعد بحمده والملائكة من خيفته ويرسل الصواعق فيصيب بها من يشاء وهم يجادلون في الله وهو شديد المحال

translation: To Him (alone) is the true prayer (or call); and those whom they invoke other than Him do not respond to them with a thing, except like one who stretches his hands towards water (from afar), that it may reach his mouth, but it will never reach it. And the supplication of the disbelievers is but in error.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the exclusivity of true worship and supplication to Allah (God). It highlights the futility of seeking help from any other besides Him. The verse employs a powerful analogy: someone stretching their hands out to water from afar, hoping it will reach their mouth. Just as the water cannot reach them in that manner, so too are the prayers and supplications directed to anything other than Allah ultimately fruitless and unproductive. The 'those whom they invoke other than Him' refers to idols, false deities, or anything which people mistakenly place their hopes and trust in besides the One True God. The last part of the verse, 'And the supplication of the disbelievers is but in error,' underscores that the entire premise of their worship is fundamentally flawed and misguided because they are directing their devotion to something that has no power to respond or benefit them. In essence, the verse is a call to sincerity in worship and a warning against misdirected faith.
orig: له دعوة الحق والذين يدعون من دونه لا يستجيبون لهم بشيء إلا كباسط كفيه إلى الماء ليبلغ فاه وما هو ببالغه وما دعاء الكافرين إلا في ضلال

translation: And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or unwillingly, and their shadows, in the mornings and the afternoons.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the absolute and universal sovereignty of Allah. It emphasizes that all creation, without exception, is in a state of submission to Him. The prostration (sujood) here signifies this submission, which is not just a physical act of prayer but a reflection of the innate nature of existence. The verse points out that even those who may not consciously acknowledge Allah or follow His commands are, in essence, submitting to His will and design. 

Here's a breakdown of the key elements:

* **"And to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and the earth..."**: This establishes that every single being in the universe, from the smallest particle to the largest celestial body, is in submission to Allah's will. This submission is not limited to humans, but encompasses all creation.

* **"...willingly or unwillingly..."**: This is a crucial distinction. 'Willingly' refers to those who consciously and lovingly submit to Allah through faith and obedience. 'Unwillingly' refers to those who, despite perhaps rejecting Allah through their actions or beliefs, are still subject to His natural laws and will. Their very existence and all they experience are ultimately within His decree. Even those who deny Him are submitting to Him through the inevitability of natural laws, such as death, aging, or being sustained by His creation.

* **"...and their shadows, in the mornings and the afternoons."**: This seemingly simple addition emphasizes the vastness of Allah's dominion and the constant, inescapable nature of submission. Shadows, as a creation that depends entirely on something else for its very being, represent the dependence of all things on Allah. The mention of 'mornings and afternoons' implies that this submission is perpetual, occurring at all times. This part could also be interpreted as a sign of God's power and control, as even something as seemingly insignificant as a shadow is a sign of His existence and control of creation, that is subservient to His will at all times. Also, shadows are a passive submission, something that does not willingly submit. Therefore, it is an extension of the phrase 'willingly or unwillingly' that highlights the point.

In summary, the verse serves as a powerful reminder that nothing exists outside the scope of Allah’s power and control. The submission to Him is not merely an act of worship for believers, but the very essence of existence for all creation, whether consciously acknowledged or not.
orig: ولله يسجد من في السماوات والأرض طوعا وكرها وظلالهم بالغدو والآصال

translation: Say, 'Who is the Lord of the heavens and the earth?' Say, 'Allah.' Say, 'Then have you taken besides Him allies who do not possess for themselves any benefit or any harm?' Say, 'Is the blind equal to the seeing? Or is darkness equal to light? Or have they attributed to Allah partners who created like His creation, so that the creation seemed similar to them?' Say, 'Allah is the Creator of all things, and He is the One, the Prevailing.'
interpretation: This verse is a powerful declaration of God's absolute sovereignty and a refutation of polytheism. It begins with a rhetorical question compelling the listener to acknowledge God as the sole Lord of the heavens and the earth, emphasizing His exclusive claim to creation and control. The verse then challenges the logic of associating partners with God. It questions the very nature of these 'allies' or idols, highlighting their utter powerlessness to benefit or harm even themselves, let alone others.  The analogy of the blind and the seeing, and darkness and light, underscores the absurdity of comparing the true God with false deities.  These idols, representing ignorance and spiritual darkness, are contrasted with the clarity of faith in the One God, who is the source of all light and knowledge. Furthermore, the verse refutes the notion that any other being or entity possesses creative power comparable to God’s, exposing the flawed reasoning that leads to polytheism. If there were truly other creators, wouldn't the creations be distinct and not mistaken for God’s?  The verse concludes by reaffirming God's unique position as the creator of everything and His absolute dominion as 'The One, The Prevailing' (al-Wahid al-Qahhar), solidifying the concept of Tawhid (Oneness of God) and His unquestionable supremacy. The verse essentially serves as an invitation to recognize the inherent logic and truth of monotheism, urging people to abandon false beliefs and turn wholeheartedly to the one true God.
orig: قل من رب السماوات والأرض قل الله قل أفاتخذتم من دونه أولياء لا يملكون لأنفسهم نفعا ولا ضرا قل هل يستوي الأعمى والبصير أم هل تستوي الظلمات والنور أم جعلوا لله شركاء خلقوا كخلقه فتشابه الخلق عليهم قل الله خالق كل شيء وهو الواحد القهار

translation: He sends down water from the sky, and valleys flow according to their capacity, and the torrent carries a swelling foam. And from that which they heat in the fire, desiring adornments or utensils, is a foam like it. Thus does Allah present the truth and falsehood. As for the foam, it vanishes, [passing away]; but as for that which benefits the people, it remains in the earth. Thus does Allah present the examples.
interpretation:
This verse uses vivid imagery to illustrate the difference between truth and falsehood, and their respective fates. It begins by describing the natural process of rain descending from the sky, filling valleys according to their size. The resulting torrent carries a foam, which is a temporary and insubstantial byproduct of the powerful flow. Similarly, the process of refining metals in fire, to create ornaments or tools, also produces a type of foam. Both foams, created through powerful forces, are transient and ultimately useless.

The verse then explicitly states that "Thus does Allah present the truth and falsehood." The foam, representing falsehood, is superficial, loud, and initially prominent, but it is ultimately ephemeral and "vanishes, [passing away]" becoming worthless and forgotten. Conversely, "that which benefits the people," represented by the water itself, which sustains life and enables growth, remains in the earth. This symbolizes the truth, which is solid, enduring, and beneficial. It may not be as flashy or immediately attention-grabbing as falsehood, but it has lasting value and impact. 

The verse concludes by emphasizing that Allah provides these types of examples for people to learn from. The analogy of water and foam, metalworking and waste, serves as a powerful reminder that appearances can be deceiving. True value and lasting impact are not found in what is loud or superficial but in what provides genuine benefit and endures over time. The verse encourages critical thinking and the pursuit of that which is truly beneficial and righteous, which are the essence of the truth, rather than being swayed by the ephemeral nature of falsehood. Thus, this verse serves as a constant reminder to prioritize the enduring and beneficial, not the fleeting and valueless.
orig: أنزل من السماء ماء فسالت أودية بقدرها فاحتمل السيل زبدا رابيا ومما يوقدون عليه في النار ابتغاء حلية أو متاع زبد مثله كذلك يضرب الله الحق والباطل فأما الزبد فيذهب جفاء وأما ما ينفع الناس فيمكث في الأرض كذلك يضرب الله الأمثال

translation: For those who have responded to their Lord is the best [reward], but those who did not respond to Him - if they had all that is in the earth entirely and the like of it with it, they would [gladly] offer it as ransom. Those will have the worst account, and their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the resting place.
interpretation:
This verse contrasts the destinies of those who heed God's call and those who reject it. It highlights the vast difference in outcomes based on their response to divine guidance. On one hand, the verse promises 'the best reward' (al-Husna) for those who 'respond to their Lord' (istajabu li-rabbihim), indicating blessings in this life and the hereafter for those who obey God and follow His commands. This encompasses acts of faith, righteous deeds, and submission to His will.

On the other hand, the verse describes the fate of those who 'did not respond to Him' (lam yastajibuu lahu). It paints a stark picture of their remorse and regret on the Day of Judgment. The verse states that even if they possessed everything on earth and an equal amount more, they would willingly give it all as a ransom to escape punishment. This emphasizes the enormity of the consequences of rejecting God's guidance. The phrase 'the worst account' (su' al-hisab) indicates a harsh reckoning for their deeds, and their ultimate abode is 'Hell' (Jahannam), described as a 'wretched resting place' (bi'sa al-mihad). This vivid imagery reinforces the severity of the punishment awaiting those who turn away from God.

Therefore, the verse serves as a warning and a reminder about the critical importance of accepting and acting upon God's guidance. It emphasizes that worldly possessions and material wealth are ultimately insignificant in the face of divine judgment, and true success lies in aligning oneself with God's will.
orig: للذين استجابوا لربهم الحسنى والذين لم يستجيبوا له لو أن لهم ما في الأرض جميعا ومثله معه لافتدوا به أولئك لهم سوء الحساب ومأواهم جهنم وبئس المهاد

translation: Is one who knows that what has been revealed to you from your Lord is the truth like one who is blind? Only those of understanding will remember.
interpretation: This verse presents a stark contrast between two types of people: those who possess knowledge and understanding of the divine revelation (the Qur'an), and those who are spiritually blind, lacking such insight. The verse is rhetorical, implying that these two groups are fundamentally different and unequal in their perception of truth. It emphasizes that recognizing the Qur'an as the truth, divinely sent by God, requires intellectual and spiritual openness. Those with 'ulu al-albab' (those of understanding, or people of intellect and insight) are the ones who can truly reflect on and be reminded by the Qur'an’s message and embrace its wisdom. The verse essentially suggests that the ability to recognize the truth is not merely about physical sight but requires a certain level of intellectual capacity, spiritual awareness, and a willingness to accept guidance, whereas ignoring it demonstrates a profound spiritual blindness that renders one incapable of perceiving the truth.
orig: أفمن يعلم أنما أنزل إليك من ربك الحق كمن هو أعمى إنما يتذكر أولو الألباب

translation: Those who fulfill the covenant of Allah and do not break the pact.
interpretation: This verse describes a key characteristic of righteous individuals: their unwavering commitment to fulfilling their obligations. 'Those who fulfill the covenant of Allah' refers to people who uphold their promises and agreements made with God, which encompasses adherence to His commandments, beliefs, and moral principles outlined in the Quran and Sunnah (Prophet Muhammad's teachings). This goes beyond mere lip service; it implies a deep inner dedication to living by God's guidance. 'And do not break the pact' emphasizes the importance of maintaining integrity and trustworthiness. The 'pact' (al-meethaq) refers not only to agreements made directly with God, such as the declaration of faith (shahada), but also to broader covenants and contracts one makes with others, representing the commitment to fulfilling one's duties and obligations in all aspects of life. Breaking this pact is viewed as a sign of hypocrisy and a serious transgression. The verse highlights the importance of consistency and faithfulness in one's relationship with God and fellow humans. It emphasizes that true piety is demonstrated through actions, and that a person's character should be marked by trustworthiness and reliability. Therefore, this verse is a call for believers to uphold their responsibilities, whether spiritual or worldly, and to be people of their word. It promotes a life of honesty, faithfulness, and steadfastness in fulfilling all covenants and commitments.
orig: الذين يوفون بعهد الله ولا ينقضون الميثاق

translation: And those who join that which Allah has commanded to be joined and fear their Lord and are afraid of the evil of [their] account.
interpretation: This verse describes a group of believers characterized by three key virtues: maintaining connections, fearing God, and being concerned about their judgment. The phrase "join that which Allah has commanded to be joined" primarily refers to maintaining kinship ties (silat ar-rahim), which is highly emphasized in Islam. However, it also encompasses a broader sense of upholding all divinely ordained bonds, including those of faith, community, and human relationships. This act of connection is intertwined with a deep awareness of God's presence and a reverence for Him ("fear their Lord"). This fear isn't one of terror but rather of accountability and a desire to please Him. The verse concludes by mentioning their fear of the "evil of [their] account," highlighting their consciousness of the Day of Judgment and the implications of their actions. They are not complacent or presumptuous but are mindful that their deeds will be scrutinized. This fear motivates them to live righteously and strive to fulfill their obligations towards God and His creation. Essentially, this verse portrays individuals who are not only connected to their families and communities but are also deeply rooted in their relationship with God, seeking His pleasure and fearing His judgment.
orig: والذين يصلون ما أمر الله به أن يوصل ويخشون ربهم ويخافون سوء الحساب

translation: And those who are patient, seeking the countenance of their Lord, and establish prayer, and spend from what We have provided for them, secretly and openly, and repel evil with good - those will have the good consequence of [this] home.
interpretation:
This verse describes the qualities of those who will be successful in the Hereafter. It highlights five key characteristics that lead to a good end in 'the abode' (referring to the Hereafter or Jannah). 

First, it emphasizes 'patience' (sabru) done 'seeking the countenance of their Lord.' This isn't passive suffering; it's about actively enduring trials and tribulations with the intention of pleasing God. It involves perseverance in religious duties, restraint from sin, and steadfastness in the face of difficulties. This patience is rooted in sincere devotion and striving to get close to Allah.

Second, they 'establish prayer' (aqamoo as-salata). This goes beyond merely performing the physical act of prayer; it implies establishing it with its due conditions, sincerity, and mindfulness. It emphasizes the importance of prayer as a direct connection with God, a source of strength, guidance, and purification of the soul. 

Third, they 'spend from what We have provided them, secretly and openly.' This demonstrates generosity and detachment from worldly possessions. They give in charity, both discreetly and publicly, recognizing that all wealth comes from God. This act of giving is not just about financial contribution, but also giving of one's time, knowledge, and other resources for the sake of God and others.

Fourth, they 'repel evil with good' (yadra'oona bil hasanati as-sayyi'ah). This is a crucial ethical principle. It means responding to negativity with positivity, to injustice with fairness, and to bad behavior with good manners. This emphasizes the active pursuit of good and the conscious choice to overcome wrong with virtuous actions. It requires self-control, forgiveness, and a commitment to kindness even when provoked. It is important to note that this does not negate the right to defend oneself against injustice, but rather emphasizes a preference for resolving conflict through positive action where possible.

The verse concludes by stating that 'those will have the good consequence of [this] home.' This refers to the blissful and eternal life in Paradise (Jannah). It is a promise to those who embody these virtues that they will attain a positive outcome in the afterlife, a dwelling filled with peace, joy, and the pleasure of God. Therefore, the verse not only identifies the virtuous qualities but also ties these qualities to a specific, desirable consequence, acting as both a description and an encouragement.
orig: والذين صبروا ابتغاء وجه ربهم وأقاموا الصلاة وأنفقوا مما رزقناهم سرا وعلانية ويدرءون بالحسنة السيئة أولئك لهم عقبى الدار

translation: Gardens of perpetual residence; they will enter them, as well as those who were righteous from among their fathers, their spouses, and their descendants. And the angels will enter upon them from every gate,
interpretation:
This verse describes a beautiful scene in Paradise (Jannat 'Adn), a place of eternal bliss. It highlights several key aspects:

1. **Gardens of Perpetual Residence (Jannat 'Adn):** This emphasizes the lasting nature of Paradise, not a temporary dwelling but an eternal home. 'Adn' signifies a place of permanence and stability.

2. **Who will enter:** The verse states that those who were righteous will enter, a clear message about the importance of piety and good deeds in this life to attain Paradise. But it doesn't end there. 

3. **Family Reunion in Paradise:**  It mentions those who are righteous from amongst their 'fathers', 'spouses', and 'descendants' will also enter. This suggests a reunion of believing families in Paradise, a great comfort and joy for Muslims. It emphasizes that faith and righteousness can extend across generations and relationships, binding families together in this life and the Hereafter.  It also implies that  the righteous will be accompanied by those family members who also fulfilled the conditions for entering paradise, but may have entered due to the influence and prayers of the righteous family member.

4. **Angels Entering from Every Gate:**  The image of angels entering upon the inhabitants of Paradise from every gate signifies honor, respect, and blessings. It conveys a sense of welcome, security, and serenity. It also suggests the abundance and vastness of Paradise with multiple entry points. The angels' presence reinforces the notion of this place being blessed and honored by God.

In summary, this verse provides a glimpse of the rewards awaiting the righteous, a place of eternal residence, familial reunion, and divine honor. It underscores the significance of faith, good conduct, and the importance of maintaining and nurturing faith in our family units and their generations. This verse serves as both a source of hope and a reminder of the ultimate purpose of our actions in this world.
orig: جنات عدن يدخلونها ومن صلح من آبائهم وأزواجهم وذرياتهم والملائكة يدخلون عليهم من كل باب

translation: Peace be upon you for what you patiently endured. And excellent is the final home.
interpretation: This verse, often found in descriptions of Paradise, is a greeting of welcome and commendation from the angels to the inhabitants of Jannah (Paradise). The phrase 'Peace be upon you' (Salamun 'alaykum) is a standard Islamic greeting, here used in a context of divine approval and reward. The core of the verse lies in the connection between patience ('bima sabartum') and ultimate reward ('ni'ma 'uqba ad-dar'). It emphasizes that the inhabitants of Paradise earned their place through enduring trials and tribulations with patience during their earthly lives. This patience isn't passive resignation, but rather steadfast perseverance in faith, obedience to God, and avoidance of sin, despite life's hardships. 'Ni'ma 'uqba ad-dar' (And excellent is the final home) signifies the incredible bliss and eternal happiness that awaits those who are patient. It highlights the profound contrast between the temporary struggles of this life and the permanent, unsurpassed felicity of Paradise. Thus, the verse serves as a profound encouragement for believers to remain patient during their worldly trials, assuring them that such endurance, coupled with faith, will culminate in the most magnificent reward – the final home in Paradise, where they will be greeted with divine peace and welcome.
orig: سلام عليكم بما صبرتم فنعم عقبى الدار

translation: And those who break the covenant of Allah after its confirmation and sever that which Allah has ordered to be joined and cause corruption on earth - for them is the curse, and they will have the worst home.
interpretation: This verse condemns those who violate their agreements with God and humanity, specifically highlighting three intertwined transgressions: breaking the covenant with Allah (referring to the natural disposition to acknowledge and submit to God and the specific commitments made to Him), severing ties that God commanded to be maintained (including family bonds, community connections, and relationships based on shared faith or values), and spreading corruption in the land (through oppression, injustice, and acts that disrupt the social and moral order). The verse emphasizes the severe consequences of such actions. "The curse" implies divine rejection and deprivation of God's blessings, while "the worst home" refers to a miserable and eternal abode in the afterlife. This serves as a stern warning against hypocrisy, betrayal, and actions that undermine the well-being of society and the relationship with God. The verse underscores the interconnectedness of faith, social responsibility, and individual conduct, highlighting that true devotion to God includes upholding both spiritual and ethical obligations.
orig: والذين ينقضون عهد الله من بعد ميثاقه ويقطعون ما أمر الله به أن يوصل ويفسدون في الأرض أولئك لهم اللعنة ولهم سوء الدار

translation: Allah extends provision for whom He wills and restricts [it]. And they rejoice in the worldly life, while the worldly life compared to the Hereafter is but a fleeting enjoyment.
interpretation: This verse highlights two key aspects of God's power and human perception. Firstly, it emphasizes that Allah is the sole controller of sustenance (rizq). He has absolute authority to expand or limit the means of livelihood for whomever He chooses. This is not necessarily tied to merit or piety but is a demonstration of His divine will and wisdom. Secondly, the verse addresses the human tendency to become overly engrossed and delighted in the temporary comforts and pleasures of this world, a state that often leads to neglecting the eternal life of the Hereafter. The Qur'an contrasts the fleeting and ultimately insignificant nature of worldly life (muta'a) with the permanent reality of the Hereafter. This serves as a reminder for believers to maintain perspective, avoiding excessive attachment to transient gains and instead focusing on actions that will benefit them in the Hereafter.
orig: الله يبسط الرزق لمن يشاء ويقدر وفرحوا بالحياة الدنيا وما الحياة الدنيا في الآخرة إلا متاع

translation: And those who disbelieve say, "Why has a sign not been sent down to him from his Lord?" Say, "Indeed, Allah sends astray whom He wills and guides to Himself whoever turns back [to Him]."
interpretation: This verse addresses the common demand of disbelievers for a tangible miracle or sign ('ayah') from God through the Prophet Muhammad as proof of his prophethood. They question why a miraculous sign hasn't been revealed. The response, directed to the Prophet, emphasizes God's absolute sovereignty over guidance and misguidance. It clarifies that the ability to recognize and accept the truth is not dependent on witnessing supernatural events. Rather, God leads astray those who willfully reject the truth and refuse to submit, while guiding to Himself those who sincerely turn back to Him in repentance (Arabic 'anaab'). The verse highlights the importance of inner disposition and sincere seeking of truth, rather than simply demanding outward signs. It underscores the principle of divine will, but also that human choice and inclination play a role in being guided or misguided; God's guidance is reserved for those who actively choose to turn towards Him.
orig: ويقول الذين كفروا لولا أنزل عليه آية من ربه قل إن الله يضل من يشاء ويهدي إليه من أناب

translation: Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound connection between faith, inner peace, and the remembrance of God (Allah). It speaks of two groups: the believers who actively cultivate their faith, and their inherent state of having tranquility in their hearts when they remember Allah. The verse then emphasizes a general principle: that true and lasting contentment of the heart is ultimately found through the remembrance of Allah. This remembrance isn't limited to just verbal utterances; it encompasses reflecting upon God's signs, worshipping Him sincerely, and aligning one's actions and intentions with His teachings. The phrase ' تطمئن القلوب ' (hearts are assured/find tranquility) implies a state of deep satisfaction, security, and calmness that is immune to the anxieties and uncertainties of the worldly life. This peace comes as a direct result of recognizing one's dependence on the Creator and the realization of His infinite power, mercy and wisdom. The verse is essentially an invitation to engage in the remembrance of Allah to gain a stable and peaceful heart.
orig: الذين آمنوا وتطمئن قلوبهم بذكر الله ألا بذكر الله تطمئن القلوب

translation: Those who believe and do righteous deeds - for them is blessedness and a good place of return.
interpretation: This verse highlights the inseparable link between faith (iman) and righteous actions (amal al-salih). It promises 'tuba' (blessedness), a state of joy, felicity, and spiritual well-being, and a 'husn ma'ab' (a good place of return), which refers to Paradise, to those who combine sincere belief in Allah with practical, good deeds in accordance with His guidance. The verse indicates that faith alone is insufficient; it must be manifested in outward actions that are beneficial and pleasing to God. The promise of both blessedness and a good return underscores the comprehensive reward for a life lived in submission to Allah's will, encompassing both present happiness and future eternal bliss.
orig: الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات طوبى لهم وحسن مآب

translation: Thus We have sent you (O Muhammad) to a community before which other communities have passed away, that you might recite to them what We have revealed to you, while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful. Say, "He is my Lord; there is no deity except Him. Upon Him I rely, and to Him is my return."
interpretation: This verse highlights several key aspects of the Prophet Muhammad's (peace be upon him) mission and the nature of God's message. Firstly, it emphasizes that the Prophet's mission is not unique; it is part of a continuous line of divine guidance sent to various communities throughout history. The phrase 'قد خلت من قبلها أمم' (before which other communities have passed away) underscores this historical context. Secondly, the purpose of the Prophet's mission is explicitly stated: 'لتتلو عليهم الذي أوحينا إليك' (that you might recite to them what We have revealed to you). This highlights the importance of the Quranic revelation as the core message that needs to be communicated to mankind. The verse acknowledges the reality of rejection by some: 'وهم يكفرون بالرحمن' (while they disbelieve in the Most Merciful). Despite this disbelief, the Prophet is instructed to reaffirm his own faith and commitment to God: 'قل هو ربي لا إله إلا هو عليه توكلت وإليه متاب' (Say, 'He is my Lord; there is no deity except Him. Upon Him I rely, and to Him is my return.'). This declaration emphasizes the core tenets of Islam – the Oneness of God, reliance on Him, and the ultimate return to Him. The verse thus serves both as a reaffirmation of the divine mission and as a personal declaration of faith in the face of opposition, offering a powerful model for believers.
orig: كذلك أرسلناك في أمة قد خلت من قبلها أمم لتتلو عليهم الذي أوحينا إليك وهم يكفرون بالرحمن قل هو ربي لا إله إلا هو عليه توكلت وإليه متاب

translation: And if there was a Qur'an by which the mountains could be moved, or the earth could be cleaved, or the dead could be made to speak, [it would be this Qur'an]. But to Allah belongs the command entirely. Have not those who believed despaired that if Allah willed, He could have guided all mankind? And those who disbelieve will continue to be struck by calamity because of what they have done, or it will descend close to their homes, until the promise of Allah comes to pass. Indeed, Allah does not break His promise.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the immense power and authority of the Quran, suggesting that it is of such magnitude that it could even perform seemingly impossible feats like moving mountains or making the dead speak. However, the verse immediately clarifies that all power and command ultimately belong to Allah. The purpose of this statement is not to belittle the Quran, but rather to emphasize Allah's absolute sovereignty and to underscore that the Quran's power is derived from Him, making it a testament to His omnipotence and wisdom. 

Furthermore, the verse addresses the believers' potential frustration and disappointment that, despite the clarity of the message, not everyone accepts Islam. The question "Have not those who believed despaired that if Allah willed, He could have guided all mankind?" implies that guidance is a matter of Allah's will and not dependent on the Quran's inherent power alone.
