This is not merely a declaration of God's mercy; it is an active affirmation of his complete trust in God's ultimate benevolence, even in the midst of intense suffering. By calling God 'أَرْحَمُ الرَّاحِمِينَ' (the Most Merciful of the merciful), Job implicitly acknowledges that God’s mercy is limitless, unbounded, and encompasses all creation. It is a superlative form indicating that God's mercy is far greater than any other form of mercy. The verse thus conveys several key themes: the importance of patience and reliance on God during times of hardship; the power of supplication to God as the sole source of help and relief; and the unwavering belief in God’s boundless mercy, even in the face of adversity. It also serves as a reminder that even prophets face severe trials, and that suffering can be a test of faith. The verse encourages believers to emulate Job's model of patience and devotion in their own lives. Job's story and this verse in particular serve as an inspiration to remain steadfast in faith and to seek God's help when afflicted with trials, placing trust in His boundless mercy.
orig: وأيوب إذ نادى ربه أني مسني الضر وأنت أرحم الراحمين

translation: So We responded to him, and We removed what affliction was upon him, and We gave him [back] his family and the like of them with them, as a mercy from Us and a reminder for the worshippers [of Allah].
interpretation: This verse recounts the story of Prophet Job (Ayyub) after his immense suffering and patience. 'So We responded to him' signifies Allah's acceptance of Job's supplication. 'We removed what affliction was upon him' highlights the lifting of the various trials and difficulties he faced, including illness and hardship. 'And We gave him [back] his family and the like of them with them' indicates a miraculous restoration not just of his original family but also an increase, possibly through children or a similar number of people. This return of family is described as 'a mercy from Us,' emphasizing Allah’s compassion and boundless grace towards His sincere servants. The verse concludes with 'and a reminder for the worshippers [of Allah],' indicating that Job's story serves as a powerful lesson in patience, unwavering faith, and the reward that awaits those who remain steadfast in their worship of Allah, particularly during times of adversity. The verse is not just a historical narrative but also a source of encouragement for believers facing trials, urging them to remain patient and supplicate to Allah with unwavering hope.
orig: فاستجبنا له فكشفنا ما به من ضر وآتيناه أهله ومثلهم معهم رحمة من عندنا وذكرى للعابدين

translation: And Ishmael, and Idris, and Dhul-Kifl, all were among the patient.
interpretation: This verse highlights three prophets: Ishmael (Isma'il), Idris (Enoch), and Dhul-Kifl (often understood to be Ezekiel or Joshua), emphasizing their shared quality of patience (sabr). 'Sabr' in Arabic encompasses not only endurance but also steadfastness, perseverance, and resilience in the face of adversity and divine trials. The verse serves to exemplify the admirable nature of these prophets, pointing to their unwavering commitment to God's will, even amidst hardship. The inclusion of these particular figures, each with their own unique historical and spiritual contexts, underscores the universality and importance of patience as a virtue for all believers. It suggests that true piety involves not just faith but also the capacity to withstand challenges with fortitude and unwavering devotion. The verse also subtly hints at the potential for divine reward associated with such perseverance. The phrase 'all were among the patient' indicates they were exemplary models of sabr, not merely individuals who possessed it.
orig: وإسماعيل وإدريس وذا الكفل كل من الصابرين

translation: And We admitted them into Our mercy. Indeed, they were of the righteous.
interpretation: This verse speaks of individuals who have earned Allah's mercy due to their righteousness. The phrase "We admitted them into Our mercy" (وأدخلناهم في رحمتنا) indicates a divine action, emphasizing that entering Allah's mercy is a privilege bestowed by Him. This mercy is not merely a passive attribute but an active force that encompasses and elevates those who are deemed worthy. The subsequent statement, "Indeed, they were of the righteous" (إنهم من الصالحين), explains the reason for this divine favor. The term "al-Salihin" (الصالحين) refers to those who are righteous in their beliefs, actions, and character, striving to fulfill their obligations towards God and their fellow beings. This highlights the direct correlation between righteousness and the attainment of divine mercy. The verse serves both as a description of the rewards for piety and as an encouragement for believers to strive for righteousness in order to be encompassed by God's mercy, implying that being righteous is a condition for receiving such grace. It is a powerful statement affirming that God's mercy is available to those who pursue a life of devotion and goodness.
orig: وأدخلناهم في رحمتنا إنهم من الصالحين

translation: And [mention] the man of the fish, when he went away in anger and thought that We would not decree [anything] upon him. Then he called out within the darknesses, "There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers."
interpretation:
This verse recounts the story of Prophet Jonah (Yunus, ذو النون - 'the one of the fish'), peace be upon him. It highlights a crucial moment in his prophetic journey and contains powerful lessons. The narrative unfolds as follows:

1. **"And [mention] the man of the fish, when he went away in anger..."**: This refers to Jonah's departure from his people in Nineveh, who had refused to heed his message of monotheism. His departure was fueled by anger and frustration, highlighting a very human struggle of a prophet.

2. **"...and thought that We would not decree [anything] upon him..."**: This is a critical point. Jonah, in his anger, assumed that Allah would not bring any hardship or consequences upon him for leaving his mission. The word 'نقْدِر' (naqdir) has a broad range of meanings, encompassing decree, power, and control. The verse suggests Jonah’s error was in thinking that Allah's plan wouldn't impact him personally after he left. This reveals a misunderstanding of Allah’s complete authority and omnipresence.  It wasn't that Jonah doubted Allah's power but rather misunderstood how Allah's decree would play out.

3. **"Then he called out within the darknesses..."**: This describes Jonah's supplication while trapped inside the belly of the whale, within the darkness of the sea and the night.  The plural 'darknesses' (الظلمات) emphasizes the overwhelming nature of his predicament and his feeling of being engulfed.

4. **"..."There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers."**: This is the core of Jonah's repentance. It is a profound expression of Tawhid (monotheism). He acknowledges Allah's absolute oneness and transcendence ('There is no deity except You; exalted are You'). He also admits his mistake and wrongdoing ('Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers'). This acknowledgement signifies the turning point of his trials and his sincere return to Allah. This is a very important element as it reveals his humility and his realization that his frustration and anger made him fall short of his obligations.

**Overall Interpretation:** The verse is not merely a historical anecdote but a spiritual lesson. It teaches that:

*   **Prophets are not infallible:** Even a prophet can experience human emotions such as anger and make mistakes in understanding God’s plan.
*   **Humility and repentance are crucial:** When faced with adversity, one must turn to God in sincere supplication, acknowledging their shortcomings and seeking His forgiveness.
*   **God's power is absolute:** He is in complete control of all affairs, and no one can escape His decree.
*   **Tawhid is the ultimate refuge:** Recognizing Allah as the sole deity is the cornerstone of faith and a source of strength in times of hardship.

This story serves as a reminder that even when we feel lost or overwhelmed, true solace and redemption can be found by humbly acknowledging our dependence on Allah and turning to Him with sincere repentance. It is not only a story about Jonah's rescue but also a profound lesson on faith, humility, and the importance of remaining steadfast in our connection with Allah.
orig: وذا النون إذ ذهب مغاضبا فظن أن لن نقدر عليه فنادى في الظلمات أن لا إله إلا أنت سبحانك إني كنت من الظالمين

translation: So We responded to him, and saved him from the distress. And thus do We save the believers.
interpretation: This verse, in its immediate context, refers to Prophet Jonah (Yunus) when he was in the belly of the whale. The phrase 'So We responded to him' indicates that God answered Jonah's prayer and plea for forgiveness while he was in distress. 'And saved him from the distress' explicitly describes God’s act of rescuing Jonah from his perilous situation.  The verse then transitions to a general principle with the statement 'And thus do We save the believers.' This signifies that God's mercy and deliverance are not exclusive to prophets but are also available to all believers who turn to Him in sincerity and faith during times of hardship. The verse acts as a powerful source of hope and reassurance to believers: just as God responded to Jonah and rescued him, God will also respond to and aid believers who turn to Him with sincere faith and devotion when they face difficulties. It highlights the importance of supplication (dua) and trust in God's power and mercy, emphasizing that God's promise of salvation extends to all who believe and seek His help. The verse also implies that the type of distress may vary, but the principle of divine deliverance remains consistent for believers. Ultimately, it encourages steadfast faith and resilience in the face of adversity, with the assurance of God’s assistance.
orig: فاستجبنا له ونجيناه من الغم وكذلك ننجي المؤمنين

translation: And [mention] Zechariah, when he called to his Lord, "My Lord, do not leave me alone [with no heir], while You are the best of inheritors."
interpretation: This verse recounts the supplication of Prophet Zechariah (Zakariya) to God. He is expressing his concern about not having an heir to carry on his legacy and the divine message after him. The phrase "do not leave me alone" highlights his human vulnerability and longing for offspring. However, he does not simply ask for a child; he acknowledges God's ultimate authority and wisdom by saying, "while You are the best of inheritors." This portion of his dua shows a profound recognition of God's sovereignty and the temporary nature of earthly possessions and lineage. Zechariah understands that ultimately, all things return to God, the true inheritor of everything. His plea is not born out of fear of being forgotten, but rather from his desire to ensure the continuation of God's message and the righteous path. The verse showcases a beautiful blend of human yearning and complete trust in God's plan, illustrating an ideal model of supplication (dua) in Islam. It also implies that offspring are not merely a matter of biological inheritance, but can also be viewed as a means of carrying on the legacy of good deeds and devotion to God. God's response to this prayer is mentioned later in the Qur'an, where he blesses Zechariah with a son, Prophet John (Yahya).
orig: وزكريا إذ نادى ربه رب لا تذرني فردا وأنت خير الوارثين

translation: So We responded to him, and We granted him John, and amended for him his wife. Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds and supplicate Us in hope and fear, and they were to Us humbly submissive.
interpretation:
This verse recounts the story of Prophet Zakariya (Zechariah) and his wife, highlighting their righteousness and God's response to their supplication. The verse's structure reveals a profound message about the relationship between piety and divine favor. 

*   **"So We responded to him..."** This phrase signifies that God answered Zakariya's prayer. The previous verses in the chapter describe Zakariya's yearning for a child, especially a righteous heir. This response demonstrates that God listens to and answers the prayers of His devoted servants.

*   **"...and We granted him John..."** This is the fulfillment of Zakariya's supplication, the birth of Prophet Yahya (John the Baptist). The name itself is given by God, signifying His direct involvement in this blessing. The gift of a son is not just a biological event; it's a divine bestowal.

*   **"...and amended for him his wife."** This speaks to the miraculous transformation of Zakariya's wife, who was previously barren. It underscores God's power to alter circumstances and overcome seemingly impossible barriers. This amendment goes beyond simply enabling conception, implying an overall improvement in her condition and capability.

*   **"Indeed, they used to hasten to good deeds..."** This is the reason why God answered their prayer and granted them these blessings. Their eagerness to perform good deeds demonstrates their active faith and striving towards righteousness. They didn't wait for opportunities but sought them out.

*   **"...and supplicate Us in hope and fear..."** Their supplication was characterized by both hope (raġban) for God's mercy and reward and fear (rahban) of His punishment and displeasure. This balanced approach reflects true submission and trust in God, acknowledging His dual attributes of mercy and justice. Hope motivates them to seek God's favors, while fear prevents them from straying from His path. It shows a balanced approach in their relationship with their Lord.

*   **"...and they were to Us humbly submissive."** The final phrase encapsulates their complete submission to God (khashi'een). Khushoo' signifies a state of humility, reverence, and heartfelt devotion. This was not a superficial submission, but one that stemmed from a deep understanding of God's majesty and their own dependence on Him. They were not just performing outward acts of worship but were truly submissive in their hearts.


In essence, this verse highlights the rewards of a life dedicated to good deeds, sincere supplication, and humble submission to God. It's a powerful reminder that God answers the prayers of those who strive to please Him and that seemingly impossible situations can be transformed by His will. It also sets an example of the perfect relationship with God through the prophets Zakariya and his family.
orig: فاستجبنا له ووهبنا له يحيى وأصلحنا له زوجه إنهم كانوا يسارعون في الخيرات ويدعوننا رغبا ورهبا وكانوا لنا خاشعين

translation: And [mention] the one who guarded her chastity, so We blew into her [garment] through Our angel, and We made her and her son a sign for the worlds.
interpretation: This verse refers to Mary (Maryam), the mother of Jesus ('Isa). It highlights her piety and chastity ('ahsanat farjaha' - guarded her private part). The phrase 'fanfakna fiha min ruhina' (We blew into her through Our angel) describes the miraculous conception of Jesus, emphasizing that it was a divine act, not a biological one. The 'ruhina' (from Our spirit) is understood not as a part of God's essence but as a created spirit, a command and act of God. Finally, the verse states that both Mary and her son Jesus were made 'aya lil'alameen' (a sign for the worlds), indicating that their miraculous birth and, implicitly, Jesus' message and ministry, serve as a powerful sign and lesson for all of humanity. It underscores God's power, the importance of chastity and piety, and the divine origins of Jesus.
orig: والتي أحصنت فرجها فنفخنا فيها من روحنا وجعلناها وابنها آية للعالمين

translation: Indeed, this, your religion, is one religion, and I am your Lord, so worship Me.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the unity of God and the unity of the message delivered by all prophets. The phrase 'Indeed, this, your religion, is one religion' highlights that despite the various prophets and messengers sent throughout history, the core message they delivered was singular: the absolute oneness of God (Allah) and the necessity of worshipping Him alone. The verse then directly states 'and I am your Lord, so worship Me,' reinforcing this monotheistic principle and commanding direct worship to Allah as the sole deity. This verse serves as a reminder to believers to avoid divisiveness and to focus on the fundamental principle of Tawhid (the oneness of God). It also stresses the responsibility of humanity to recognize and submit to their Creator, the one and only God. The emphasis is on the common origin and purpose shared by all of humanity, as well as the singular source of truth and guidance.
orig: إن هذه أمتكم أمة واحدة وأنا ربكم فاعبدون

translation: And they have divided their affair among themselves, [while] all will return to Us.
interpretation: This verse highlights a state of disunity and discord among people regarding their beliefs and practices, particularly concerning religion. The phrase 'they have divided their affair among themselves' refers to their fragmentation into different sects, groups, and viewpoints, often contradicting each other and losing sight of a unified truth or purpose. This division is portrayed as a deviation from the guidance that they should have been following. However, the verse concludes with 'all will return to Us,' a crucial reminder of accountability. Despite their disunity and conflicting beliefs, everyone will ultimately be brought back to God for judgment. This emphasizes that their differences will not negate their responsibility before God and that their ultimate return is to Him alone. Thus, the verse serves as a warning against division and a reminder of the final reckoning.
orig: وتقطعوا أمرهم بينهم كل إلينا راجعون

translation: So whoever does righteous deeds while being a believer, there will be no rejection of his effort, and indeed, We are recording it for him.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the crucial link between faith and good deeds in Islam. It conveys a powerful message of divine justice and reward. Firstly, it highlights that merely performing good actions is insufficient; true acceptance and reward are contingent upon the doer being a 'mu'min' (believer), meaning one who has genuine faith in God and His message. The phrase 'fa la kufraan li sa'yih' (there will be no rejection of his effort) is significant, assuring believers that their righteous deeds, done with sincere faith, will not be wasted or ignored by God. Instead, they are acknowledged and cherished. The verse concludes with 'wa innaa lahu kaatiboon' (and indeed, We are recording it for him), reinforcing the idea that God meticulously records every deed. This underscores the responsibility and accountability of every individual in the eyes of God. It also provides comfort and encouragement to believers, assuring them that their acts of devotion and kindness, done with faith, will be fully recognized and rewarded by God. This verse serves as a cornerstone of Islamic thought, emphasizing both the importance of faith and action as essential components of a successful spiritual life and ultimate salvation.
orig: فمن يعمل من الصالحات وهو مؤمن فلا كفران لسعيه وإنا له كاتبون

translation: And it is forbidden for a city which We have destroyed that they should not return.
interpretation: This verse speaks of the divine decree concerning destroyed communities. The word 'haram' (forbidden) in this context implies a divine law or decree, making it impossible or highly improbable for the inhabitants of a destroyed city to return to their previous state or dwelling. The verse suggests finality in destruction; once a community has reached a point of divine annihilation, there is no possibility of them being restored or returning as they were before. It is not simply about a physical return to a location, but also implies an inability to revive the community’s essence, culture, or power. This can be understood as a warning, indicating the consequences of actions that lead to widespread destruction, reflecting the divine justice where severe consequences follow severe transgressions. Some interpretations also view it as referring to the inevitable return of all individuals to God on the Day of Judgement, as this is a return that everyone must make, despite earthly destruction. The 'return' could thus also hint at the accountability that destroyed communities (and, by extension, all people) will face before their Lord.
orig: وحرام على قرية أهلكناها أنهم لا يرجعون

translation: Until when Gog and Magog are let loose and they rush down from every height.
interpretation: This verse, found in Surah Al-Anbiya (21:96), describes a future event associated with the end times. The 'opening' or 'release' of Gog and Magog signifies a dramatic and chaotic period. 'Gog and Magog' (Ya'juj wa Ma'juj) are often understood to represent powerful, numerous, and destructive forces that will be unleashed upon the world. The phrase 'they rush down from every height' (min kulli hadabin yansiloon) vividly portrays their overwhelming and rapid descent, suggesting an unstoppable and widespread advance.  Traditionally, this is interpreted to mean a time of immense turmoil, conflict, and upheaval preceding the Day of Judgment. It's important to note that interpretations vary, with some regarding them as literal tribes and others as metaphorical representations of evil or disorder. The core meaning, however, consistently points to a period of intense global instability and the collapse of established order. The verse serves as a warning of the trials and tribulations that will come before the final reckoning.
orig: حتى إذا فتحت يأجوج ومأجوج وهم من كل حدب ينسلون

translation: And the true promise has drawn near; then suddenly the eyes of those who disbelieved will stare in horror, [saying], "Woe to us! We had been heedless of this; rather, we were wrongdoers."
interpretation: This verse describes the imminent arrival of the Day of Judgment, referred to as 'the true promise.' The phrase 'drawn near' signifies its close proximity, emphasizing the urgency and reality of the event. The verse then paints a vivid picture of the disbelievers' reaction when confronted with the undeniable truth. Their eyes will be 'staring in horror' (shaakhisatan absaaruhum), indicating shock and disbelief as the reality of the Day overwhelms them. This is followed by a lament and admission of their past mistakes. They exclaim, 'Woe to us! We had been heedless of this,' acknowledging their negligence and ignorance of the warnings given to them. They conclude with, 'rather, we were wrongdoers,' admitting their culpability and oppression by denying the truth. The verse serves as a stark warning and reminder of the consequences of disbelief and heedlessness towards divine guidance. It highlights the inescapable reality of the Day of Judgment and emphasizes the importance of acting righteously in this life. The use of the word 'wailuna' (woe to us) expresses profound regret and anguish. The 'promise' is the promise of resurrection and judgment, which will reveal the truth, leaving no room for denial from those who rejected it during their lifetime. The verse calls on reflection and sincere contemplation of what awaits those who reject the divine message.
orig: واقترب الوعد الحق فإذا هي شاخصة أبصار الذين كفروا يا ويلنا قد كنا في غفلة من هذا بل كنا ظالمين

translation: Indeed, you [disbelievers] and what you worship other than Allah are the fuel of Hell. You will be entering it.
interpretation: This verse is a stark warning directed towards those who associate partners with Allah and worship anything besides Him. The word 'إنكم' (Indeed you) refers to the disbelievers and polytheists. 'وما تعبدون من دون الله' (and what you worship other than Allah) encompasses all idols, false deities, and objects of worship that are attributed divine status apart from the One God, Allah. The term 'حصب جهنم' (fuel of Hell) vividly paints a picture of these beings – both the worshippers and their worshipped – becoming the very material that feeds the fires of Hell. This is a powerful metaphor highlighting the futility and ultimate damnation of associating partners with God. 'أنتم لها واردون' (You will be entering it) makes it clear that this is not merely a theoretical punishment; the disbelievers and the objects they worshipped will definitely enter Hell. The verse emphasizes the absolute oneness of Allah and the dire consequences of shirk (associating partners with Allah), underscoring the importance of pure monotheism in Islam. It is not meant to condemn the worshipers in the sense that they are pre-destined for hell, but to warn them and give them a chance to reconsider their worship and belief before death arrives.
orig: إنكم وما تعبدون من دون الله حصب جهنم أنتم لها واردون

translation: Had these [false deities] been gods, they would not have entered it [Hell], and all of them will abide therein eternally.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful refutation of polytheism and idol worship. It asserts that if the entities people worshipped besides Allah were truly gods, they would not be subjected to the punishment of Hell. The fact that they, along with their worshippers, will be cast into Hell and remain there forever proves their falsity and lack of divine power. The verse highlights the fundamental difference between the one true God (Allah) and all other purported deities. It underscores the absolute sovereignty and uniqueness of Allah, who is the only one worthy of worship. Therefore, the core message of this verse is that the fate of both the false gods and those who worship them is eternal damnation, clearly establishing their inadequacy as divine entities and affirming the monotheistic principle of Islam.
orig: لو كان هؤلاء آلهة ما وردوها وكل فيها خالدون

translation: For them therein will be a (deep) sighing and they therein will not hear.
interpretation: This verse describes a state of profound suffering and isolation experienced by the inhabitants of Hell. The phrase 'لهم فيها زفير' (for them therein will be a deep sighing) refers to the sounds of anguish and deep breaths, indicative of intense pain and distress. The term 'زفير' (zafeer) specifically denotes a drawn-out, heavy exhalation, implying not just any sigh, but one born of great agony. This suggests the sheer physical and emotional torment experienced in the afterlife.  The second part of the verse, 'وهم فيها لا يسمعون' (and they therein will not hear), highlights a sense of detachment and desolation. This 'not hearing' can be interpreted on multiple levels.  Firstly, they may not hear anything that could offer them solace or relief.  Secondly, it could mean they are so consumed by their own suffering that they are unable to perceive their surroundings, as if their pain has deafened them to all else.  Finally, some interpretations suggest that they may not hear the appeals or cries for mercy, either from themselves or from others.  Taken together, the verse paints a picture of intense suffering, isolation, and an utter lack of any hope or escape. It emphasizes the severity of the punishment awaiting those who disobey God and warns against the consequences of their actions.
orig: لهم فيها زفير وهم فيها لا يسمعون

translation: Indeed, those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us - they will be far removed from it [Hellfire].
interpretation: This verse speaks about a group of people who have been divinely favored and destined for Paradise. The phrase 'those for whom the best [reward] has preceded from Us' refers to those who have earned God's favor through their righteous actions and sincere faith, and whose ultimate reward in Paradise has already been decreed or 'written' by God. The expression 'they will be far removed from it [Hellfire]' emphasizes that these individuals are protected from the torments of Hellfire. They are so favored that they are kept far from it and are thus clearly destined for the pleasure and bliss of Paradise. This verse offers a profound message of hope and assurance to the believers, highlighting God's mercy and justice in rewarding those who strive to please Him. It also implies that a righteous path is the key to divine favor and salvation.
orig: إن الذين سبقت لهم منا الحسنى أولئك عنها مبعدون

translation: They will not hear its faintest sound, while they are, in that which their souls desire, abiding eternally.
interpretation: This verse describes the blissful state of the inhabitants of Paradise. It highlights two key aspects of their eternal reward. Firstly, "They will not hear its faintest sound" refers to the complete absence of any negative or undesirable experience. The 'it' here refers to the fire of Hell, meaning they are completely shielded from its torment and even its slightest indication. This underscores the absolute peace and security they experience. Secondly, "while they are, in that which their souls desire, abiding eternally" emphasizes the fulfillment of all their desires in Paradise. They will have everything they could possibly wish for, and this state of contentment and satisfaction will be unending. The word 'khaledoon' (abiding eternally) further reinforces that this joy and fulfillment are permanent and not transient. The verse paints a picture of perfect happiness, security, and eternal bliss, serving as a powerful incentive for believers to strive for this reward in the afterlife.
orig: لا يسمعون حسيسها وهم في ما اشتهت أنفسهم خالدون

translation: The Great Terror will not grieve them, and the angels will receive them, [saying], "This is your Day which you were promised."
interpretation: This verse describes the blissful state of the righteous on the Day of Judgment. The phrase "لا يحزنهم الفزع الأكبر" (The Great Terror will not grieve them) signifies that they will be spared the immense fear and panic that will engulf others when the final hour arrives. This terror, "الفزع الأكبر", refers to the cataclysmic events of the Day of Resurrection, which will be terrifying for those who have not prepared for it. Instead of experiencing fear, the righteous will be greeted by angels, "وتتلقاهم الملائكة" (and the angels will receive them). This reception is not just a casual welcome; it's a grand welcoming ceremony, a sign of honor and divine acceptance. The angels will proclaim, "هذا يومكم الذي كنتم توعدون" (This is your Day which you were promised). This declaration highlights the fulfillment of God's promises to the believers and their righteous deeds. It's a day of joy, reward, and vindication, contrasting sharply with the terror experienced by the wicked. The verse therefore paints a vivid picture of the starkly different fates awaiting the righteous and the unrighteous on the Day of Judgment, emphasizing the importance of faith and righteous actions in securing divine favor and eternal happiness.
orig: لا يحزنهم الفزع الأكبر وتتلقاهم الملائكة هذا يومكم الذي كنتم توعدون

translation: On the Day when We will roll up the heaven like the rolling up of a scroll of writings. Just as We began the first creation, We will repeat it. [That is] a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We will do it.
interpretation: This verse vividly describes the cataclysmic end of the world and the beginning of a new creation on the Day of Judgment. The image of 'rolling up the heaven like a scroll' signifies the complete annihilation of the existing cosmos, emphasizing the immense power and authority of God. The phrase 'Just as We began the first creation, We will repeat it' highlights God's ability to bring about existence from non-existence and emphasizes the cyclical nature of creation and recreation. This is a clear statement that the resurrection is not a new event that God is incapable of, rather, it is just as easy for God to recreate as it was to create the first time. Furthermore, the declaration 'a promise binding upon Us. Indeed, We will do it' serves as an affirmation of God's commitment to this process, assuring believers of the certainty of the Day of Judgment and reinforcing the power and infallibility of God's will. It underscores the inevitability of the event and the inescapable accountability of humanity.
orig: يوم نطوي السماء كطي السجل للكتب كما بدأنا أول خلق نعيده وعدا علينا إنا كنا فاعلين

translation: And We have already written in the book of Psalms, after the Reminder, that the earth shall be inherited by My righteous servants.
interpretation: This verse speaks of divine decree and promise. The phrase "We have already written" emphasizes the certainty of this event as something predetermined by God. The "book of Psalms" ( الزبور - Zabur) refers to the scripture revealed to Prophet David (peace be upon him), highlighting the continuity of this message across divine revelations. "After the Reminder" (من بعد الذكر - min ba'di al-dhikr) likely refers to the prior divine scriptures, potentially including the Torah, suggesting this promise was not novel but reiterated. The core message is that the earth will ultimately be inherited by "My righteous servants" (عبادي الصالحون - 'ibadi al-salihun). This signifies not a literal inheritance of land ownership in a materialistic sense, but rather a state of dominion, influence, and guidance stemming from righteousness, piety, and adherence to God's commands. It implies a future where those who are dedicated to good and to God's will will hold sway and be inheritors of a just and blessed world order. This is not a guaranteed temporal victory for a specific group of Muslims, but a wider concept of how goodness, guided by God, will ultimately prevail over evil. It emphasizes the reward and ultimate triumph of good character and righteous action, rather than a political or geographical conquest, though some may interpret it through a more literal lens. The verse provides hope and motivation for the believers that ultimately good will prevail as per God's plan.
orig: ولقد كتبنا في الزبور من بعد الذكر أن الأرض يرثها عبادي الصالحون

translation: Indeed, in this is a message for a people who are devoted worshippers [of God].
interpretation: This verse, "إن في هذا لبلاغا لقوم عابدين" (Inna fee hatha la balaghan liqawmin 'abideen), is a powerful statement emphasizing that the message of the Quran (implied by 'this', hatha) contains sufficient guidance and a clear communication (balagh) for those who are sincerely devoted worshippers ('abideen). The term 'abideen' denotes not just those who perform rituals, but those who are deeply committed to the worship of God with sincerity and devotion. The verse implies that those who approach the Quran with genuine piety and a desire to understand will find within it all the necessary direction for their spiritual and worldly lives. It highlights the Quran's role as a complete and sufficient message, requiring no external additions or alterations for those who are rightly guided and truly seeking God. The emphasis is on the receptive heart and genuine devotion as a prerequisite for benefiting fully from the Quran's message.
orig: إن في هذا لبلاغا لقوم عابدين

translation: And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.
interpretation: This verse (21:107) from the Quran highlights the central role of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as a divine mercy for all of creation, not just for Muslims or even humanity, but 'to the worlds' (العالمين). The word 'rahmah' (رحمة), translated as mercy, encompasses a wide range of meanings, including compassion, kindness, benevolence, and divine grace. It signifies that the Prophet's mission, teachings, and very presence are a blessing and a source of good for all beings. This is understood to manifest in several ways: firstly, through the Quran which is regarded as guidance and healing, secondly, through his practical example of noble character which he showed throughout his life and called on the people to emulate; and thirdly, by liberating humanity from the darkness of ignorance and oppression towards the light of knowledge, justice, and faith. It implies that the Prophet's message is not limited by time or space, and its benefits extend to all of creation in the past, present and future. Therefore, the verse underscores the universality of the Prophet's mission and emphasizes the compassionate nature of Islam, moving away from any interpretation that may limit its scope of compassion to a singular group.
orig: وما أرسلناك إلا رحمة للعالمين

translation: Say, "It is only revealed to me that your god is one God. So will you then submit [to Him]?"
interpretation: This verse (Qur'an 21:108) is a powerful declaration of the core message of Islam: Tawhid, the absolute oneness of God (Allah). It instructs the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to declare that his revelation emphasizes the singular nature of the divine. The word 'yuha' (يُوحَىٰ) highlights that this understanding is not from human reasoning but is divinely revealed. The phrase 'innama ilahukum ilahun wahid' (إِنَّمَا إِلَٰهُكُمْ إِلَٰهٌ وَاحِدٌ) asserts definitively that the God of humanity is one and the same, rejecting any polytheistic beliefs. The concluding rhetorical question 'fahal antum muslimun' (فَهَلْ أَنتُم مُّسْلِمُونَ) serves as a call to action and a pointed inquiry, inviting the audience to acknowledge this truth and submit themselves to God's will, which is the very essence of the word 'Muslim'. This verse encapsulates the central tenet of Islamic faith and calls upon all humanity to embrace monotheism and willingly submit to the one true God.
orig: قل إنما يوحى إلي أنما إلهكم إله واحد فهل أنتم مسلمون

translation: But if they turn away, then say, "I have warned you on equal terms, and I know not whether what you are promised is near or far."
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and, by extension, all those who convey the message of Islam. It outlines a clear course of action when confronted with rejection. The phrase "فإن تولوا" (fa'in tawallaw) - "But if they turn away" - acknowledges the possibility that the message will not be received or accepted by all. In this case, the Prophet is instructed to declare "فقل آذنتكم على سواء" (faqul a'dhantukum 'ala sawa') - "then say, 'I have warned you on equal terms.'" This implies that the message has been clearly and unequivocally communicated, leaving no room for ambiguity or doubt about its content and implications. The phrase "على سواء" (ala sawa') highlights the justice and fairness in the way the warning is delivered; all are equally informed and accountable. Furthermore, the Prophet is to disclaim knowledge of when the promised consequences will occur, stating "وإن أدري أقريب أم بعيد ما توعدون" (wa in adri aqarib am ba'eed ma tu'adoon) - "and I know not whether what you are promised is near or far". This emphasizes the divine timing of events and the Prophet's role as a messenger, not as someone who can determine the exact moment of fulfillment. In essence, the verse combines a firm declaration of responsibility with humility before God. It conveys that the Prophet has fulfilled his duty to warn people, while also acknowledging that the ultimate fate and timing of events are in the hands of God. The message also implies that disbelief has consequences and that the ultimate reckoning is certain, even if its timing is not known to the messenger. This should provide a perspective on the importance of responding positively to divine guidance while there is still time.
orig: فإن تولوا فقل آذنتكم على سواء وإن أدري أقريب أم بعيد ما توعدون

translation: Indeed, He knows what is spoken aloud and what you conceal.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes God's absolute and comprehensive knowledge. 'He knows what is spoken aloud' (الجهر من القول) highlights that nothing escapes His awareness, even the most public and overt declarations. 'And what you conceal' (ما تكتمون) emphasizes His knowledge extends to the most hidden thoughts, intentions, and secrets within the human heart. This is a powerful reminder of God's omniscience, which is a fundamental aspect of His divine nature. The verse serves as both a source of comfort for the believer, knowing that God is fully aware of their struggles and needs, and a warning to be mindful of their inner state and not just outward actions, as God sees both. It implies a call for sincerity and piety, urging believers to cultivate a pure heart and avoid hypocrisy, since all actions and even intentions are known to the Almighty. This knowledge should inspire both fear of accountability and hope in His mercy and forgiveness.
orig: إنه يعلم الجهر من القول ويعلم ما تكتمون

translation: And I do not know, perhaps it is a trial for you and an enjoyment for a time.
interpretation: This verse is typically understood as a reflection on the uncertainty surrounding divine decrees and the potential for both trials and temporary benefits within the human experience. The phrase "And I do not know" emphasizes the limits of human knowledge and the exclusive nature of God's understanding of events and their ultimate purpose. The "it" in the verse refers to an event or a situation that is unclear in its immediate impact or long-term consequences. The verse suggests that what appears as a negative or undesirable situation ('fitna', often translated as 'trial' or 'temptation') could actually be a test from God, meant to refine and elevate the believer. This trial may be coupled with or followed by some 'muta'a ila hin', which is temporary enjoyment or benefit, not necessarily negating the difficult experience but acknowledging that even hardship can have temporal relief and even, perhaps surprisingly, lead to eventual blessings. The 'ila hin' ('for a time') implies that both the trial and the enjoyment associated with it are not eternal and are ultimately part of God's grand design, emphasizing the transient nature of worldly affairs. Thus, this verse encourages acceptance, patience, and reliance on God's wisdom, even in the face of uncertainty and hardship. It highlights that believers should not be disheartened by seemingly negative events, as those might be a path towards growth and ultimately, divine reward.
orig: وإن أدري لعله فتنة لكم ومتاع إلى حين

translation: He said, "My Lord, judge with truth." And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one whose help is sought against what you describe.
interpretation: This verse contains two distinct parts, each carrying significant meaning. The first part, "He said, 'My Lord, judge with truth,'" signifies a plea or invocation. The speaker, often understood to be a prophet or a righteous individual facing opposition or false accusations, is appealing to God for a just and righteous judgment. They are not seeking vengeance, but rather a judgment based on truth and justice, a rectification of the falsehoods being propagated against them. They are submitting their situation to the divine arbiter, recognizing God's ultimate authority and wisdom in discerning the truth. The second part, "And our Lord is the Most Merciful, the one whose help is sought against what you describe," is a statement of faith and reliance. 'Our Lord' refers to Allah, emphasizing the shared relationship between believers and their creator. The phrase 'Most Merciful' highlights God's compassion and forgiveness, suggesting that while seeking justice, the believer is also acknowledging God's mercy as a core attribute. The concluding part, 'the one whose help is sought against what you describe,' further emphasizes the speaker's reliance on Allah. This signifies that the speaker is acknowledging the accusations and lies directed at them ('what you describe') and is seeking Allah's help and protection against their effects. They recognize their own limitations and completely depend on God's assistance to overcome the challenges presented by the false narratives. In essence, this verse embodies a profound reliance on God for truth, justice, and support, particularly in the face of adversity and falsehood. It demonstrates an understanding of God's justice, mercy, and power as the ultimate recourse for the believer.
orig: قال رب احكم بالحق وربنا الرحمن المستعان على ما تصفون

translation: O mankind, fear your Lord. Indeed, the earthquake of the Hour is a terrible thing.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful call to humanity to be mindful of their relationship with God, specifically by developing 'Taqwa', often translated as 'fear' but more accurately understood as 'God-consciousness' or 'piety'. It highlights the impending reality of the Day of Judgment, referred to here as 'the Hour', and emphasizes the immense severity of the earthquake that will accompany it. This earthquake is not just a physical phenomenon but a cosmic event signifying the end of the world as we know it. The purpose of describing the magnitude of this event is to instill a sense of urgency and responsibility in people, prompting them to reconsider their actions and strive to live righteously before facing their Lord. The verse is not meant to inspire literal fear in the sense of panic, but rather a reverential awe and awareness of the consequences of one's deeds, ultimately encouraging individuals to seek God's mercy and guidance.
orig: يا أيها الناس اتقوا ربكم إن زلزلة الساعة شيء عظيم

translation: On the Day you see it, every nursing mother will be distracted from that which she was nursing, and every pregnant woman will lay down her burden, and you will see the people [appearing] intoxicated, and they are not intoxicated, but the punishment of Allah is severe.
interpretation:
This verse describes the terrifying events of the Day of Judgment. It paints a picture of utter chaos and distress, highlighting the sheer magnitude of the cataclysmic events that will unfold. 

The phrase 'every nursing mother will be distracted from that which she was nursing' illustrates the extreme panic and fear that will grip even the most maternal and nurturing individuals. The bond between a mother and child, typically considered one of the strongest, will be broken due to the overwhelming terror. Similarly, 'every pregnant woman will lay down her burden' signifies the immense distress that will force even pregnant women to abandon their natural concern for their unborn child. They will be overwhelmed by the horrors of the day and will simply collapse, unable to carry the weight of their pregnancies.

The verse continues with 'and you will see the people [appearing] intoxicated, and they are not intoxicated.' This imagery vividly conveys the state of confusion, bewilderment, and disorientation that people will experience. They will seem drunk or mentally unstable, not from alcohol or any substance, but from the sheer terror and trauma of the Day of Judgment. Their state is a result of the overwhelming and terrifying nature of the events occurring, demonstrating how the divine power can deeply affect the physical and psychological state of humanity.

The verse concludes with 'but the punishment of Allah is severe,' emphasizing that the apparent chaos and terror are not just random events but are the consequence of divine justice. This is a powerful reminder of the accountability that everyone will face on that Day and the severe nature of the consequences of neglecting God's commands. It underscores the gravity of the Day of Judgment and the importance of living a life in accordance with divine guidance. The verse serves as a powerful warning and a call to reflection, urging individuals to be mindful of their actions and to seek Allah's mercy and forgiveness before that inevitable Day arrives. The imagery, while distressing, is designed to inspire awe and fear of Allah, ultimately leading to a more righteous path.
orig: يوم ترونها تذهل كل مرضعة عما أرضعت وتضع كل ذات حمل حملها وترى الناس سكارى وما هم بسكارى ولكن عذاب الله شديد

translation: And among the people are those who dispute about Allah without knowledge and follow every rebellious devil.
interpretation: This verse highlights two significant deviations from the path of truth and guidance. Firstly, it speaks about people who engage in arguments and debates about Allah (His existence, attributes, or divine will) without any genuine knowledge or understanding. This indicates a reliance on speculation, baseless claims, or inherited misconceptions, rather than a grounded comprehension of Islamic teachings and evidence. Such disputation is condemned as it often leads to misguidance and the spread of misinformation. Secondly, the verse identifies another group who, instead of seeking knowledge and truth from reliable sources, follow 'every rebellious devil'. This refers to those who are swayed by the whispers and temptations of Satan, which can manifest in various forms of falsehood, immorality, and disbelief. The verse emphasizes that true faith and understanding necessitate seeking knowledge from authentic sources and resisting the influence of those who actively seek to mislead. Therefore, the verse serves as a warning against both ignorant debates and the blind following of misguided influences, urging people to rely on sound knowledge and sincere devotion to God.
orig: ومن الناس من يجادل في الله بغير علم ويتبع كل شيطان مريد

translation: It is decreed for him that whoever takes him as a patron, then he will mislead him and guide him to the punishment of the Blaze.
interpretation: This verse refers to Satan (Iblis) or a powerful misleading force. It states that it is divinely ordained that anyone who takes Satan as a protector, ally, or leader (i.e., follows his temptations and guidance) will inevitably be led astray from the righteous path. Furthermore, this verse emphasizes that following Satan’s guidance ultimately leads to the severe punishment of Hellfire (specifically described as 'the Blaze'). This underscores the consequences of disobedience to God and the dangers of aligning oneself with evil forces. The verse highlights that Satan’s promises of pleasure and ease are deceitful, and his influence will ultimately drag his followers to eternal suffering. The meaning also emphasizes the free choice that humans have, choosing between God’s path and the path of Satan. This verse is a warning and a reminder of the importance of seeking guidance from God alone.
orig: كتب عليه أنه من تولاه فأنه يضله ويهديه إلى عذاب السعير

translation: O mankind, if you are in doubt about the Resurrection, then consider that We created you from dust, then from a sperm-drop, then from a clinging clot, then from a lump of flesh, formed and unformed - that We may make [it] clear to you. And We settle in the wombs whom We will for a specified term, then We bring you out as a child, then [We develop you] that you may reach your maturity. And among you is he who is taken in [early] death, and among you is he who is returned to the most decrepit [old] age, so that he knows nothing after [having had] knowledge. And you see the earth barren, but when We send down upon it rain, it stirs and swells and puts forth every kind of beautiful growth.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful address to humanity, urging reflection on the reality of resurrection by pointing to the observable evidence of creation. The verse starts by addressing those who doubt the resurrection, a common objection raised against the message of prophets. It presents the process of human creation as a testimony to God's power and ability to bring life from non-existence, the same way He can bring life again in the Resurrection. The stages of creation, from dust to a sperm-drop, a clot, and a lump of flesh, both formed and unformed, underscore the meticulous and intentional nature of God's creation. The phrase "that We may make [it] clear to you" highlights that this process serves as a sign for mankind to understand God’s power and wisdom. The verse also reminds us that God determines the term of life within the womb and the time of birth, demonstrating His absolute control over life. The human lifecycle is then described, including childhood, maturity, death, and for some, old age where mental faculties diminish. This journey serves to illustrate human's inherent vulnerability and dependence on God. Finally, the verse draws an analogy between the resurrection and the revitalization of barren land by rain. Just as dry land springs back to life with rain, so too will humans be resurrected on the Day of Judgment, thus solidifying the central point of the verse: that if God can create life from nothing and then cause barren land to produce life, then surely resurrection is not only possible but also probable. Ultimately, this verse is a compelling argument for the resurrection, grounded in the observable natural world and the detailed process of human creation, reminding mankind of their complete reliance on the Divine Power and the inevitability of accountability.
orig: يا أيها الناس إن كنتم في ريب من البعث فإنا خلقناكم من تراب ثم من نطفة ثم من علقة ثم من مضغة مخلقة وغير مخلقة لنبين لكم ونقر في الأرحام ما نشاء إلى أجل مسمى ثم نخرجكم طفلا ثم لتبلغوا أشدكم ومنكم من يتوفى ومنكم من يرد إلى أرذل العمر لكيلا يعلم من بعد علم شيئا وترى الأرض هامدة فإذا أنزلنا عليها الماء اهتزت وربت وأنبتت من كل زوج بهيج

translation: That is because Allah is the Truth, and that He gives life to the dead, and that He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse powerfully establishes the absolute truth and sovereignty of Allah. The phrase 'That is because Allah is the Truth' asserts that Allah's existence, power, and attributes are not based on conjecture or perception, but are the ultimate and unshakeable reality. It contrasts with all false deities and transient aspects of the world, emphasizing that Allah alone is the source of all truth and reality. The subsequent statement, 'and that He gives life to the dead,' highlights Allah's power over life and death, demonstrating His capacity to resurrect individuals on the Day of Judgment. This act is not merely a physical revival but also a testament to His limitless creative capability. Finally, 'and that He is over all things competent' underscores Allah's all-encompassing power and ability. It confirms that there is nothing beyond His control or comprehension; He is capable of executing His will in every aspect of existence. Taken together, these three assertions provide a solid foundation for belief in Allah by emphasizing His truth, His life-giving power, and His absolute control over all creation. This verse serves as a profound reminder of Allah's supreme position and calls for humanity to recognize and submit to His ultimate authority.
orig: ذلك بأن الله هو الحق وأنه يحيي الموتى وأنه على كل شيء قدير

translation: And that the Hour is coming, there is no doubt about it, and that Allah will resurrect those in the graves.
interpretation: This verse is a powerful affirmation of core Islamic beliefs. It asserts two fundamental tenets: the inevitability of the Day of Judgment (the Hour) and the reality of resurrection. The phrase 'لا ريب فيها' (la rayba fiha), meaning 'there is no doubt about it,' emphasizes the absolute certainty of the Hour's arrival. It's not presented as a possibility but as a guaranteed future event. This is designed to instill a sense of urgency and accountability in believers. The second part, 'وأن الله يبعث من في القبور' (wa anna Allaha yab'athu man fil-qubur), which translates to 'and that Allah will resurrect those in the graves', further reinforces the concept of accountability. It highlights Allah's power to bring back to life those who have died, underscoring that death is not the end, but rather a transition to a final accounting before Allah. This belief in resurrection serves as a significant motivator for righteous behavior and a deterrent against wrongdoing. The verse aims to instill faith in Allah's promises and warnings, reminding people of the ultimate consequences of their actions in this life.
orig: وأن الساعة آتية لا ريب فيها وأن الله يبعث من في القبور

translation: And among the people are those who dispute about Allah without knowledge or guidance or an enlightening Scripture.
interpretation:
This verse highlights a critical issue: the presence of individuals who engage in arguments about Allah (God) without a proper foundation. It identifies three key deficiencies that characterize such disputants:

1. **Without knowledge (بغير علم):** They lack genuine understanding of Allah, His attributes, and His teachings. Their arguments are based on ignorance, conjecture, or hearsay, rather than sound reasoning and evidence.

2. **Without guidance (ولا هدى):** They are not following the path of divine guidance revealed through prophets and scriptures. They are not seeking to understand Allah through the channels He has established for His guidance.

3. **Without an enlightening Scripture (ولا كتاب منير):** They have no access to or disregard divinely revealed books, which provide clear and illuminating explanations about Allah and the purpose of life. These scriptures serve as a light, guiding believers to the truth.

The verse condemns those who argue for the sake of argument, motivated by pride, stubbornness, or a desire to mislead, rather than a sincere pursuit of truth. It serves as a warning against baseless discourse on matters of faith and encourages seeking knowledge, following divine guidance, and referring to revealed scriptures as sources of authentic understanding. The implication is that such arguments are not only futile, but also potentially harmful, leading both the disputer and those swayed by their arguments away from the truth.
orig: ومن الناس من يجادل في الله بغير علم ولا هدى ولا كتاب منير

translation: Turning away disdainfully to lead others astray from the path of God. For him is disgrace in this world, and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning Fire.
interpretation: This verse describes the actions and fate of a specific type of arrogant and obstinate individual. The phrase "Turning away disdainfully" (ثاني عطفه) vividly portrays someone who, full of pride, physically turns his body away, refusing to listen or heed guidance. This act symbolizes their rejection of truth and their condescending attitude toward those who follow the path of God. The key motivation behind this behavior is "to lead others astray from the path of God" (ليضل عن سبيل الله). This indicates a deliberate and malicious intention to divert people from righteousness, not simply personal deviation. The verse then outlines the consequences: "For him is disgrace in this world" (له في الدنيا خزي), suggesting that their actions will ultimately lead to public shame and humiliation even in their earthly life. Furthermore, on the Day of Resurrection, a far more severe punishment awaits them: "and We will make him taste on the Day of Resurrection the punishment of the burning Fire" (ونذيقه يوم القيامة عذاب الحريق). This imagery of burning fire emphasizes the severe torment they will endure for their intentional misguidance and rejection of divine truth. The verse highlights the interconnectedness of actions and consequences, emphasizing that those who arrogantly reject truth and actively mislead others will face both worldly disgrace and eternal punishment in the afterlife. It is a stern warning against pride, obstinacy, and deliberately hindering others from following God's path.
orig: ثاني عطفه ليضل عن سبيل الله له في الدنيا خزي ونذيقه يوم القيامة عذاب الحريق

translation: That is for what your hands have put forth, and that Allah is not ever unjust to [His] servants.
interpretation: This verse addresses the consequences of one's actions. The phrase 'That is for what your hands have put forth' signifies that the outcome, whether positive or negative, is a direct result of the deeds a person has committed in their life. It emphasizes personal responsibility and accountability for one's actions. The latter part, 'and that Allah is not ever unjust to [His] servants,' serves as a crucial qualifier. It assures that Allah's judgments are perfectly just and equitable. Any hardship or perceived injustice is not from divine unfairness, but rather a consequence of the individual's own choices. Allah does not wrong anyone, and the results they receive are a reflection of their deeds. This verse underscores the Islamic concept of divine justice, where individuals are responsible for their actions, and Allah's justice ensures that no one is dealt with unfairly. It also serves as a reminder to strive for righteousness, as good deeds will ultimately bring about positive outcomes, and to fear misdeeds which result in negative consequences. The message is not fatalistic, but empowering, encouraging individuals to take control of their destinies by making good choices, always aware that Allah is the all-just judge.
orig: ذلك بما قدمت يداك وأن الله ليس بظلام للعبيد

translation: And among the people is he who worships Allah on the fringe (or with doubt). If good befalls him, he is content with it; but if a trial afflicts him, he turns back on his face (to disbelief). He has lost [this] world and the Hereafter. That is the manifest loss.
interpretation: This verse describes a particular type of believer whose faith is shallow and conditional. The phrase 'على حرف' (ala harf) which I translated as 'on the fringe', literally means 'on an edge' or 'on the side.' This conveys the idea that their faith isn't deeply rooted in conviction or understanding. Instead, it's a surface-level adherence that wavers with their circumstances. They only maintain their devotion when life is going well. They are content and feel at peace with their belief when they experience worldly blessings like health, wealth, and success. However, if they face hardship, tribulation, or a test from God, their faith crumbles, and they revert to disbelief or stray from the path of righteousness. The phrase 'انقلب على وجهه' (inqalaba ala wajhih) which is translated as 'turns back on his face' depicts this sudden and dramatic reversal. Their faith is contingent on their personal benefit and not based on the love and fear of God. Ultimately, this unstable faith leads to significant loss in both worlds. 'خسر الدنيا والآخرة' (khasira al-dunya wal-akhira) means they lose the benefits of this worldly life that can be derived from righteous actions and they also lose the eternal rewards of the Hereafter. The closing statement 'ذلك هو الخسران المبين' (dhalika huwa al-khusranu al-mubin) emphasizes the clear and obvious nature of their loss, highlighting the grave consequences of superficial faith.
orig: ومن الناس من يعبد الله على حرف فإن أصابه خير اطمأن به وإن أصابته فتنة انقلب على وجهه خسر الدنيا والآخرة ذلك هو الخسران المبين

translation: He invokes besides Allah that which can neither harm him nor benefit him. That is the extreme straying.
interpretation: This verse speaks about the act of worshipping or calling upon entities other than Allah (God). It highlights the futility and irrationality of such actions. The verse points out that these false deities or objects of worship are powerless, being unable to cause harm or bring benefit to the one who supplicates them. The phrase 'extreme straying' (ضلال البعيد) emphasizes the severity of this deviation from the correct path of monotheism (Tawhid). It underscores the distance one places between oneself and the true guidance of God by directing devotion and supplication towards powerless beings. Essentially, the verse serves as a powerful condemnation of idolatry and polytheism, urging believers to turn solely to Allah for their needs and acknowledging His absolute power and dominion.
orig: يدعو من دون الله ما لا يضره وما لا ينفعه ذلك هو الضلال البعيد

translation: He calls upon one whose harm is nearer than his benefit. How evil an ally and how evil a companion!
interpretation: This verse criticizes the practice of seeking help or devotion from beings or entities that are more likely to bring harm or disadvantage than any benefit. It condemns such reliance as misguided and foolish. The phrase 'how evil an ally' refers to the one being supplicated or relied upon, highlighting their ineffectiveness and potential to cause negative outcomes. The phrase 'how evil a companion' emphasizes the detrimental nature of such a relationship, suggesting that the one sought out is not only unhelpful but also a bad influence or associate. The verse serves as a warning against misplaced trust and devotion, particularly towards idols or false deities that ultimately lead to more harm than good. It encourages believers to seek guidance and support from sources that are truly beneficial and righteous.
orig: يدعو لمن ضره أقرب من نفعه لبئس المولى ولبئس العشير

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds to gardens beneath which rivers flow. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation: This verse highlights the ultimate reward for believers who couple their faith with righteous actions. It emphasizes God's unwavering promise of paradise (Jannat), a place of unimaginable beauty with rivers flowing beneath it, for those who live according to His guidance. The phrase 'Indeed, Allah does what He wills' underscores His absolute sovereignty and power, and reminds believers that their reward is entirely dependent on His grace and that His plans are always perfectly executed. This statement also subtly reminds the reader that Allah is not bound by any limitations and what He promises will indeed come to pass.  It serves as both an assurance for the believers and a reminder of God's limitless authority.
orig: إن الله يدخل الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار إن الله يفعل ما يريد

translation: Whoever thinks that Allah will not help him in this world and the Hereafter, let him stretch a rope up to the sky, then let him cut it. Then let him see whether his plan will remove that which enrages him.
interpretation: This verse presents a challenge to those who doubt Allah's support and victory for His believers. It uses a hyperbolic image to highlight the futility of trying to escape or circumvent Allah's will. The 'stretching a rope to the sky and cutting it' is a metaphor for any desperate attempt to thwart divine decree. The core message is: if someone believes Allah won't aid believers in this life or the next, let them try to sever the connection between the heavens and earth, symbolic of cutting themselves off from divine support and providence. The verse then asks them to observe if their actions actually alleviate their rage and frustration. It's a rhetorical question, implying that their efforts are ultimately pointless. Essentially, the verse assures the believers of Allah's support and warns the disbelievers of the ineffectiveness of their plots against the divine plan. It emphasizes that true power and victory lie with Allah, not in futile human schemes. The verse encourages faith and trust in Allah and discourages despair in the face of adversity.
orig: من كان يظن أن لن ينصره الله في الدنيا والآخرة فليمدد بسبب إلى السماء ثم ليقطع فلينظر هل يذهبن كيده ما يغيظ

translation: And thus We have sent it down as clear verses, and indeed, Allah guides whom He wills.
interpretation: This verse highlights two key aspects of divine guidance. First, it emphasizes the clarity of the Quran itself, described as 'clear verses' (آيات بينات). This suggests that the Quran's message is accessible and understandable, not obscure or convoluted. The use of 'We sent it down' (أنزلناه) implies a divine origin, further reinforcing the Quran's authority. Second, the verse acknowledges that while the Quran provides the path, ultimately 'Allah guides whom He wills' (يهدي من يريد). This doesn't suggest randomness, but rather a divine wisdom in choosing who is receptive to guidance. 'Wills' (يريد) here implies not merely a desire, but an active choice from God based on his comprehensive knowledge and justice. Therefore, the verse indicates that guidance involves both a clear message from God (the Quran) and an act of divine facilitation. It encourages engagement with the Quran, while also humbling believers by reminding them that ultimate guidance is from God and not merely a result of their own efforts.
orig: وكذلك أنزلناه آيات بينات وأن الله يهدي من يريد

translation: Indeed, those who have believed and those who were Jews and the Sabians and the Christians and the Magians and those who associated others with Allah - indeed, Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection. Indeed Allah is, over all things, Witness.
interpretation: This verse outlines a broad spectrum of religious groups and belief systems existing at the time of revelation, including Muslims, Jews, Sabians (a group with varied beliefs, often involving astral worship), Christians, Magians (Zoroastrians), and those who associated partners with God (polytheists). The verse doesn't pass judgment on the truth or falsehood of these different beliefs but instead defers that judgment to God on the Day of Resurrection. The phrase 'Indeed Allah will judge between them on the Day of Resurrection' emphasizes that ultimate truth and final reckoning belong to God alone. This verse is not a statement of religious relativism but rather an acknowledgement of the diversity of belief systems and a declaration that it is God's prerogative to decide on the validity of their beliefs and actions. The final statement, 'Indeed Allah is, over all things, Witness', underscores that God is fully aware of everyone's actions and intentions, making his judgment fair and just. The verse does not negate the Islamic emphasis on monotheism but acknowledges the reality of a diverse religious landscape and affirms God's final authority in judging the beliefs of all humanity.
orig: إن الذين آمنوا والذين هادوا والصابئين والنصارى والمجوس والذين أشركوا إن الله يفصل بينهم يوم القيامة إن الله على كل شيء شهيد

translation: Do you not see that to Allah prostrates whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth and the sun, the moon, the stars, the mountains, the trees, the moving creatures and many of the people? But many are those upon whom punishment is deserved. And he whom Allah humiliates - for him there is no bestower of honor. Indeed, Allah does what He wills.
interpretation:
This verse paints a powerful picture of the universal submission to Allah. It highlights the cosmic order, where all of creation, from the celestial bodies like the sun, moon, and stars, to the natural world including mountains, trees, and animals, instinctively and willingly prostrate to Allah, acknowledging His absolute sovereignty and power.  

The mention of "many of the people" acknowledges that not all of humanity is in alignment with this universal submission. Some actively choose to rebel, leading to the consequence of deserving punishment. The verse emphasizes a clear distinction between those who willingly surrender to Allah and those who reject Him.

The following statement, "And he whom Allah humiliates - for him there is no bestower of honor," underscores the absolute power of Allah in determining honor and disgrace.  No earthly power can elevate someone whom Allah has chosen to humiliate, nor can anyone diminish the honor granted by Allah. 

The verse concludes with "Indeed, Allah does what He wills," reaffirming His complete freedom and authority. He is not bound by any external factors; He acts according to His wisdom and purpose. This assertion emphasizes that the entire process of prostration, submission, honor, and humiliation is entirely within Allah's control and serves His divine plan. 

In essence, this verse is a profound reminder of Allah's omnipotence and the universality of His dominion, while also serving as a warning to humanity about the consequences of rejecting His guidance and choosing disobedience.
orig: ألم تر أن الله يسجد له من في السماوات ومن في الأرض والشمس والقمر والنجوم والجبال والشجر والدواب وكثير من الناس وكثير حق عليه العذاب ومن يهن الله فما له من مكرم إن الله يفعل ما يشاء

translation: These two are adversaries who dispute concerning their Lord. But those who disbelieve will have garments of fire cut out for them, and scalding water will be poured over their heads.
interpretation: This verse (22:19) uses the image of disputing adversaries to highlight the fundamental division between believers and disbelievers. 'These two adversaries' refers to the opposing groups, one believing in the oneness of God (Tawhid) and the other rejecting it. This struggle concerning 'their Lord' is the core of their disagreement, representing the conflict between faith and disbelief. The verse then pivots to describe the severe consequences for the disbelievers in the afterlife. They will be punished with 'garments of fire cut out for them', suggesting a punishment that is both confining and intensely painful. Furthermore, 'scalding water will be poured over their heads', emphasizing the all-encompassing nature of their torment. The imagery used here vividly conveys the horrific nature of Hellfire for those who persistently deny God. The verse functions as a powerful warning, illustrating the grave consequences of disbelief and highlighting the importance of recognizing and submitting to the will of God. It serves as a stark contrast to the rewards promised to believers, though not described in this specific verse, which often include gardens of paradise and eternal bliss.
orig: هذان خصمان اختصموا في ربهم فالذين كفروا قطعت لهم ثياب من نار يصب من فوق رءوسهم الحميم

translation: Wherewith that which is in their bellies and their skins will be melted.
interpretation: This verse, typically found in the context of describing the punishments of Hellfire, vividly depicts the torment of the damned. The word 'يُصْهَرُ' (yus'haru) translates to 'will be melted,' but carries a stronger connotation of being utterly consumed by intense heat, like metal being smelted in a furnace. The verse indicates that the fire's intensity will penetrate not only the external skin ('الْجُلُودُ' - al-julūd) but will also reach and melt what is within their bellies ('مَا فِي بُطُونِهِمْ' - mā fī buṭūnihim). This isn't just about physical pain; the imagery emphasizes the complete and utter destruction and anguish that the inhabitants of Hell will experience, signifying a punishment that spares no part of their being. The verse serves as a powerful reminder of the consequences of rejecting God's guidance and serves as a warning to those who might be tempted to deviate from the straight path. The melting is not just literal; it can also represent the breaking down of their internal self, the destruction of their inner being due to the consequences of their actions, making their pain and suffering complete and all-encompassing.  The vivid imagery is intended to evoke a deep sense of dread and encourage reflection on one's actions.
orig: يصهر به ما في بطونهم والجلود

translation: And for them are maces of iron.
interpretation: This verse, "وَلَهُم مَّقَامِعُ مِنْ حَدِيدٍ" (Wa lahum maqāmiʿu min ḥadīd), describes a harsh aspect of the punishment awaiting the inhabitants of Hell in Islamic eschatology. The phrase "مَقَامِعُ (maqāmiʿu)" refers to maces, clubs, or instruments of striking and beating. The specification that these maces are "مِنْ حَدِيدٍ (min ḥadīd)" - of iron - emphasizes their severity and the extreme pain they will inflict. This is not simply a description of a physical object, but a symbolic representation of the agonizing and merciless nature of the torment in Hell. It serves to illustrate the consequences of rejecting God's guidance and committing evil deeds in this life. The verse highlights the contrast between God's mercy and justice. While He is merciful to those who seek His forgiveness and follow His path, His justice demands a fitting recompense for those who reject Him. The 'maces of iron' are therefore not just instruments of pain, but symbols of the divine retribution awaiting those who earned it. It is also a reminder for believers of the importance of good actions and avoidance of sin to protect oneself from such dire consequences.
orig: ولهم مقامع من حديد

translation: Every time they desire to get out of it from anguish, they will be returned to it, and [it will be said], 'Taste the punishment of the burning fire!'
interpretation: This verse describes the torment of the inhabitants of Hell. It highlights their hopeless plight, where they are repeatedly afflicted with intense suffering.  The phrase 'كلما أرادوا أن يخرجوا منها من غم أعيدوا فيها'  (Every time they desire to get out of it from anguish, they will be returned to it) depicts a cycle of despair. They desperately seek escape from their pain, but are perpetually thrust back into the torment. This cyclical torment emphasizes the inescapable nature of their punishment.  The concluding phrase, 'وذوقوا عذاب الحريق' (and [it will be said], 'Taste the punishment of the burning fire!'), acts as a pronouncement of their punishment, emphasizing the intensity of the Hellfire. The word 'ذوقوا' (taste) here implies a direct, personal experience of the suffering, not merely an abstract concept. The verse, therefore, paints a vivid picture of the agonizing and relentless nature of Hellfire, where there is no respite or hope of escape.
orig: كلما أرادوا أن يخرجوا منها من غم أعيدوا فيها وذوقوا عذاب الحريق

translation: Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds to gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearl, and their garments therein will be of silk.
interpretation:
This verse describes the reward that Allah promises to those who believe and do good works. The key elements are:

*   **"Indeed, Allah will admit those who believe and do righteous deeds..."**: This establishes a clear link between faith (iman) and righteous actions (amal al-salih). It's not enough to simply believe; faith must be manifested in good deeds. This highlights the importance of actively living a life pleasing to Allah.

*   **"...to gardens beneath which rivers flow..."**: This describes Paradise (Jannah). The image of gardens with flowing rivers is a common depiction of the lushness, beauty, and abundance found in the afterlife. The rivers symbolize the sustenance and life-giving aspects of Paradise, contrasting with the arid conditions often faced in this world.

*   **"...wherein they will be adorned with bracelets of gold and pearl..."**: This describes the luxurious adornments of the people in Paradise. Bracelets of gold and pearl are symbols of beauty, honor, and high status. This suggests that the inhabitants of Paradise will be richly rewarded and respected.

*   **"...and their garments therein will be of silk."**: Silk, a fine and luxurious fabric, symbolizes the comfort and ease that the believers will experience in Paradise. It speaks to the physical and material blessings that await them. The overall tone of this verse is one of immense joy, reward, and honor. It motivates believers to strive for righteousness in this life, reminding them of the magnificent rewards Allah has promised for the Hereafter. The verse not only describes the physical characteristics of Paradise, but it also implicitly underscores the connection between belief, righteous actions, and divine reward.
orig: إن الله يدخل الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار يحلون فيها من أساور من ذهب ولؤلؤا ولباسهم فيها حرير

translation: And they were guided to good speech, and they were guided to the path of the Praiseworthy (Allah).
