The 'ihsan' (good doing) here isn't simply fulfilling a minimum requirement; it denotes a striving for perfection and a sincere devotion in performing good deeds. 

Therefore, this verse asserts that God's reward for those who perform good actions with sincerity and excellence is a firm promise. The verse doesn’t specify the exact nature of the reward, but it implies that the reward is commensurate with the quality and sincerity of the good actions, a principle of justice that is core to Islamic theology. The emphasis on 'We reward' and 'in this manner' reinforces that divine recompense is a fundamental aspect of God's design. It acts both as an encouragement for believers to strive for good and a reassurance that their righteous deeds will not go unnoticed. Furthermore, it serves as a reminder that ethical conduct and striving for excellence (ihsan) are essential components of a fulfilling life, not just in this world but also in the hereafter.
orig: إنا كذلك نجزي المحسنين

translation: Indeed, they were two of Our believing servants.
interpretation: This verse, "إنهما من عبادنا المؤمنين" (Innahuma min 'ibadina al-mu'mineen), speaks of two individuals (implied from the dual form 'inhuma') who are specifically described as being 'of Our believing servants.' The use of 'Our servants' ('ibadina) emphasizes their complete submission and devotion to God, while 'believing' (mu'mineen) highlights their sincere faith and conviction in the divine message. This verse typically appears in contexts where the individuals being referred to are exemplary figures known for their piety and dedication to God. It serves to underscore their high spiritual standing and serves as an example for others to emulate. The specific individuals referred to will vary depending on the particular context in the Qur'an where this phrase is found but, the core message remains the same, it is a divine certification and commendation of faith and service to God.
orig: إنهما من عبادنا المؤمنين

translation: And indeed, Elias was among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse affirms the prophethood of Elias (Elijah). It is a straightforward declaration that he was one of the messengers sent by God. The phrase 'lamin al-mursalin' (among the messengers) emphasizes that he was part of a long line of prophets and messengers tasked with conveying divine guidance. It highlights his status as a chosen individual selected to deliver God's message to his people. The verse, while concise, underscores the importance of recognizing and respecting the role of all prophets, including Elias, as divine envoys. It serves to reinforce the concept of prophetic continuity within the Islamic framework.
orig: وإن إلياس لمن المرسلين

translation: When he said to his people, "Will you not fear Allah?"
interpretation:
This verse, 'إذ قال لقومه ألا تتقون' (idh qaala li-qawmihi ala tattaqoon), is a common phrase used by various prophets in the Quran when addressing their respective communities. It literally translates to "When he said to his people, 'Will you not fear [Allah]?'". The key concept here is 'taqwa' (تقوى), often translated as 'fear', but it carries a deeper meaning of God-consciousness, piety, righteousness, and awareness of one's accountability before God. It’s not a servile fear but rather a profound sense of reverence and responsibility that motivates one to act in accordance with divine guidance.

The verse highlights the core message of prophets: to remind their people to be mindful of God and His commands. It is not merely a question about being afraid of divine punishment, but a call to self-reflection and moral rectitude. The use of 'ala' (ألا) before 'tattaqoon' (تتقون) adds emphasis, suggesting a sense of astonishment or urgency on the part of the prophet. He is essentially saying, "Shouldn't you, given your intellect and the signs around you, be conscious of your duty to God and act accordingly?" The verse implies that the people's actions or beliefs were contrary to God's will and therefore lacked this critical sense of 'taqwa'. It's a foundational call for ethical behavior rooted in faith, and underscores the importance of striving to please God in all aspects of life, not out of fear of punishment but from a love and recognition of His grace and power. This phrase often sets the stage for the prophets to further elaborate on their message and call their people to repentance.
orig: إذ قال لقومه ألا تتقون

translation: Do you invoke Ba'al and abandon the Best of Creators?
interpretation: This verse is a rebuke, specifically directed towards those who worshipped Ba'al, a deity associated with fertility and storms in ancient cultures. The core message is a powerful condemnation of idolatry and polytheism. The verse questions the rationale behind turning to a created being (Ba'al) for assistance and devotion while neglecting the One who is "ahsan al-khaliqeen" – the Best of Creators.  This phrasing emphasizes God's unique and superior creative power, implying that He is the only one truly worthy of worship and devotion. The question is rhetorical, intended to highlight the irrationality of choosing a false deity over the true God. It underscores the Islamic concept of Tawhid (Oneness of God) and the imperative to direct all worship solely to Him. The verse calls upon people to reflect on the source of creation and sustenance, urging them to abandon false gods and return to the worship of the one and only God, the most perfect creator. The use of the word "Ba'al" here serves as an example of any false deity or object of worship, not limited to the specific historical context. Thus, it provides a timeless lesson against associating partners with God in worship and relying on entities other than Him for help or guidance.
orig: أتدعون بعلا وتذرون أحسن الخالقين

translation: Allah is your Lord and the Lord of your first forefathers.
interpretation:
This verse emphasizes the absolute and encompassing Lordship of Allah. It asserts that He is not only the Lord of the present generation ('your Lord') but also the Lord of all previous generations ('the Lord of your first forefathers'). This highlights several key aspects of Islamic theology:

1. **Divine Sovereignty:** Allah's Lordship is universal and transcends time. It is not limited to a particular people or period, but extends to all of humanity, past, present, and future. This underscores His supreme authority and power.

2. **Continuity of Divine Guidance:** The phrase 'first forefathers' implies that the message of Tawhid (Oneness of God) has been consistent throughout history. Although the specific prophets and messengers have varied, the fundamental principle of worshipping Allah alone has been the core message of all divine revelations. It connects the present generation to the previous generations through the same divine Lord.

3. **Rejection of Ancestor Worship:** The verse implicitly rejects the practice of worshipping ancestors or idols. By stating that Allah is the Lord of both the present and previous generations, it redirects worship and submission solely towards Him, the ultimate Creator and Sustainer of all.

4. **Reminder of Mortality and Lineage:** The mention of 'first forefathers' serves as a reminder of human mortality and the continuity of life from past generations. It urges people to reflect on their purpose in life and their relationship with their Creator, rather than being solely focused on the material world or the practices of their ancestors if those practices deviate from divine guidance.

In essence, this verse is a powerful declaration of Allah's unwavering Lordship over all of humanity, emphasizing the importance of worshipping Him alone and following the timeless message of Tawhid, consistent through the generations.
orig: الله ربكم ورب آبائكم الأولين

translation: And they denied him, so they will surely be brought [to punishment].
interpretation: This verse speaks of a situation where a messenger of God (implied, such as a prophet) is rejected and disbelieved by his people. The phrase 'they denied him' (فَكَذَّبُوهُ) signifies a deliberate rejection of the truth presented to them. The consequence of this denial is explicitly stated: 'they will surely be brought [to punishment]' (فَإِنَّهُمْ لَمُحْضَرُونَ). The word 'muhdarun' (مُحْضَرُونَ) literally means 'those who are brought forth' or 'those who are made present.' In this context, it implies being brought to the presence of God for judgment and punishment for their disbelief. The use of 'la-' (لَ) before 'muhdarun' (مُحْضَرُونَ) intensifies the certainty of this event, emphasizing the inevitability of their accountability. Therefore, the verse serves as a warning to those who reject divine messengers and their messages, highlighting the grave consequences of disbelief and the certainty of divine retribution.
orig: فكذبوه فإنهم لمحضرون

translation: Except the servants of Allah, the chosen ones.
interpretation: This verse, "إلا عباد الله المخلصين" (illa 'ibaada Allahi al-mukhlasin), is often found within passages discussing the consequences of disbelief or misguidance. It serves as a crucial exception, highlighting a group who are exempt from negative outcomes. The literal translation points to 'except the servants of Allah, the purified/sincere ones' or 'the chosen ones'. The key word here is 'al-mukhlasin'. It implies a level of devotion and sincerity that goes beyond mere outward observance. These are individuals whose hearts are purified and dedicated solely to Allah, meaning that their faith is sincere, their actions are solely for His sake, and their worship is free from any form of hypocrisy or association with others. They are often described as being sincere in their belief, actions and intentions towards Allah and their commitment to following the divine guidance given in the Qur'an and sunnah of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). Thus, they are distinguished and spared from whatever punishment or trial is being discussed in the context of the passage where this verse appears. The verse emphasizes that genuine, pure devotion to Allah offers protection and elevates one's status in His eyes, demonstrating the significance of sincerity in worship and faith.
orig: إلا عباد الله المخلصين

translation: And We left for him [a good remembrance] among later generations.
interpretation: This verse, "وتركنا عليه في الآخرين" (Wa tarakna `alayhi fi al-akhirin), typically refers to a prophet, such as Noah or Abraham, after they have faced trials and fulfilled their mission. The verse signifies that God established a positive legacy for them among those who would come after them. It emphasizes the enduring impact of their righteousness, their dedication to God, and their perseverance in the face of adversity. The "good remembrance" is not just about their names being remembered, but also about the positive influence they continue to have through their examples, teachings, and the messages they conveyed. This verse is a testament to the idea that good deeds and commitment to God's will have a lasting effect that transcends time, and acts as encouragement for future generations to emulate the virtues of the prophets and righteous people before them. It also implies a continued blessing from God upon them and the continuation of their divine purpose even after their departure from this world. It also serves as a reminder to believers that their lives too will have an effect and their deeds will leave a mark; therefore, it emphasizes the importance of good actions.
orig: وتركنا عليه في الآخرين

translation: Peace be upon the family of Yasin.
interpretation:
This verse, "Salamun 'ala Ali Yasin" (سلام على إل ياسين), is found in Surah As-Saffat (37:130) of the Quran. The core meaning is a declaration of peace, safety, and blessings being bestowed upon "Ali Yasin," which literally translates to "the family of Yasin" or "the descendants of Yasin."  The interpretation of who is being referred to by "Yasin" is a matter of scholarly debate.  

Here are the main interpretations:

1. **Yasin as Prophet Muhammad (PBUH):**  The most widely accepted interpretation among many scholars is that 'Yasin' is another name for Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). This is supported by other verses which often address the prophet by titles and descriptions. This reading implies that the verse is a blessing upon the Prophet Muhammad's family and descendants and, by extension, upon the believers who follow his path.

2.  **Yasin as a specific family:** Some scholars believe 'Yasin' to refer to a particular family lineage within the progeny of the Prophet (PBUH) or a righteous family known for their devotion. This interpretation highlights the concept of piety being passed down through generations.

3.  **Yasin as a title:** Yet another perspective is that 'Yasin' could be a descriptive title, meaning something like 'the righteous ones', rather than a personal name. Thus, this interpretation expands the scope to encompass all virtuous and righteous people who follow the true path.

In essence, irrespective of the precise person or group referred to by “Ali Yasin”, the verse serves as a divine blessing and a declaration of peace. It underscores the importance of honoring the Prophet's legacy (according to the first interpretation) and the significance of righteousness. Regardless of the scholarly viewpoint, the message remains consistent: God’s peace and blessings are upon those associated with piety and divine guidance.
orig: سلام على إل ياسين

translation: Indeed, thus do We reward the doers of good.
interpretation: This verse, "إنا كذلك نجزي المحسنين" (Inna kadhalika najzi al-muhsineen), is a powerful statement about divine justice and the reward for excellence in conduct (ihsan). The word 'inna' (indeed, verily) emphasizes the certainty and truth of the statement. 'Kadhalika' (thus, like that) refers back to examples of divine reward mentioned in previous verses or the general concept of divine justice established throughout the Qur'an. 'Najzi' (We reward) indicates that the reward is a direct action by God. 'Al-muhsineen' (the doers of good) refers to those who strive for excellence in their actions, both in their worship and in their dealings with others. Ihsan is a comprehensive concept encompassing sincerity, devotion, and perfection in one’s work. It goes beyond merely fulfilling obligations and seeks to perform actions in the best possible manner. Therefore, this verse conveys that God rewards those who strive for ihsan. This reward is not limited to the afterlife but can also be manifested in this world through blessings, guidance, and inner peace. The verse serves as an encouragement for believers to strive for excellence in all their actions and to have hope in God’s just and generous reward.
orig: إنا كذلك نجزي المحسنين

translation: Indeed, he was one of Our believing servants.
interpretation:
This verse, "إنه من عبادنا المؤمنين" (Innahu min 'ibadina al-mu'mineen), is a common phrase found in the Quran, often used to describe prophets and righteous individuals. The literal translation conveys that the person being referred to was 'indeed' or 'verily' 'from' 'Our' ('us', meaning God) 'servants' 'the believing ones.' This indicates a very high status in the sight of God.

The key elements of interpretation are:

*   **'Innahu' (Indeed, he):** This emphasizes the truth and certainty of the statement, leaving no room for doubt regarding the described person’s character.

*   **'Min 'ibadina' (from Our servants):**  'Ibad' signifies servitude, emphasizing the person's humility, complete submission, and devotion to God. Being called a 'servant of God' is a great honor. This also suggests a close relationship and special care from God.

*   **'Al-mu'mineen' (the believing ones):** This highlights the importance of having strong faith in God. It’s not just any kind of service, but the service of a believer – one who holds true conviction and trust in God and acts upon their faith. This also means that the actions and deeds of this individual were in accordance with the teachings and commandments of God, showcasing not only belief but sincere and conscious practice of faith.

Therefore, the verse is not just a simple statement but rather a commendation of high praise, highlighting their devotion and dedication. The individual was a sincere, faithful servant of God who demonstrated strong belief through their actions and obedience. It's often used within stories of prophets or people with exemplary faith, as a means of emphasizing their righteousness and as a model for all believers to aspire towards.

In short, it’s a strong affirmation of their excellent standing before God, due to their sincere faith and devoted service.
orig: إنه من عبادنا المؤمنين

translation: And indeed, Lot was among the messengers.
interpretation: This verse, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:133), is a straightforward declaration affirming the prophethood of Lot (Lut). It firmly establishes him as one of the messengers sent by God, similar to many other prophets mentioned in the Quran. The verse is brief and emphatic, using the particle 'إنّ' (indeed) to underscore the certainty of his status. The statement serves to validate his divine mission and implicitly supports the narrative of his story, which includes his struggle against his people's immorality and his eventual salvation along with his believing family members (except his wife). This verse also contributes to the broader message of the Quran: affirming the prophethood of all the messengers sent by God and that they all shared the same core message of worshipping One God and behaving righteously.
orig: وإن لوطا لمن المرسلين

translation: When We saved him and his family, all of them.
interpretation: This verse refers to the time when Allah (God) saved a specific prophet and his family from a great calamity or punishment that befell his people. The context, which would be found in the surrounding verses and the relevant surah (chapter) of the Qur'an, is essential to understanding which prophet this is referring to. Generally, this type of verse highlights Allah's mercy and favor towards His messengers and their close family who followed the right path, even when the majority of their people chose disbelief and faced divine retribution. The emphasis on saving 'all of them' underscores the completeness of the salvation and the special protection granted to the righteous.
orig: إذ نجيناه وأهله أجمعين

translation: Except an old woman among those who remained behind.
interpretation: This verse, \"إلا عجوزا في الغابرين\" (illa 'ajoozan fi al-ghabireen), is typically found within narratives of divine destruction or punishment, specifically referencing the story of Lot and his people. The word \"عجوزا\" ('ajoozan) translates to 'an old woman,' and \"الغابرين\" (al-ghabireen) means 'those who remained behind' or 'those who stayed back.' In this context, the \"old woman\" is Lot's wife. The exception highlights her fate: unlike Lot and his righteous family who were instructed to leave, Lot's wife was not saved. She was included among those who remained behind, implying she was not a believer and shared the fate of the wicked people who were destroyed. This verse emphasizes the importance of inner faith and righteousness in escaping divine punishment, rather than merely being a relative of a righteous person. It serves as a reminder that true salvation lies in one's own actions and belief, not merely familial or social connections. The verse carries a stern warning about the consequences of aligning oneself with the wicked and disregarding divine guidance.
orig: إلا عجوزا في الغابرين

translation: Then We destroyed the others.
interpretation: This verse, "Then We destroyed the others," (ثم دمرنا الآخرين) is typically found in the context of narratives describing the fate of past peoples who rejected their prophets and disobeyed God's commands. The word 'dammarnā' (دمرنا) signifies a complete and utter destruction, implying a devastating end. 'Al-ākharīn' (الآخرين), meaning 'the others,' refers to the disbelievers or those who opposed the divine message within the specific story being narrated.  The verse highlights a divine pattern of justice where those who persistently reject guidance and engage in transgression are ultimately held accountable. It serves as a cautionary tale for subsequent generations, emphasizing the consequences of disobedience and the ultimate power and sovereignty of God. The specific identity of 'the others' varies depending on the surrounding verses; it could be the people of Noah, Ad, Thamud, or other communities that faced divine punishment. The core message, however, remains consistent: persistent disbelief and wrongdoing lead to destruction, while submission to God brings safety and salvation.
orig: ثم دمرنا الآخرين

translation: And indeed, you pass by them in the morning.
interpretation: This verse, typically found in Surah As-Saffat (37:137) and similar verses elsewhere, refers to the ruins and remnants of past civilizations that were destroyed due to their rejection of God's messengers and their disobedience. The 'you' in this context is generally understood to be the people of Makkah, particularly during the Prophet Muhammad's time, who would often travel past these desolate places during their journeys, particularly in the morning when they would leave their homes. The verse serves as a reminder of the fate that befalls those who transgress against God, highlighting the power of God and the transience of worldly power. It encourages reflection on the lessons of history and serves as a warning not to follow the path of those who were destroyed for their arrogance and disobedience. Furthermore, it implicitly urges belief and righteousness before one faces a similar fate. The specific locations implied vary among commentators, with some referencing the people of Aad, Thamud, or the cities destroyed by the Prophet Lut. The core message remains the same - that past destruction is a clear sign and lesson for those who are willing to learn from it.
orig: وإنكم لتمرون عليهم مصبحين

translation: And in the night, will you not then use your reason?
interpretation:
This verse, 'وبالليل أفلا تعقلون' (Wa bil layli afala ta'qiloon), is a powerful rhetorical question found in the Quran, often in the context of discussing signs from God within the natural world. The verse is segmented in two parts:

*   **'وبالليل' (Wa bil layli):** This translates to 'And in the night' or 'And by the night'. It points to the night as a specific time, setting it up as an object of contemplation.

*   **'أفلا تعقلون' (Afala ta'qiloon):** This is a rhetorical question meaning 'Will you not then use your reason?' or 'Do you not understand?'. The word 'ta'qiloon' comes from the root 'aql', which implies the act of intellectual understanding, reasoning, and using one's cognitive abilities. It's not simply 'seeing' but understanding with clarity and purpose.

Taken together, the verse highlights the night as a sign requiring reflection. The night, with its darkness, stillness, and the celestial bodies, provides ample opportunity for contemplation. It encourages humanity to move beyond merely observing the night to actively ponder its significance and the divine wisdom that it embodies. The rhetorical question challenges the reader to use their God-given intellect to recognize the signs and lessons woven into the very fabric of existence. The use of "reason" highlights the Islamic emphasis on understanding one's environment and purpose rather than simply blind acceptance.

In essence, the verse is not just about the night itself, but about urging us to utilize our intellect to discover the meaning and signs embedded within the natural order, ultimately pointing to the Creator and His wisdom.
orig: وبالليل أفلا تعقلون

translation: And indeed, Jonah was among the messengers.
interpretation:
This verse, "Wa 'inna Yunusa lamina al-mursaleen,"  is a concise affirmation of the prophethood of Jonah (Yunus).  It falls within a section of the Quran (typically in Surah As-Saffat, 37:139-148) that recounts the stories of various prophets, emphasizing their status as chosen messengers of God. The verse's significance lies in several key aspects:

1. **Confirmation of Prophethood:** The phrase "lamina al-mursaleen" (among the messengers) directly establishes Jonah as a prophet sent by God, thereby confirming his divine mission and the truthfulness of his message. This is crucial in Islamic theology, as it distinguishes prophets from ordinary individuals and highlights their unique role in guiding humanity.

2. **Part of a Chain of Prophecy:** By placing Jonah within the broader group of messengers, the verse subtly reinforces the continuity of divine revelation throughout history. It connects Jonah's prophetic experience to that of other prophets mentioned in the Quran, such as Noah, Abraham, Moses, and Jesus, all of whom shared the task of conveying God's message to their respective peoples.

3. **Emphasis on Divine Authority:** The use of "inna" (indeed, verily) in the Arabic text strengthens the assertion that Jonah was indeed a messenger of God. It is a linguistic device that underscores the certainty and unquestionable nature of the statement, reinforcing the divine authority behind Jonah's mission.

4. **Moral and Spiritual Lesson:** Though concise, the verse serves as a reminder of the importance of following divine guidance and the consequences of disobedience. Jonah's story, while not fully elaborated in this specific verse, is well-known within the Quran and provides valuable lessons regarding patience, faith, and submission to God's will.

5. **Part of the Overall Narrative:**  This verse is often seen as a preamble to the later verses detailing Jonah's trials, the whale story, and his eventual repentance. It establishes him first as a messenger with divine backing before moving on to the difficulties of his prophethood.

In conclusion, this seemingly simple statement  is a powerful declaration affirming Jonah's prophethood, linking him to the overall tradition of divine messengers, and highlighting a fundamental Islamic tenet about the role of prophets as intermediaries between God and humanity.
orig: وإن يونس لمن المرسلين

translation: When he fled to the laden ship.
interpretation: This verse, specifically 'Idh abaqa ila al-fulki al-mashhoon' (إذ أبق إلى الفلك المشحون), refers to a specific event in the story of the Prophet Yunus (Jonah), peace be upon him. 'Abaqa' (أبق) means 'he fled' or 'he ran away'. 'Al-fulk al-mashhoon' (الفلك المشحون) translates to 'the laden ship,' meaning a ship that was full or heavily loaded. Therefore, the verse describes the moment when Yunus, feeling overwhelmed or frustrated with his mission to his people, decided to leave his post and board a ship that was already full of passengers and cargo. This action is presented in the Qur'an not as a direct command from God, but as a moment where Yunus acted independently of divine guidance, which ultimately led to his trials including being swallowed by a whale. The verse highlights the human aspect of even the prophets, that they could face moments of vulnerability and make choices that may not align with God's will at that moment. It serves as a reminder of the importance of patience, perseverance, and trust in God's plan, even when faced with difficulties or a lack of immediate results. It also indirectly underscores the importance of fulfilling one's assigned duties and trusting in Allah’s judgment. The 'laden ship' setting emphasizes the extent of Yunus’ decision, highlighting the deliberate nature of his departure.
orig: إذ أبق إلى الفلك المشحون

translation: Then he drew lots and was among the losers.
interpretation: This verse is part of the story of Prophet Yunus (Jonah) peace be upon him, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:141). The context is that Yunus, feeling overwhelmed or perhaps acting impetuously, boarded a ship that later faced a severe storm. To lighten the load and appease the turbulent sea, the passengers decided to draw lots to determine who should be thrown overboard. The verse states that Yunus participated in this drawing of lots (فساهم) and, as a result, he was among those who were defeated (من المدحضين) or 'among the losers'. The 'losing' here means that the lot fell on him, indicating he was chosen to be cast into the sea. This verse highlights the divine decree that was working in this event, as Yunus himself was not intending to be cast into the sea but was led there by the divine will through the apparent random chance of the lot drawing. The verse doesn't imply he did anything wrong, but shows that Allah’s plan is working in ways beyond human comprehension. It's important to understand that Yunus's story is not about punishment, but rather a process of spiritual growth and submission to Allah. His later repentance and acceptance by God show Allah's mercy and wisdom in the events that unfolded.
orig: فساهم فكان من المدحضين

translation: Then the fish swallowed him, and he was blameworthy.
interpretation: This verse, from Surah As-Saffat (37:142), describes the consequence faced by Prophet Yunus (Jonah). After disobeying God's command to deliver his message to the people of Nineveh, he fled on a ship. Due to a severe storm, the crew decided to cast lots to determine who was responsible, and the lot fell upon Yunus. He was then thrown into the sea, where he was swallowed by a large fish (whale or whale-like creature). The phrase "وهو مليم" (wa huwa muleem) translates to "and he was blameworthy" or "while he was blameworthy" and highlights that Yunus's swallowing was not random but a divine consequence for his disobedience. It signifies that he had brought this upon himself and that his experience in the fish's belly was a form of divine correction and introspection. The verse serves as a powerful reminder of the importance of obedience to God's commands, and it preludes Yunus's repentance and eventual deliverance.
orig: فالتقمه الحوت وهو مليم

translation: Then had he not been of those who glorify Allah,
interpretation: This verse (فلولا أنه كان من المسبحين) is typically part of a larger narrative in the Quran, often relating to Prophet Jonah (Yunus). The phrase 'had he not been of those who glorify Allah' (min al-musabbihin) specifically refers to Jonah's consistent devotion and remembrance of God, which manifested through his acts of 'tasbih' - glorifying, praising, and declaring the perfection of God. The implied meaning is that if Jonah had not been among those who regularly and sincerely engaged in this form of worship, then he would not have been saved from the hardship he faced (being swallowed by the whale). The verse highlights the immense value of consistent remembrance and glorification of God, especially in times of distress, and suggests that such practice is a means of obtaining divine mercy and deliverance. It implies that Jonah's past good deeds and habit of glorifying God served as a kind of spiritual insurance policy, earning him Allah's favor and leading to his eventual release. The 'then' (fa) at the beginning further suggests that the following verses will explain the outcome of this consistent glorification, further stressing its significance.
orig: فلولا أنه كان من المسبحين

translation: He would have remained in its belly until the Day they are resurrected.
interpretation: This verse is part of a longer passage often referring to the story of Prophet Jonah (Yunus) and the whale (or large fish). It highlights the immense power of God and the consequences of disobedience or being in a state not completely in line with God's will.  Specifically, this verse states that had God not chosen to show mercy, or had Jonah not repented, he would have remained within the belly of the creature until the Day of Resurrection. The verse emphasizes God’s complete control over the creation and the consequences of divine will. It is not necessarily a literal description of the specific fish being a 'jail' until the resurrection, but rather an illustration of the magnitude of God’s ability. The core meaning emphasizes the temporary nature of hardship through God’s grace, and the dire consequences that would occur if God did not extend such mercy. It also implicitly teaches the value of sincere repentance and seeking God's forgiveness.
orig: للبث في بطنه إلى يوم يبعثون

translation: Then We cast him onto the open shore, and he was ill.
interpretation: This verse, part of the story of Prophet Yunus (Jonah) in the Qur'an (specifically, Surah As-Saffat, 37:145), describes his condition after being swallowed by the whale (or large fish) and then expelled. The Arabic word 'فنَبَذْنَاهُ' (fanabadhnahu) means 'then We cast him', 'We threw him out', or 'We ejected him', emphasizing that it was a divine act. 'بالعَرَاء' (bil-'araa') translates to 'onto the open shore', 'in the open land', or 'in a bare place', highlighting his vulnerability and exposure after his ordeal. The final part, 'وهو سقيم' (wa huwa saqeem), means 'and he was ill' or 'and he was sick'. This indicates the physical toll his time within the fish had taken on him. The verse signifies several key points: Firstly, it demonstrates divine intervention in both the engulfing and the expulsion of Yunus, emphasizing that these events are controlled by God. Secondly, it showcases the consequences of disobedience and the need for repentance, as Yunus' illness is linked to his initial flight from his assigned duty. Lastly, the scene of him being cast onto the open shore in a weakened state highlights his total dependence on God and paves the way for his subsequent recovery and the acceptance of his repentance.
orig: فنبذناه بالعراء وهو سقيم

translation: And We caused to grow over him a gourd vine.
interpretation: This verse refers to the story of Prophet Jonah (Yunus) when he was cast from the whale or large fish. After his ordeal, he was weak and vulnerable. Allah, in His mercy, caused a gourd vine to grow over him. This vine provided him with shade from the harsh sun and its fruits provided him with nourishment. The 'yaqteen' (يقطين), typically understood as gourd, pumpkin, or squash, is significant not just for its immediate benefit but also as a symbol of Allah's care and provision even in the most dire of circumstances. It emphasizes the divine compassion and the nurturing aspect of Allah's power. Furthermore, it's interpreted by some scholars as an example of how Allah can swiftly create what is needed when it is needed, highlighting His complete control over nature and events. The verse acts as a reminder that even after facing hardship, Allah can restore, heal, and provide comfort and sustenance.
orig: وأنبتنا عليه شجرة من يقطين

translation: And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more.
interpretation: This verse, specifically referring to the Prophet Jonah (Yunus), describes the size of the population he was sent to preach to. The phrasing "a hundred thousand or more" indicates a very large number, emphasizing the vastness of the task entrusted to him. The use of "or more" suggests that the exact number was perhaps unknown or not the primary point of emphasis; rather, it highlights the significant scope of his mission. Some commentators interpret 'or more' as signifying that the actual number could have been considerably higher, perhaps even doubling that figure. Additionally, this verse serves as a reminder of the power and reach of Allah's message, extending to large populations. It contrasts with Jonah's initial despair and demonstrates that despite initial negative reactions, large-scale conversions were possible after he repented and followed Allah’s commands. It also emphasizes the importance of perseverance in conveying Allah’s message.
orig: وأرسلناه إلى مائة ألف أو يزيدون

translation: So they believed, and We granted them enjoyment for a time.
interpretation: This verse, found in multiple locations in the Quran (e.g., Surah As-Saffat 37:148, Surah Al-Muminun 23:44), describes a situation where a group of people initially rejected a prophet's message but later chose to believe. The phrase 'فآمنوا' (fa'amanu) signifies their acceptance of faith. The subsequent phrase 'فمتعناهم إلى حين' (famatta'nahum ila heen) then highlights the consequence of their belief - that Allah granted them 'enjoyment' or 'provision' ('متعناهم' - matta'nahum) for a specified period ('إلى حين' - ila heen). This 'time' is often interpreted as their lifespan in this world or a particular period within their lives before their death or before a specific event mentioned in the context of the Surah. The verse underscores a recurring theme in the Qur'an: divine mercy and reward for those who choose to believe. However, the 'enjoyment' is temporary and limited to worldly life, emphasizing the importance of the Hereafter and the ultimate rewards awaiting the believers.
orig: فآمنوا فمتعناهم إلى حين

translation: Then ask them, "Does your Lord have daughters while they have sons?"
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed to those who ascribed daughters to God and claimed sons for themselves. It highlights the illogical and arrogant nature of their beliefs. They considered daughters inferior, yet they attributed them to God, while they chose to have sons for themselves, who they perceived as superior. The verse underscores the absurdity of their dualistic thinking and challenges their flawed understanding of divine attributes. It serves to demonstrate that God is far above any such gender distinctions and human perceptions of value.
orig: فاستفتهم ألربك البنات ولهم البنون

translation: Or did We create the angels as females while they were witnesses?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed to those who attributed female gender to angels, a belief prevalent in pre-Islamic Arabia. The verse challenges their claim by highlighting the absurdity of such an assertion. The question implies that if God had created angels as females, He would have done so publicly and with witnesses. Since there was no such witnessing, it follows that the claim is baseless and a product of their own conjecture. The verse underscores the divine origin of the creation and the lack of human knowledge of its specific details unless revealed. Furthermore, it refutes the pagan belief system that placed female deities or entities in association with the Divine. The implication is clear: such a claim is an act of assigning gender to those beyond the human understanding of gender, in the context of attributing partners to God which the Qur'an refutes.
orig: أم خلقنا الملائكة إناثا وهم شاهدون

translation: Verily, it is from their fabrication that they say:
interpretation: This verse highlights the act of deliberate falsehood and fabrication by those being referred to (often understood as those who reject the truth or oppose the Prophet). The phrase 'من إفكهم' (min ifkihim) translates to 'from their fabrication,' indicating that their statements are not based on truth or evidence, but rather are concocted lies and misrepresentations. The use of 'ليقولون' (liyaqulun) - 'they say' - in the present tense, emphasizes the ongoing nature of this deceptive behavior. The verse serves as a warning about the spread of falsehood and a condemnation of those who knowingly engage in such practices. The 'إفك' (ifk) is not simply a mistake or error; it is a deliberate fabrication designed to mislead or harm. This verse underscores the importance of truthfulness and the severe consequences of spreading falsehoods, especially when it relates to matters of faith and divine revelation.
orig: ألا إنهم من إفكهم ليقولون

translation: Allah has begotten a son, and indeed, they are liars.
interpretation: This verse is a direct refutation of the claim that Allah has a son. It emphatically rejects the concept of God having offspring, which was a belief held by some during the time of the Prophet Muhammad and still exists in various forms in some religions. The Quran stresses the absolute oneness (Tawhid) and transcendence of Allah, asserting that He is unique, eternal, and has no partners, family, or progeny. The phrase 'indeed they are liars' underscores the falsehood of the claim, portraying it as a deliberate misrepresentation of God's nature. This verse is a clear example of the Quran's emphasis on the pure monotheism that is the foundation of Islam.
orig: ولد الله وإنهم لكاذبون

translation: Has He chosen daughters over sons?
interpretation: This verse, found in Surah As-Saffat (37:153), is a rhetorical question posed to challenge the polytheistic beliefs of the Arabs of that time. They attributed daughters to God, viewing them as inferior while desiring sons for themselves. The verse highlights the absurdity of this belief, suggesting that if God were to choose offspring, He would not select the type that they themselves deemed less desirable. It's not a literal question implying God has taken daughters, but rather a powerful tool used to expose the hypocrisy and flawed logic of their idolatrous practices. The verse emphasizes God's absolute transcendence and refutes the idea that He could have any needs or desires similar to human beings, including a preference for one gender over another. Ultimately, the verse serves to underscore God's perfection and uniqueness, while simultaneously debunking the flawed conception of deity common among the polytheists.
orig: أصطفى البنات على البنين

translation: What is the matter with you? How do you judge?
interpretation:
This verse, "ما لكم كيف تحكمون" (Mā lakum kayfa taḥkumūn), is a rhetorical question often found in the Quran, designed to challenge the listener's logic, reasoning, and the validity of their judgements or beliefs.  

**Breakdown of the words:**
*   **ما لكم (Mā lakum):** Literally "What is to you?" or "What is the matter with you?" It expresses a sense of astonishment or disapproval at the listener's current state or position.
*   **كيف (Kayfa):** "How?"
*   **تحكمون (Taḥkumūn):** "You judge" (plural). 

**Interpretation:**

The verse is not simply asking how someone makes a judgment, but rather questioning the *basis* and *justification* of their decision. It implies that the judgment or belief being held is flawed, illogical, or contrary to what should be considered right or reasonable, given evidence, reason or God’s guidance. The phrase 'what is the matter with you' suggests a state of confusion, misguided thinking, or a deviation from truth or righteousness. The verse serves as a prompt for introspection and calls for an honest reassessment of the grounds on which judgments are made. It is often used in situations where people are being criticized for embracing falsehood, neglecting their responsibilities, or misinterpreting divine messages.

In the Quranic context, this verse often appears in relation to the rejection of prophets, denial of the truth, or making false judgments about God's signs. It urges believers and non-believers to think deeply and examine their convictions, to engage their intellect, and to base their beliefs on sound principles instead of prejudice, blind following or self-interest. The implied answer is that they are not judging correctly and should change their ways.

Therefore, the verse functions as a powerful call for self-reflection, critical thinking, and a move toward fair and just assessments based on truth and divine guidance, not personal whim or erroneous assumptions. It also carries a warning against hasty and unreasoned judgements.
orig: ما لكم كيف تحكمون

translation: Then will you not remember?
interpretation: This verse, "أفلا تذكرون" (Afala tadhakkarun), is a rhetorical question often used in the Quran to prompt reflection and contemplation. The core meaning is an appeal to the listener's intellect and memory, urging them to consider the signs of God's power, wisdom, and mercy that are present in the world around them and within themselves. It suggests a failure to use reason or recall past lessons or experiences, ultimately hindering their ability to perceive the truth. The phrase isn't just about remembering facts; it's about remembering the deeper implications and lessons embedded within those facts. The context in which it appears usually highlights specific signs or events – for instance, creation, natural phenomena, historical narratives, or moral principles. By asking, "Then will you not remember?", the Quran is inviting individuals to engage in a process of active reflection and to come to a conclusion about the truth that has been revealed to them. It's a call to awaken the dormant consciousness and move towards belief, understanding, and righteous action. The lack of remembering here implies not merely forgetting, but a willful neglect or disregard of the evidence and guidance presented to them. The verse carries a tone of reproach, subtly indicating the responsibility that comes with the capacity for reason and remembrance.
orig: أفلا تذكرون

translation: Or do you have a clear authority?
interpretation: This verse is a rhetorical question posed to those who reject the message of the Prophet Muhammad and the truth of Islam. It challenges them to produce any legitimate evidence or authority that justifies their opposition and their adherence to false beliefs or practices. The word 'سلطان' (sultan) refers to a clear, compelling proof or authority, not just political power. 'مبين' (mubeen) emphasizes the clarity and explicitness of this proof. The verse implies that they have no such evidence, and their rejection is based solely on unfounded claims, inherited traditions, or personal desires, not on sound reasoning or divine guidance. Therefore, it serves as a sharp rebuke and a call for honest self-reflection.
orig: أم لكم سلطان مبين

translation: Then bring your scripture, if you should be truthful.
interpretation: This verse is a challenge often directed towards those who deny or question the divine origin of the Qur'an or the message of the Prophet Muhammad. It's a call to produce a scripture of similar eloquence, wisdom, and guidance from their own sources, if they claim to possess the truth. The underlying message is that if their claims are genuine, they should be able to substantiate them with a divine text of their own, proving they also have a source of revelation or knowledge comparable to what is presented in the Quran. Failing to produce such a book indicates the truthfulness of the claim made by the Prophet Muhammad and the Quran itself and the falsity of the claims of those who deny it.
orig: فأتوا بكتابكم إن كنتم صادقين

translation: And they have claimed a kinship between Him and the jinn, while the jinn know well that they will be brought [to judgment].
interpretation: This verse addresses the polytheists of Mecca who falsely claimed a familial relationship or close kinship between God and the jinn. This claim was likely part of their polytheistic beliefs where they attributed divine or semi-divine status to the jinn and perhaps even suggested they had some control or influence over God’s affairs. The verse vehemently rejects this notion, asserting that the jinn themselves know they are subservient to God and will be brought forth for judgment. This implies the absurdity of claiming a divine link to entities that are not only created by God but also accountable to Him. The verse serves to refute polytheistic beliefs, reassert God's absolute uniqueness and supremacy, and emphasize the ultimate accountability of all beings before Him.
orig: وجعلوا بينه وبين الجنة نسبا ولقد علمت الجنة إنهم لمحضرون

translation: Glory be to Allah, far above what they describe.
interpretation:
This verse, "SubhanAllah 'amma yasifun," is a powerful declaration of God's transcendence and absolute perfection.  The phrase 'SubhanAllah' (Glory be to Allah) is an expression of glorification and affirmation of God's purity and freedom from any imperfection or deficiency.  The phrase 'amma yasifun' (far above what they describe) refers to the descriptions and attributions of God given by human beings, often based on limited human understanding or flawed analogies. It implies that no human description can ever truly capture the essence or magnificence of God.  

This verse serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it emphasizes the inadequacy of human language to fully comprehend God's majesty. Our limited minds and vocabulary cannot encapsulate the divine reality. Secondly, it cautions against anthropomorphism or attributing human-like qualities or limitations to God.  Such descriptions are invariably flawed and diminish God's absolute uniqueness. Lastly, it directs believers to contemplate the divine beyond the constraints of human comprehension, urging a humble and awe-inspired recognition of God's exaltedness. It's a call to recognize that God is far more magnificent and sublime than we can ever imagine or express in words. The verse is often used to express disapproval of misguided theological concepts that attempt to define or limit God's attributes.
orig: سبحان الله عما يصفون

translation: Except the devoted servants of Allah.
interpretation:
This verse fragment, "إلا عباد الله المخلصين" (illa 'ibad Allah al-mukhlaseen), is typically found within larger contexts describing divine grace, rewards, or exceptions.  The core idea revolves around a distinction between those who are generally subject to a particular outcome (e.g., punishment, straying from the path) and a select group who are exempt due to their sincerity and devotion to God. 

The key terms are: 

* **إلا (illa):**  Meaning 'except' or 'but,' indicating an exception.
* **عباد الله ('ibad Allah):** Literally 'servants of Allah,' denoting those who are in a relationship of worship and submission to God.
* **المخلصين (al-mukhlaseen):** Meaning 'the devoted' or 'the purified,' referring to those who have genuine sincerity in their faith and actions. This sincerity is characterized by a pure intention aimed solely at pleasing God, without any ulterior motives like seeking praise or recognition from others.

Therefore, the verse highlights that while a general condition or outcome may apply to many, a specific group – the truly devoted servants of God – are excluded. This exclusion is a consequence of their 'ikhlas,' their pure and sincere devotion. They are not merely performing religious rituals superficially, but their hearts and actions are completely directed toward God's pleasure. They are, therefore, safeguarded from that negative outcome or are given special grace and reward. The meaning implies the importance of sincerity in one's worship and relationship with God, emphasizing that genuine devotion is the key to divine favor and protection.  This also indicates the high status and favor granted to those who attain this level of sincerity (Ikhlas).
orig: إلا عباد الله المخلصين

translation: Indeed, you and what you worship
interpretation: This verse fragment, "Fa innakum wa ma ta'budoon," is often found within larger passages of the Quran, particularly those addressing the misguided worship of idols or other deities besides Allah.  The literal translation highlights a direct connection between the disbelievers and the objects of their worship. The meaning conveyed is not merely a descriptive statement, but rather a form of reprimand or a prelude to a more severe statement. It serves to emphasize the futility and falsehood of their worship.  It implies that the idols themselves have no power or divinity, and that their worship is therefore meaningless and ultimately harmful. The context surrounding the verse usually elaborates on the consequences of this misguidance, such as being fuel for hellfire, or that they are incapable of providing any aid or benefit to their worshippers. It is a stark assertion of the oneness of God (Tawhid) and a denunciation of polytheism or any act of associating partners with God in worship.
orig: فإنكم وما تعبدون

translation: You are not, with respect to it, tempters.
interpretation: This verse, "ما أنتم عليه بفاتنين" (Mā antum 'alayhi bi-fātineen), typically appears in contexts where the disbelievers are attempting to dissuade others from the truth, often in reference to the Prophet Muhammad's message or belief in the oneness of God. The key word here is "فاتنين" (fātineen), the plural form of "فاتن" (fātin), which means 'tempter,' 'seducer,' or 'one who causes fitna' (discord/trial/temptation).  The verse is denying the disbelievers' ability to effectively turn others away from the true path. It's important to understand that the denial is not about their intent, as they certainly *try* to tempt others. Rather, it's a denial of their *success* in that endeavor, due to the strength of the message of truth and the inherent guidance of God. The implication is that the truth is so self-evident and powerful that the disbelievers' attempts to mislead are ultimately futile. Their efforts are portrayed as ineffective and weak in the face of divine guidance and the innate human inclination towards truth. Therefore, the verse conveys both a message of reassurance to the believers and a statement of the ultimate ineffectiveness of disbelief's seductions.
orig: ما أنتم عليه بفاتنين

translation: Except he who is to enter the burning Fire.
interpretation: This verse, taken on its own, is a fragment and requires context from the surrounding verses to fully grasp its meaning. However, based on its wording, it describes an exception to a previously established group or condition. The phrase 'صال الجحيم' (ṣāli al-jaḥīm) directly translates to 'entering/roasting in the blazing fire,' and 'al-jaḥīm' is one of the names for Hellfire. Therefore, this verse is indicating an individual or group that is destined for Hellfire, contrasting them with those who might be spared or have a different fate. The broader context in which this verse appears often clarifies *who* this exception is referring to – typically, it describes those who reject the message of God, those who commit major sins, or those who are punished for their actions. Without specific context of the surah and the verse itself, we can only interpret it that as an explicit statement of divine judgment where specific individuals or group will face the punishment of hellfire. The verse serves as a potent reminder of the consequences of actions and choices in this life, according to Islamic theology, and highlights the difference in their final abode based on deeds.
orig: إلا من هو صال الجحيم

translation: And there is not one of us except that for him is a known station.
interpretation:
This verse, "وما منا إلا له مقام معلوم" (Wa ma minna illa lahu maqamun ma'loom), speaks to the structured and purposeful nature of existence, specifically within the realm of divine creation, often understood in the context of angels, but applicable more broadly.  The key phrase, "مقام معلوم" (maqamun ma'loom), signifies a 'known station' or 'assigned place'.  Here's a breakdown of the interpretation:

*   **"وما منا" (Wa ma minna) - "And there is not one of us":** This establishes the universality of the statement.  It emphasizes that what follows applies to every individual within the group being referred to, which is most often understood to be the angels in the Quranic context. However it also implies that everything in creation has been given its purpose and place. 

*   **"إلا له" (Illa lahu) - "except that for him":** This indicates that the subsequent phrase is a necessary attribute of each individual within the defined group. 

*  **"مقام معلوم" (Maqamun ma'loom) - "a known station":** This is the core of the verse. "Maqam" (مقام) refers to a place, position, or station, while "ma'loom" (معلوم) means known, defined, or established. The combination of these words implies:
    *   **Ordained Position:** Each individual, whether an angel or a created thing has been given a pre-determined role, responsibility, and function within the cosmic order. This is not arbitrary but part of the divine plan. This preordained purpose and place are not just a physical place in a particular location but a function that this created entity is supposed to perform.
    *   **No Chaos or Randomness:** The universe is not haphazard. There is a structure, a hierarchy (if we are considering angels), and a precise orchestration to creation. Everything has a place and a purpose.
    *   **Divine Knowledge:** The fact that the station is "ma'loom" (known) highlights God's encompassing knowledge of each creature and its specific role. This suggests God's detailed planning and continuous awareness of all creation.

**Contextual Considerations (While often applied to Angels):**

*  While this verse appears in a context that is often interpreted as referring to angels, who each have specific duties and locations in the heavens, the concept of "maqam ma'loom" is more general.  It can be applied to any created entity in order to emphasize that nothing was created without purpose.
* **Humanity:** Applying this concept to humanity means that each human is placed into the world with a specific and divinely purposed life to live. They have been given gifts and a place in the world to fulfill that purpose. Some take it further to mean a divinely appointed role as a form of predestination, but this idea is contentious and subject to theological debate.

**Overall, the verse signifies order, purpose, and divine knowledge underlying creation. It implies that everything has a predefined and significant role to play, not just in a general sense, but that role has been intentionally designed.** It underscores the intricate design and organization of the universe, highlighting the deliberate nature of divine creation, and should inspire a person to look for their place and purpose.
orig: وما منا إلا له مقام معلوم

translation: And indeed, it is We who are lined up (in ranks).
interpretation:
This verse, "Wa inna la nahnu as-saffoon," emphasizes the organized and disciplined nature of angels or, more broadly, beings in the divine service. The word "as-saffoon" (الصَّافُّونَ) is derived from "saffa" which means to form ranks or lines. Therefore, the literal translation speaks of those who are 'lined up'.  

Contextually, this verse is typically found in passages discussing the celestial realm and the divine order. The verse is usually understood to refer to the angels, who are constantly in a state of worship and submission to God, organized in ranks and ready to carry out His commands. It highlights their perfect obedience and their inherent orderliness, serving as a model of devotion and discipline. Some interpreters also extend its meaning to include all those who submit to God’s will and are organized in their worship and service, such as in congregational prayer (Salat) which requires standing in rows (sufuf, plural of saff). The verse serves as a reminder of the divine order and the importance of maintaining structure and discipline in one's relationship with God.
orig: وإنا لنحن الصافون

translation: And indeed, it is We who are the ones who glorify [Allah].
interpretation: This verse, "Wa inna la-nahnu al-musabbihun," emphasizes the exclusive and continuous glorification of Allah by a specific group – referred to as "We." The context in which this verse often appears within the Qur'an points towards this 'We' as referring to the angels, or possibly all of creation in a state of complete submission and praise to God. The word 'musabbihun' (المسبحون) is derived from 'tasbih' (تسبيح), which signifies glorifying God, declaring His transcendence, and affirming His perfection. It is not mere verbal recitation, but rather encompasses a state of being where the entire existence and actions are a testament to God's greatness. The verse underscores the idea that glorifying God is not a discretionary act for these specific entities, but their intrinsic and continuous nature, reflecting their perfect submission to and awareness of the Divine. It also serves as a reminder to humans to strive for such a state of devotion and submission to Allah through their actions and words, while implicitly noting the vastness of Allah's creation and His continuous glorification by others.
orig: وإنا لنحن المسبحون

translation: And indeed, they were certainly saying.
interpretation: This verse fragment, "وإن كانوا ليقولون" (Wa 'in kānū la-yaqūlūn), is typically found within a larger context in the Quran. It signifies that the people being referred to were persistently and emphatically making a certain statement or claim. The use of 'in' (وإن) followed by the past tense of 'to be' (كانوا) and the particle 'la-' (ل) preceding the verb 'to say' (يقولون) emphasizes the certainty and continued nature of their speech. Essentially, it highlights that those being talked about weren't just saying something occasionally, but that it was an ongoing, definite, and perhaps well-known claim they were making. The specific meaning of the verse heavily depends on the context of the verses immediately surrounding it in the Quran. For example, it could be referring to the disbelievers’ denial of the Prophet's message, or it might be about the justifications given by wrongdoers.  Therefore, the verse is not standalone, but rather a part of a more extended narrative within the Quran and it requires the additional surrounding verses for proper understanding.
orig: وإن كانوا ليقولون

translation: If only we had a reminder from the former peoples!
interpretation: This verse expresses a longing or regret from a group of people (often understood to be the disbelievers or those who reject the message of the Prophet Muhammad) who, upon witnessing the truth or facing consequences, wish they had received a divine reminder like the earlier nations did. The phrase "ذِكْرًا مِنَ ٱلْأَوَّلِينَ" (dhikran mina al-awwalin) refers to a 'reminder' or 'book of remembrance' or 'scripture' that was sent to previous prophets and their communities.  The sentiment implies that had they received such a clear and compelling message earlier, they might have believed and avoided their current predicament.  Essentially, it's an acknowledgement of their shortsightedness and a lament about their lack of guidance, while also subtly acknowledging the validity of the divine message now made clear to them. It can also be seen as a form of excuse-making, suggesting that they were not properly warned or had not received sufficient proof, although this argument would ultimately be rejected in the context of the Quran's overall message.
orig: لو أن عندنا ذكرا من الأولين

translation: But we are the devoted servants of Allah.
interpretation: This verse fragment, likely part of a larger dialogue or narrative within the Quran, emphasizes the speaker's (or the group's) status as sincere and devoted servants of God (Allah). The Arabic term 'al-mukhlisin' (المخلصين) carries the weight of being purified, sincere, and dedicated in their worship and devotion. It implies a level of faithfulness that goes beyond mere outward acts and encompasses a genuine inner connection with the divine. This verse is a powerful affirmation of submission and devotion to Allah, highlighting the importance of sincere worship and the pursuit of closeness to God. It can be understood as a rejection of other forms of allegiance or worship, asserting that their sole loyalty and service is to Allah alone. The phrase underscores a key theme of Islamic theology - Tawhid (Oneness of God) and the sincere dedication that should characterize a believer's relationship with their creator.
orig: لكنا عباد الله المخلصين

translation: So they disbelieved in it, and they will soon know.
interpretation: This verse speaks of a rejection of a message or sign from God. The phrase 'they disbelieved in it' (فَكَفَرُوا بِهِ) indicates an active denial and rejection of something presented to them as truth, guidance, or a divine sign. The subsequent phrase 'and they will soon know' (فَسَوْفَ يَعْلَمُونَ) is a warning, a threat, and a promise of the consequences of their disbelief. This future knowledge isn't merely about gaining information; rather, it's a reference to the painful and certain realization of the truth they rejected, likely occurring in the hereafter or through a worldly punishment. The verse highlights the inevitable accountability for denying divine truth. It also implies that the truth, though initially rejected, will eventually be made manifest, often through a means that is less desirable for the rejectors.
orig: فكفروا به فسوف يعلمون

translation: And Our word has already gone forth to Our Messengers, Our Servants.
interpretation: This verse, *wa laqad sabaqat kalimatuna li'ibadina al-mursaleen*, highlights the preordained divine plan and the unwavering support that God provides to His chosen Messengers. The phrase "Our word has already gone forth" (sabaqat kalimatuna) signifies that God's decree and promise of victory and success for His messengers were established before their very mission began. It implies that their ultimate triumph is not solely dependent on their own efforts, but is rather a guaranteed outcome backed by divine will. The term "Our Messengers, Our Servants" (li'ibadina al-mursaleen) emphasizes the close relationship between God and His prophets. They are both messengers carrying out God’s word and servants wholly devoted to Him. Therefore, this verse serves as a reassurance and a source of strength for all those who strive in God's path, particularly for the prophets, that despite hardships, God's support is guaranteed, and their efforts to spread His message will ultimately prevail. It is also a reminder of God’s absolute knowledge and power – His plans and words are set and will be fulfilled. The word 'kalimatuna' (Our word) can also refer to the promise of victory or the support that accompanies His Messengers, depending on different interpretive schools.
orig: ولقد سبقت كلمتنا لعبادنا المرسلين

translation: Indeed, they are the ones who will be victorious.
interpretation: This verse, "إنهم لهم المنصورون" (Innahum lahum al-mansuroon), is a powerful affirmation of divine support and ultimate victory for those who are aligned with God's will. The emphasis is placed on the pronoun 'they' (هم - hum), which, in its context within the Qur'an, typically refers to the believers or those who are striving for righteousness. The phrase " لهم المنصورون" (lahum al-mansuroon) uses the emphatic 'lam' (لهم) which intensifies the meaning, meaning 'truly to them' or 'certainly they are'. 'Al-mansuroon' is the passive participle meaning 'the ones who are given victory' or 'the ones who are aided'. This implies that their victory is not solely due to their own strength or effort, but rather is a gift and divine assistance from God. The verse thus conveys a sense of assurance and encouragement, promising eventual triumph to those who remain steadfast in their faith and commitment to God's path. It highlights the belief that the righteous will ultimately prevail, even in the face of adversity. The victory is not always immediate or worldly but it also encompasses spiritual and ultimate triumph in the hereafter. It is a powerful reminder of God's promise and a source of hope for the believers.
orig: إنهم لهم المنصورون

translation: And indeed, Our soldiers - they will be the victors.
interpretation: This verse, "Wa inna jundana lahumul-ghalibun,"  is a powerful declaration of divine support and ultimate triumph for those who are aligned with God's cause. 'Jundana' (Our soldiers) is interpreted in various ways by scholars. It can refer literally to those who fight in the path of God (the 'Mujahideen'), but more broadly it signifies those who uphold truth, righteousness, and God's commands.  The 'ghalibun' (victors) refers to the ultimate success and victory that they will achieve.  This victory is not necessarily immediate or worldly but often refers to a more comprehensive and enduring triumph in the Hereafter. The verse inspires confidence and steadfastness in believers, assuring them that even amidst hardship and challenges, the ultimate victory belongs to those who are steadfast in their faith and commitment to God's way. It emphasizes that genuine strength lies in divine support, not just worldly power. It also implies a struggle and a test – that victory is earned and not simply granted. The promise is conditional upon aligning with God’s purpose. Therefore, it is not a blanket statement guaranteeing victory for anyone who claims to be a believer but a promise for those who genuinely strive on the righteous path, making God’s will supreme in their lives.
orig: وإن جندنا لهم الغالبون

translation: So turn away from them for a time.
interpretation:
This verse, "فَتَوَلَّ عَنْهُمْ حَتَّى حِينٍ" (fa-tawalla 'anhum hatta heenin), is generally understood as an instruction to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to temporarily withdraw or disengage from those who reject his message, specifically his immediate opponents. The phrase "fa-tawalla" means "so turn away" or "so withdraw". The addition of "'anhum" indicates that this withdrawal is directed away "from them," meaning the disbelievers or those actively hostile to the nascent Muslim community. However, the withdrawal is qualified by "hatta heenin," which translates to "until a time" or "for a time." This suggests that the withdrawal is not meant to be permanent, but rather a temporary measure. The 'time' (heen) itself is not explicitly defined. It can be interpreted in several ways, including: 

1.  **A period of patience:** It implies a period where the Prophet should not engage in direct confrontation or debate with them, allowing space for them to reflect and potentially reconsider their stance. 
2. **A defined future time:** It could refer to a future time when circumstances would be more favorable, such as after the Muslims had grown stronger, or when God had decreed a decisive outcome through his will. This might be through a divine intervention, a new directive, or even a change in the opposition's behavior. 
3. **A temporary reprieve:** It's also interpreted as a period of respite from the challenges and hostility of the opposition, allowing the Prophet to focus on other priorities such as building the Muslim community, receiving further revelations, and consolidating his followers. 

Fundamentally, this verse highlights the importance of strategic patience and wisdom in dealing with opposition. It does not advocate for permanent abandonment or passivity, but rather suggests a temporary withdrawal as a part of a longer-term strategy. It underscores the understanding that sometimes, engagement isn't always the most productive approach, and a pause to regroup and reassess the situation can be beneficial. The ultimate meaning rests on God's wisdom, and the specific length or nature of the "time" is left open to His discretion, reflecting the complex dynamics of the early Meccan period.
orig: فتول عنهم حتى حين

translation: And watch them, for they will soon see.
interpretation:
This verse, \"وأبصرهم فسوف يبصرون\" (Wa 'absirhum fasawfa yubsiroon), carries a dual meaning, both a command and a prophecy. 

**Translation Breakdown:**
* **وأبصرهم (Wa 'absirhum):** This part literally translates to "And watch them" or "Be observant of them." It's a directive to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), and by extension, to all believers, to observe the actions and behaviors of those who reject the message of Islam. This observation is not merely passive; it implies careful consideration and understanding of their conduct and its consequences.
* **فسوف يبصرون (fasawfa yubsiroon):** This translates to "then they will soon see." The key here is 'sawfa,' which indicates a future occurrence that is not distant.  'Yubsiroon' means 'they will see',  and not only  in the physical sense of vision, but it is also to understand, to realize, or to perceive with insight. Thus the future seeing refers not just to a physical event. 

**Interpretation:**

Taken together, the verse implies that while the disbelievers may currently be veiled from the truth, engaged in their denial and opposition to the message,  they will inevitably come to understand the reality they are currently rejecting.  This realization will come as a direct result of seeing  the consequences of their choices and actions, whether in this life or the hereafter. It is a divine guarantee, a prophecy. 

The verse also serves as a source of comfort and patience for believers.  It reminds them that despite the current resistance and difficulties,  the truth will ultimately prevail, and those who deny it will eventually recognize their error. The imperative "Watch them" isn't about gloating or hatred, but about learning from their path and remaining steadfast on the path of truth. The verse provides assurance that Allah's justice will be manifested.  It is therefore a powerful message of patience, vigilance and hope in the eventual revelation of Truth.
orig: وأبصرهم فسوف يبصرون

translation: Then are they seeking to hasten Our punishment?
interpretation: This verse poses a rhetorical question to those who disbelieve and reject the divine message. It highlights their arrogance and defiance by suggesting that they are essentially daring or challenging God by desiring the arrival of the punishment they are warned about. It implies that their skepticism and rejection are not born out of genuine inquiry or doubt, but rather out of a stubborn denial that leads them to a point where they even express a desire for the consequences they are told will follow disobedience. The verse serves as a sharp rebuke and a reminder of the severity of the impending divine reckoning, emphasizing that the punishment they seemingly crave is, in fact, a terrifying prospect they should actively avoid by turning to faith.
orig: أفبعذابنا يستعجلون

translation: Then when it descends into their open space, evil will be the morning of those who were warned.
interpretation: This verse speaks of a divine punishment or calamity that is imminent upon those who were warned but disregarded the warnings. The phrase 'when it descends into their open space' (bisaahatihim) refers to the sudden arrival of this punishment in their midst, catching them unprepared. The 'open space' suggests a place where they are vulnerable and exposed, without any means of escape or defense. The expression 'evil will be the morning' (sa'a sabahu al-mundhirin) uses a literary device, referring to the morning after the punishment arrives. It suggests that this morning will be characterized by suffering, regret, and destruction for those who received warnings but did not heed them. The verse serves as a stern warning to those who reject divine guidance, highlighting the inevitable consequences of their disbelief and disobedience. It emphasizes the gravity of ignoring the messengers of God and their messages.
orig: فإذا نزل بساحتهم فساء صباح المنذرين

translation: And turn away from them for a while.
interpretation:
This verse, "وتول عنهم حتى حين" (Wa tawalla 'anhum hatta heen), is a directive, often found in the Quran, instructing the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) to turn away or disregard the actions and statements of those who oppose him or reject his message, but only for a specific, limited time (حتى حين - hatta heen). The 'while' (حين - heen) is deliberately vague, suggesting it is a period set by God's wisdom, not a permanent abandonment. It doesn't indicate a complete and final break, but rather a temporary withdrawal from direct confrontation or engagement. This withdrawal could serve several purposes:

1. **Patience and Resilience:** It teaches patience and resilience in the face of opposition. Instead of engaging in futile arguments, the Prophet is instructed to step back and allow events to unfold according to God’s plan.
2. **Focus on the True Message:** By turning away from distractions, the Prophet can focus on the more critical aspects of delivering the message and organizing the Muslim community. The respite allows him to regroup and prepare for future challenges.
3. **Opportunity for Reflection and Change:** The 'while' provides an opportunity for the opponents to reflect upon their behavior and potentially change their stance. It avoids continuous antagonism, allowing time for hearts and minds to soften.
4. **Divine Wisdom and Timing:**  The length of the 'while' is left to Allah’s knowledge, implying that He determines the appropriate timing for the Prophet to re-engage with those who oppose him. This conveys the idea that the Prophet's actions are ultimately guided by divine wisdom. 

In summary, this verse is a command to be patient and strategic, not to give up on conveying the message of Islam but to wait for the right time and approach. It acknowledges the challenges of propagation and provides guidance on how to deal with opposition without succumbing to negativity or despair. The idea is temporary disengagement for a greater purpose, all within the divine will and timing.
orig: وتول عنهم حتى حين

translation: And watch, for soon they will see.
interpretation: This verse, "Wa absir fa sawfa yubsirun," is a powerful statement that combines a command to observe with a future prediction.  The initial part, "Wa absir," is a directive, often translated as 'And watch,' 'observe,' or 'be watchful.' It urges the listener, implicitly the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and by extension, his followers, to carefully scrutinize the situation or the actions of those being addressed.  The phrase "fa sawfa yubsirun" translates to 'for soon they will see.' This second part provides the reason for the watchful observation. It is a prophetic statement indicating that the truth will inevitably become clear. The 'they' in this context refers to those who are being watched - typically the disbelievers, the deniers, or those who oppose the message of Islam.  The verse implies that although they might be blind to the truth at present, the reality of the situation (either the truth of the message, the consequences of their actions, or the divine punishment) will become evident to them. It carries a sense of both patience and certainty – urging patience and trust in Allah’s plan. The emphasis on seeing suggests that the realization will be undeniable and complete. Furthermore, it suggests that the outcome isn't something obscure but something that will be readily perceivable. This verse often appears as a sort of warning and a reassurance for the believers that ultimately truth prevails, and those who oppose it will eventually witness that truth, though perhaps too late.
orig: وأبصر فسوف يبصرون

translation: Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of Might, from what they attribute [to Him].
interpretation: This verse, "Subhana Rabbika Rabbil 'Izzati 'Amma yasifun," is a powerful declaration of God's transcendence and perfection. It begins with "Subhana Rabbika," which translates to "Glory be to your Lord." The term "Subhan" signifies that God is free from all imperfections, flaws, or limitations that humans might attribute to Him. It is a declaration of His absolute purity and exalted nature. The phrase "Rabbil 'Izzati" then clarifies that this Lord is "the Lord of Might," emphasizing His supreme power, honor, and dominion. The verse concludes with "'Amma yasifun," meaning "from what they describe" or "from what they attribute [to Him]." This highlights a crucial point: that human attempts to describe or define God often fall short, sometimes even leading to anthropomorphic or inaccurate conceptions of His nature.
