orig: يسبح لله ما في السماوات وما في الأرض له الملك وله الحمد وهو على كل شيء قدير

translation: He is the One who created you, and among you are those who disbelieve and among you are those who believe. And Allah, of what you do, is Seeing.
interpretation: This verse highlights a fundamental aspect of human existence and divine knowledge. It emphasizes that God is the creator of all humanity, and within this created population, there exists a natural dichotomy: some will choose to disbelieve (kufr), while others will choose to believe (iman). This divergence is presented as an inherent part of the human experience, not as a divine decree predetermining faith or disbelief. Furthermore, the verse asserts that Allah is 'Baseer' (All-Seeing) of what people do; This implies that God observes the actions and choices of all individuals, both believers and disbelievers. This underscores accountability, as individuals will be held responsible for their actions and the faith choices they make. The verse can be interpreted as a call to reflect on one's personal beliefs and conduct, acknowledging that the choice of faith is a personal one, with ultimate responsibility resting with the individual, and God having full knowledge of human actions and intention.
orig: هو الذي خلقكم فمنكم كافر ومنكم مؤمن والله بما تعملون بصير

translation: He created the heavens and the earth in truth, and He formed you and perfected your forms; and to Him is the [final] return.
interpretation: This verse highlights several profound aspects of God's power and the human condition. Firstly, it emphasizes that the creation of the heavens and the earth is not arbitrary but purposeful ('in truth'). This implies a grand design and a meaningful existence for the universe. Secondly, it speaks of God's meticulous creation of humanity, not just as a species but as individuals with unique and perfected forms ('and He formed you and perfected your forms'). The Arabic term 'صوركم' (ṣawwarakum) which we translate as formed you also implies shaping and designing, highlighting God's active role and the beauty of human form. The word 'أحسن' (aḥsana) here indicates that this shaping and designing is not just perfect but also beautiful and refined. Therefore it is a reminder that our existence and physical form are gifts from God, which should inspire humility and gratitude. Finally, the verse concludes with a reminder that our ultimate destination is back to Him ('and to Him is the [final] return'). This underscores the temporary nature of worldly life and the accountability we will all face before our Creator. It encourages a sense of responsibility in our actions during our earthly sojourn as we will eventually all return to Allah for judgement. In essence, this verse is a potent blend of divine creation, human dignity, and ultimate accountability.
orig: خلق السماوات والأرض بالحق وصوركم فأحسن صوركم وإليه المصير

translation: He knows what is in the heavens and the earth; and He knows what you conceal and what you reveal. And Allah is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts (of men).
interpretation:
This verse emphasizes God's absolute and comprehensive knowledge. It highlights three interconnected aspects of this divine attribute:

1. **"He knows what is in the heavens and the earth"**: This establishes the vastness of God's knowledge, encompassing the entire created universe. Nothing escapes His awareness, from the grandest celestial bodies to the smallest particles on Earth. It signifies that God's knowledge is not limited to a specific place or time but is all-encompassing.

2. **"and He knows what you conceal and what you reveal"**: This part focuses on God's knowledge of human actions and intentions. It underscores that God knows both the outward acts that people display (what they 'reveal') and the inner thoughts and feelings they keep hidden (what they 'conceal'). This implies that accountability extends not just to deeds, but to the inner motivations behind them.

3. **"And Allah is All-Knowing of what is in the breasts (of men)"**: This final clause further emphasizes God's profound knowledge of human hearts and minds. The term 'breasts' here is a metaphorical reference to the inner selves of individuals, their innermost thoughts, feelings, intentions, and even the secrets they might hide from themselves. This reinforces the idea that nothing is hidden from God's knowledge, and that He is fully aware of the inner states of every individual. The phrase "All-Knowing" (عليم) stresses that this knowledge is perfect and complete.

In summary, this verse serves as a powerful reminder of God's omnipresence and omniscience. It encourages believers to be mindful of their actions and intentions, knowing that God is aware of everything, both outwardly and inwardly, fostering a sense of accountability and inspiring them towards righteous behavior with sincerity. It also conveys a sense of comfort and security to those who are sincere and might face injustices, knowing that their true intentions are known to God, even if unseen by others.
orig: يعلم ما في السماوات والأرض ويعلم ما تسرون وما تعلنون والله عليم بذات الصدور

translation: Has there not come to you the news of those who disbelieved before? So they tasted the evil consequences of their conduct, and for them is a painful punishment.
interpretation:
This verse is a reminder and a warning, drawing parallels between past generations who rejected divine guidance and their ultimate fate, and the present audience. It highlights a pattern of cause and effect: disbelief (kufr) leads to negative consequences in this life ('tasted the evil consequences') as well as in the afterlife ('painful punishment').

The verse uses the past tense to refer to previous disbelievers, suggesting that their stories are readily available and should serve as cautionary tales. 'The news' (naba') implies that the information about their fates is not obscure, but widely known. 'Tasted the evil consequences of their conduct' suggests that the negative outcomes were immediate and tangible in their lives, not just a future punishment. This might refer to calamities, defeats, or societal breakdowns. Finally, 'painful punishment' explicitly warns of severe torment in the Hereafter.

The key takeaway from this verse is to learn from history and to recognize that disbelief carries both temporal and eternal repercussions. It encourages reflection on the consequences of choosing a path that rejects divine guidance and instead promotes righteousness and submission to God.
orig: ألم يأتكم نبأ الذين كفروا من قبل فذاقوا وبال أمرهم ولهم عذاب أليم

translation: That is because their messengers used to come to them with clear proofs, but they said, "Are mere mortals going to guide us?" So they disbelieved and turned away, and Allah was not in need of them. And Allah is Free of need, Praiseworthy.
interpretation: This verse describes the reason for the punishment or consequences faced by those who rejected the truth. It highlights a pattern of behavior where messengers, chosen by God, were sent with clear signs (Bayyinat) and proofs demonstrating the truth of their message. Instead of accepting guidance, the people dismissed the messengers with arrogance, questioning how fellow humans could guide them ('Are mere mortals going to guide us?'). This reveals a lack of humility and a prideful rejection of divine guidance. Consequently, they chose disbelief (Kafaru) and turned away (Tawallaw) from the truth. The verse then emphasizes God's absolute self-sufficiency and independence. Their actions had no negative impact on God; rather, they only harmed themselves. Allah is declared to be 'Ghaniyy' (Free of Need) and 'Hameed' (Praiseworthy), highlighting His perfection and deserving of all praise regardless of people's belief or disbelief. The verse serves as a warning against arrogance, the rejection of divinely sent messengers and a reminder of God's absolute power and perfection.
orig: ذلك بأنه كانت تأتيهم رسلهم بالبينات فقالوا أبشر يهدوننا فكفروا وتولوا واستغنى الله والله غني حميد

translation: Those who disbelieve claim that they will not be resurrected. Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected, then you will surely be informed of what you did. And that, for Allah, is easy.'
interpretation: This verse addresses a core tenet of Islamic belief: the Day of Resurrection. It highlights the disbelief of some who reject the possibility of being raised again after death. The verse begins by stating that those who disbelieve (those who explicitly deny God or reject the Prophet's message) assert that they will not be resurrected. In response, God instructs the Prophet (peace be upon him) to vehemently affirm the reality of the Resurrection with a strong oath: 'Say, 'Yes, by my Lord, you will surely be resurrected.'' The use of 'by my Lord' emphasizes the certainty of the event and invokes the divine power and authority to bring it to pass. Furthermore, the verse states that after being resurrected, they will be fully informed about their actions. This implies accountability for their deeds in the worldly life. Finally, the verse ends by saying 'And that, for Allah, is easy,' underscoring God's omnipotence and capability to carry out the Resurrection and Judgement. In essence, this verse serves as a powerful declaration of the Day of Resurrection, challenging the deniers and emphasizing that everyone will be held responsible for their actions before God. It aims to provide a firm assurance for the believers, while being a stark warning to those who disbelieve.
orig: زعم الذين كفروا أن لن يبعثوا قل بلى وربي لتبعثن ثم لتنبؤن بما عملتم وذلك على الله يسير

translation: So believe in Allah and His Messenger and the Light which We have sent down. And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.
interpretation:
This verse is a call to sincere faith and conscious action. It has three main parts:

1.  **'So believe in Allah and His Messenger...'**: This emphasizes the foundational pillars of Islam: belief in the Oneness of God (Allah) and acceptance of Prophet Muhammad as His final Messenger. This belief is not merely intellectual assent but a deep, heartfelt conviction that shapes one's life.

2.  **'...and the Light which We have sent down.'**: The "Light" (an-Nūr) refers to the Quran. It illuminates the path to truth, righteousness, and guidance. It is a divine revelation that provides clarity and dispels the darkness of ignorance and misguidance. It also implies adherence to the teachings of the Quran, not just reading it.

3.  **'And Allah is All-Aware of what you do.'**: This is a constant reminder of God's omnipresence and perfect knowledge. It is not just about the external actions but also the intentions, thoughts, and feelings that motivate those actions. This awareness should instill a sense of accountability and encourage believers to strive for excellence in their conduct. The phrase 'what you do' (ta'maloon) is very general and includes both good and bad deeds. The implication is a warning against bad deeds and a motivation to engage in good deeds, as Allah is aware of all.

In summary, the verse urges believers to have sincere faith, embrace the guidance of the Quran, and act consciously, knowing that Allah is fully aware of their deeds and intentions. It calls for a holistic approach to faith, encompassing belief, guidance, and accountability.
orig: فآمنوا بالله ورسوله والنور الذي أنزلنا والله بما تعملون خبير

translation: The Day He will gather you for the Day of Gathering - that is the Day of Deprivation. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness - He will remove from him his misdeeds and admit him to gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. That is the great attainment.
interpretation: This verse from Surah At-Taghabun (The Mutual Loss and Gain) describes the Day of Judgment, emphasizing its nature as a 'Day of Gathering' and 'Day of Deprivation' (Taghabun). The gathering aspect refers to the assembly of all humanity before God for judgment. The 'deprivation' aspect is interpreted in multiple ways: it signifies the loss that disbelievers will experience due to not having invested in righteous deeds for the Hereafter, the regret and loss felt by those who wasted their lives, and the immense disparity in outcome between the righteous and the wicked. The verse then shifts to the reward promised to those who believe in Allah and perform righteous actions. Their misdeeds will be forgiven, and they will be granted entry into Paradise, a blissful abode characterized by flowing rivers and eternal residence. This reinforces the fundamental Islamic doctrine of divine justice and the ultimate success (Fawz al-Azeem) of those who submit to God and strive for righteousness. The verse highlights the importance of faith and good deeds as the path to salvation and ultimate triumph over loss and regret on the Day of Judgment.
orig: يوم يجمعكم ليوم الجمع ذلك يوم التغابن ومن يؤمن بالله ويعمل صالحا يكفر عنه سيئاته ويدخله جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار خالدين فيها أبدا ذلك الفوز العظيم

translation: And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs - those are the companions of the Fire; they will abide therein eternally, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation: This verse describes the fate of those who reject faith (kufr) and actively deny God's clear signs (ayatina). The word 'kufr' here encompasses both disbelief in God's existence and rejection of the prophetic message and revealed scriptures. 'Ayatina' refers to the various signs of God's existence, power, and guidance, which could be manifest in the natural world, historical events, or the Quran itself. The verse asserts that these disbelievers and deniers will be 'ashab al-nar' (companions of the Fire), meaning they will be inhabitants of hell. Their punishment is described as 'khalidin fiha' (abiding therein eternally), indicating its permanence. The concluding phrase 'wa bi'sa al-masir' (and wretched is the destination) emphasizes the severe and undesirable nature of their ultimate end. This verse serves as a stern warning about the consequences of rejecting divine truth and highlights the importance of faith and acceptance of God's signs.
orig: والذين كفروا وكذبوا بآياتنا أولئك أصحاب النار خالدين فيها وبئس المصير

translation: No calamity befalls except by Allah's permission. And whoever believes in Allah - He will guide his heart. And Allah is Knowing of all things.
interpretation: This verse addresses the nature of trials and the role of faith in navigating them. It asserts that nothing happens in the universe, including hardships and calamities ( مصيبة - musiba), without Allah's decree and permission (بإذن الله - bi-ithnillah). This is not to imply that Allah is the source of evil, but rather that He is the ultimate orchestrator of all events, allowing things to occur within His grand plan and wisdom. The verse then connects faith (ومن يؤمن بالله - wa man yu'min billah) to inner peace and guidance (يهد قلبه - yahdi qalbahu). This means that genuine belief in Allah, acknowledging His power and wisdom, leads to a tranquil heart and acceptance of His decree. This acceptance doesn't imply passivity; instead, it allows a believer to face difficulties with patience and resilience, knowing that even in trials there is divine purpose. The concluding phrase (والله بكل شيء عليم - wallahu bikulli shay'in 'aleem) emphasizes Allah's all-encompassing knowledge, affirming that nothing is hidden from Him and that all events, including those that seem chaotic or negative, occur with His full awareness and understanding. Therefore, while acknowledging that difficulties are part of life, the verse ultimately offers comfort and assurance by emphasizing reliance on Allah, His control over all matters, and the peace that comes from faith.
orig: ما أصاب من مصيبة إلا بإذن الله ومن يؤمن بالله يهد قلبه والله بكل شيء عليم

translation: And obey Allah and obey the Messenger, but if you turn away, then upon Our Messenger is only the clear notification.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the dual obligation of obedience to both God (Allah) and His Messenger (Prophet Muhammad). It highlights that true faith requires adherence to divine guidance as revealed in the Quran and the prophetic teachings (Sunnah). The verse also clarifies that the Prophet's role is limited to conveying the divine message clearly and understandably. If people choose to disregard this message and turn away from obedience, the responsibility for their actions rests with them. The Prophet's duty is fulfilled by delivering the message, and he is not accountable for people's choices to accept or reject it. The verse subtly warns against disobedience, suggesting it leads to negative consequences for the individual, not for the Prophet or God. The phrase 'clear notification' emphasizes the comprehensibility of the message, implying no ambiguity or justification for rejection.
orig: وأطيعوا الله وأطيعوا الرسول فإن توليتم فإنما على رسولنا البلاغ المبين

translation: Allah! There is no god but He. And upon Allah, let the believers rely.
interpretation: This verse emphasizes the core tenet of Islam: Tawhid, the absolute oneness of God. It declares that Allah is the sole deity, negating the existence of any other god. The phrase 'La ilaha illa Huwa' (There is no god but He) is the essence of the Islamic creed, affirming God's unique and unrivaled divinity. Furthermore, the verse instructs believers to place their trust (tawakkul) solely in Allah. This reliance is not passive; rather, it's an active engagement with life while having complete faith that all outcomes ultimately rest in God's hands. Believers are encouraged to strive and make effort, but with the understanding that the ultimate success and sustenance are from Allah alone. The verse connects the affirmation of God's oneness with the necessity of complete reliance upon Him, highlighting that true faith manifests in both belief and action.
orig: الله لا إله إلا هو وعلى الله فليتوكل المؤمنون

translation: O you who have believed, indeed, among your wives and your children are enemies to you, so beware of them. But if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses believers, highlighting a challenging reality: that even those closest to us, our spouses and children, can sometimes act as 'enemies.' This doesn't necessarily imply active hostility, but rather, they can be a source of distraction, temptation, or hinderance to our devotion to Allah and our righteous conduct. The verse urges caution and awareness regarding their potential negative influence. However, it immediately follows with a powerful call for forgiveness, pardon, and overlooking their faults. This emphasis on forgiveness is crucial. Instead of harboring resentment or seeking revenge, the verse encourages believers to emulate Allah's attributes of forgiveness and mercy. The ultimate message is one of balance: while we must be mindful of potential negative influences even from loved ones, we are also commanded to practice compassion and forgiveness. The closing with 'Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful' serves as both a reminder of God's nature and an encouragement to adopt these qualities ourselves, reflecting a profound understanding of human relationships and their potential complexities within a faith-based context.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا إن من أزواجكم وأولادكم عدوا لكم فاحذروهم وإن تعفوا وتصفحوا وتغفروا فإن الله غفور رحيم

translation: Your wealth and your children are but a trial, and Allah has with Him a great reward.
interpretation: This verse highlights a crucial aspect of the human condition: that our possessions (wealth) and our offspring (children), while often perceived as blessings, are essentially a test (fitna) from Allah. They can easily become sources of distraction, attachment, and even wrongdoing if not handled with the right intention and consciousness of Allah. The 'fitna' here implies a test or trial that can lead a person astray from the path of righteousness if they become overly focused on accumulating worldly gains or prioritizing their children over their religious obligations. The verse emphasizes that the true and lasting reward (ajr 'azeem) lies with Allah, suggesting that our efforts should be directed towards pleasing Him rather than fixating on temporary worldly matters. It serves as a reminder that the love for wealth and children should not overshadow our love for and obedience to Allah, and that our focus should remain on the eternal life to come and the reward in the hereafter.
orig: إنما أموالكم وأولادكم فتنة والله عنده أجر عظيم

translation: So fear Allah as much as you are able and listen and obey and spend [in the way of Allah]; it is better for yourselves. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.
interpretation: This verse encompasses several crucial aspects of a believer's relationship with Allah and their fellow beings. Firstly, it commands 'fear Allah as much as you are able,' which emphasizes that the obligation of God-consciousness is not burdensome. It's tailored to individual capacity, acknowledging that people have different abilities and circumstances. It doesn't demand perfection but sincere effort within one's means. The verse then links this fear with practical actions: 'listen,' 'obey,' and 'spend.' 'Listen' refers to hearing and understanding the divine guidance, both the Quran and the Prophet's teachings. 'Obey' implies acting upon this guidance in all aspects of life, demonstrating submission to Allah's will. 'Spend' highlights the importance of charity and generosity, using one's wealth for the benefit of others and the cause of Islam. This spending is described as 'better for yourselves,' underscoring that giving, paradoxically, benefits the giver spiritually and sometimes even materially. The verse concludes with a powerful statement on self-purification and success. It states that 'whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul' – meaning those who overcome their innate tendency towards miserliness and greed – 'it is those who will be the successful.' This connects inner purification with ultimate success in this life and the hereafter. This protection from stinginess is achieved through conscious effort, self-discipline, and seeking refuge in Allah. Thus, the verse advocates a holistic approach to faith, where inner consciousness of Allah leads to practical actions and culminates in spiritual and worldly success. It emphasizes that true piety is not just about religious rituals but also about social responsibility and internal cleansing.
orig: فاتقوا الله ما استطعتم واسمعوا وأطيعوا وأنفقوا خيرا لأنفسكم ومن يوق شح نفسه فأولئك هم المفلحون

translation: If you lend to Allah a good loan, He will multiply it for you and forgive you. And Allah is Most Appreciative, Most Forbearing.
interpretation: This verse uses the metaphor of a 'loan' to Allah to encourage acts of charity and kindness, particularly towards the needy. It highlights that when someone gives for the sake of Allah, with sincerity and good intentions (a 'good loan'), the reward from Allah is not only multiplied (often interpreted as manyfold both in this life and the hereafter), but also combined with divine forgiveness. The verse concludes by emphasizing two attributes of God: 'Shakur' (Most Appreciative), indicating that Allah deeply values even small acts of goodness and rewards them abundantly, and 'Haleem' (Most Forbearing), signifying His patience and graciousness towards human shortcomings. Thus, the verse motivates believers towards generosity, assures them of immense reward, and underscores Allah's forgiving and appreciative nature. It implies that giving is not a loss but an investment with Allah, yielding both material and spiritual benefits.
orig: إن تقرضوا الله قرضا حسنا يضاعفه لكم ويغفر لكم والله شكور حليم

translation: Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, the Exalted in Might, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse describes some of the attributes of God (Allah). "عالم الغيب والشهادة" ( 'Alim al-Ghaib wa ash-Shahadah) translates to 'Knower of the unseen and the witnessed'. This signifies God's comprehensive knowledge, encompassing everything that is hidden (ghaib), such as the future, the contents of hearts, and things beyond human perception, as well as everything that is apparent and witnessed (shahadah) in the observable world. There is nothing outside of His knowledge. "العزيز الحكيم" ('Al-'Aziz al-Hakim) translates to 'the Exalted in Might, the Wise'. 'Al-'Aziz' denotes that God is All-Powerful, possessing ultimate strength and dominion, and that He is invincible. 'Al-Hakim' indicates that He is All-Wise, meaning that all His actions, decrees, and creation are based on perfect wisdom and purpose. Therefore, this verse conveys that God is not only all-knowing but also possesses absolute power and perfect wisdom in all His actions and judgments. It emphasizes the comprehensiveness and perfection of His attributes, highlighting His sovereignty and the meticulous design of the universe. The combination of these attributes encourages believers to trust in God's plan and to submit to His will, understanding that His knowledge and wisdom are superior.
orig: عالم الغيب والشهادة العزيز الحكيم

translation: O Prophet, when you [or the believers] divorce women, divorce them for their prescribed waiting period and count the waiting period accurately, and fear Allah, your Lord. Do not turn them out of their [husbands'] houses, nor should they themselves leave [during that period] unless they commit a clear immorality. And those are the limits of Allah, and whoever transgresses the limits of Allah has certainly wronged himself. You know not; perhaps Allah will bring about after that a [different] matter.
interpretation:
This verse from Surah At-Talaq (The Divorce) outlines crucial guidelines for divorce in Islam, emphasizing both legal procedure and the moral implications. The verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) as a leader and model, but its instructions apply to all believers. 

The primary focus is on a regulated divorce process, specifically concerning the 'iddah' or waiting period. This period, during which the divorced woman is to remain in the husband's home, is not arbitrary. Its purpose is multi-faceted:

1.  **Reconciliation Window:** The most important aspect is the opportunity for reconciliation. This 'waiting period' aims to provide space for both parties to reconsider their decision. The verse states, 'You know not; perhaps Allah will bring about after that a [different] matter,' highlighting the possibility of reunion and reinforcing that divorce should not be impulsive or final. Staying in the same household might help facilitate this possibility.

2.  **Determining Pregnancy:** The 'iddah' also helps ascertain if the woman is pregnant, which has implications for child support and lineage.

3.  **Protection and Respect:** Keeping the woman in her marital home during this period provides her with a measure of protection and support at a vulnerable time, preventing immediate displacement and ensuring a stable environment. It also underscores respect for the divorced woman.

4.  **Strict Adherence:** The verse stresses the importance of accurately counting the 'iddah' and observing its regulations, highlighting the need to approach divorce with mindfulness and responsibility.

5.  **Exception for 'Clear Immorality':** The only exception for the woman to leave the marital home is in the case of 'a clear immorality.' While the interpretation of this term varies among scholars, it is generally understood to encompass grave offenses like adultery or significant misbehavior that breaches the sanctity of the household.

6.  **Transgressing God's Boundaries:** The verse concludes with a stern warning: Those who transgress the prescribed limits of Allah 'have wronged themselves.' This emphasizes that these are not merely rules of social conduct but moral and divine guidelines. Ignoring or circumventing them has harmful consequences on the individual and society, reflecting the importance of adhering to God's laws even in matters as difficult as divorce. 

In essence, this verse underscores the gravity of divorce in Islam, seeking to minimize its occurrence, ensure just and humane treatment of women, and offer a chance for reconciliation. It provides a framework that balances the rights of both spouses while discouraging the hasty dissolution of marriage.
orig: يا أيها النبي إذا طلقتم النساء فطلقوهن لعدتهن وأحصوا العدة واتقوا الله ربكم لا تخرجوهن من بيوتهن ولا يخرجن إلا أن يأتين بفاحشة مبينة وتلك حدود الله ومن يتعد حدود الله فقد ظلم نفسه لا تدري لعل الله يحدث بعد ذلك أمرا

translation: Then, when they have reached their term, either retain them in a good manner or separate from them in a good manner. And bring to witness two just men from among you and establish the testimony for [the sake of] God. That is instructed to whoever believes in God and the Last Day. And whoever fears God - He will make for him a way out.
interpretation: This verse, primarily concerning divorce ('when they have reached their term,' refers to the waiting period or 'iddah' after divorce), outlines the ethical and legal procedures for handling the conclusion of a marriage. It emphasizes the importance of acting with 'ma'ruf' (goodness, kindness, fairness, and well-recognized proper conduct).  Specifically, it dictates two possibilities when a divorced woman completes her waiting period: either the husband reconciles and takes her back (retention in a good manner), or the couple formally separates (separation in a good manner). Crucially, these actions must be done in a respectful and just way, avoiding any harm or bitterness.  The verse then mandates bringing two just witnesses from the Muslim community to witness either the reconciliation or the final divorce, further highlighting the need for transparency and accountability, and that the testimony is done justly and righteously for God, not personal bias. This testimony provides legal validity to the divorce process and protects the rights of both parties. The verse concludes with a powerful message: these instructions are a guidance for believers in God and the Day of Judgment. Furthermore, it provides a promise to those who fear God (act with piety and consciousness of God in all actions). God will make 'a way out' (a solution and relief from their hardship, a means of resolving their difficulties). This final statement not only provides comfort and hope but also reinforces the idea that following God's law is the best way to achieve ease and positive outcomes, and encourages all believers to behave ethically throughout their lives, especially within the family unit during separation and divorce. It also alludes to the idea that God guides those who seek guidance and follow the rules with piety.
orig: فإذا بلغن أجلهن فأمسكوهن بمعروف أو فارقوهن بمعروف وأشهدوا ذوي عدل منكم وأقيموا الشهادة لله ذلكم يوعظ به من كان يؤمن بالله واليوم الآخر ومن يتق الله يجعل له مخرجا

translation: And He will provide for him from where he does not expect. And whoever relies upon Allah - then He is sufficient for him. Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for all things a decree.
interpretation: This verse highlights the profound concept of divine provision and the importance of trust in Allah. The phrase 'He will provide for him from where he does not expect' emphasizes that Allah's sustenance is not limited to our perceived means. He can provide for us in ways we cannot even imagine, underscoring His limitless power and knowledge. This is often understood as a reassurance to those who are struggling financially or facing challenges. The verse then links this divine provision to 'trust in Allah.' The statement 'whoever relies upon Allah - then He is sufficient for him' establishes that true reliance, or tawakkul, upon Allah is the key to finding sufficiency and peace in life. It's not a passive waiting, but rather active striving while knowing that the ultimate outcome is in Allah's hands.  The final part, 'Indeed, Allah will accomplish His purpose. Allah has already set for all things a decree,' reinforces Allah's sovereignty and preordainment. Everything in the universe, including our sustenance and life events, is part of His plan. He will certainly bring about what He has willed and there's a divine decree (qadar) for every aspect of existence. This reinforces the idea that trusting in Allah does not negate the need for effort, but provides a sense of security in the knowledge that even when the outcome is beyond our immediate control, it is aligned with His will and wisdom. The verse as a whole emphasizes the importance of tawakkul (reliance on Allah), which combines sincere effort with full confidence in Allah's planning and provision, and a deep understanding of the divine decree.
orig: ويرزقه من حيث لا يحتسب ومن يتوكل على الله فهو حسبه إن الله بالغ أمره قد جعل الله لكل شيء قدرا

translation: And those of your women who have despaired of menstruation, if you doubt, then their period of waiting is three months, and for those who have not menstruated. And for those who are pregnant, their term is until they give birth. And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him of his matter ease.
interpretation:
This verse outlines the waiting periods ('iddah) for women in the context of divorce or the death of a husband. It addresses three specific situations:

1. **Women who have reached menopause (yaisna min al-maheedh):** For women who have despaired of menstruation, meaning they are past childbearing age, the waiting period is three months. The phrase "if you doubt" suggests that if there is uncertainty about whether a woman is truly past menopause, this three-month waiting period should be observed.

2. **Women who have not yet menstruated (wal-laa'ee lam yahidn):** This refers to girls who have not yet reached puberty and therefore haven't experienced menstruation. Their waiting period is also three months, aligning with those who have passed menopause. This shows consistency in a time-based waiting period.

3. **Pregnant Women (wa ulat al-ahmaal):** For pregnant women, the waiting period extends until they give birth. This acknowledges the biological reality of pregnancy and ensures the lineage of the child is clear.

The verse concludes with a general principle: "And whoever fears Allah - He will make for him of his matter ease." This serves as both a reminder and encouragement for believers to be mindful of God's laws and guidance. Those who adhere to His commands, including these specific rules concerning divorce and waiting periods, will find ease in their affairs. The final phrase is a strong encouragement to follow Allah's guidance in all aspects of life, including the complex issue of family matters.

In essence, this verse provides clear guidelines regarding the 'iddah of divorced or widowed women based on their biological circumstances. The purpose of these waiting periods is to ensure certainty regarding parentage, protect the rights of women and children, and foster order and stability in society, all while emphasizing taqwa (fear of God) as the foundation for leading a righteous life. The focus on ease suggests that God's commands are not meant to be burdensome but are rather a pathway to stability, justice, and ultimately a better life.
orig: واللائي يئسن من المحيض من نسائكم إن ارتبتم فعدتهن ثلاثة أشهر واللائي لم يحضن وأولات الأحمال أجلهن أن يضعن حملهن ومن يتق الله يجعل له من أمره يسرا

translation: That is the command of Allah, which He has sent down to you. And whoever fears Allah - He will remove from him his misdeeds and amplify for him his reward.
interpretation: This verse highlights the divine origin of the commandments and teachings within the Quran, emphasizing that they are not of human origin but are sent down by Allah. The verse presents a clear link between piety (taqwa, fearing Allah) and its positive consequences. 'Taqwa' here encapsulates a state of being conscious of God's presence and acting in accordance with His will. For those who maintain this consciousness and strive to please God, Allah promises two significant benefits: firstly, the expiation ('yakaffir 'anhu sayyi'aatihi') or removal of past sins and misdeeds. This signifies divine forgiveness and a cleansing of the individual's spiritual record. Secondly, the verse assures an increased reward ('wa yu'zim lahu ajraan') - a greater recompense than what their actions might naturally warrant. This emphasizes Allah's generosity and boundless grace towards those who sincerely seek His pleasure. Essentially, the verse is a call to action - a motivator to live a life of piety and obedience, assuring believers that their efforts will not only be acknowledged but will also result in forgiveness and amplified reward.
orig: ذلك أمر الله أنزله إليكم ومن يتق الله يكفر عنه سيئاته ويعظم له أجرا

translation: House them where you dwell, according to your means, and do not harm them in order to make things difficult for them. And if they are pregnant, then provide for them until they deliver their burden. Then if they suckle for you, give them their due payment. And consult among yourselves in a reasonable manner. But if you disagree, then there may suckle for him another woman.
interpretation:
This verse outlines the responsibilities of husbands towards their divorced wives, specifically focusing on their housing and financial well-being, especially during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The verse emphasizes several key points:

1. **Housing:** Divorced wives should be housed in a manner comparable to the husband's own living conditions, based on his financial capacity ('according to your means'). This provision ensures the wife has a safe and dignified place to stay. Importantly, the verse strictly prohibits harming or mistreating them to make their living situation difficult, indicating an emphasis on humane treatment.

2. **Financial Support during Pregnancy:** If the divorced wife is pregnant, the husband is obligated to provide for her needs until she gives birth. This obligation acknowledges the vulnerability of pregnant women and the necessity of their well-being, emphasizing the importance of supporting both mother and child.

3. **Compensation for Breastfeeding:** If the divorced wife chooses to breastfeed the child, she is entitled to fair compensation for her efforts. This payment is not merely a token but an acknowledgement of her labor and a crucial part of the child's well-being. The verse doesn't automatically require mothers to breastfeed, but if they choose to, fair remuneration is obligated.

4. **Mutual Consultation and Resolution:** The verse encourages amicable consultation between the parents ('consult among yourselves in a reasonable manner') regarding arrangements related to the child's care, including breastfeeding. This promotes cooperation and healthy communication even after divorce. However, it also acknowledges that disputes might arise. Therefore, it states that if an agreement on breastfeeding and compensation cannot be reached, another woman can be employed to nurse the child ('if you disagree, then there may suckle for him another woman'). This flexibility ensures the infant's nutritional needs are always met.

In essence, this verse highlights Islam's commitment to the well-being of divorced women and their children. It emphasizes the importance of financial security, dignified living conditions, fair compensation, and cooperative parenting, even in the face of separation. The verse reflects a balanced approach that considers both the practical aspects of the situation and the emotional needs of everyone involved.
orig: أسكنوهن من حيث سكنتم من وجدكم ولا تضاروهن لتضيقوا عليهن وإن كن أولات حمل فأنفقوا عليهن حتى يضعن حملهن فإن أرضعن لكم فآتوهن أجورهن وأتمروا بينكم بمعروف وإن تعاسرتم فسترضع له أخرى

translation: Let the wealthy man spend according to his wealth, and the one whose provision is restricted should spend from what Allah has given him. Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it. Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease.
interpretation: This verse outlines a principle of social responsibility and divine providence related to spending and financial capacity. It establishes that those blessed with wealth ('dhu sa'a') should spend generously from their abundance. This spending isn't defined arbitrarily; it's 'min sa'atihi' (from his wealth), implying a proportionality where giving scales with capacity. Conversely, those with limited resources ('man qudira 'alayhi rizquhu') are not obligated to the same extent. They are to spend 'mimma atahu Allah' (from what Allah has given them), demonstrating that all provision, large or small, is from God and should be used to benefit others as much as possible within one's means. The verse then transitions to emphasize divine justice and the principle that 'Allah la yukallifu nafsan illa ma ataha' (Allah does not burden any soul beyond what He has given it). This highlights that financial obligations are tailored to individual circumstances, and God does not expect anyone to give beyond their capability. Finally, the verse concludes with a hopeful promise: 'sayaj'alu Allahu ba'da 'usrin yusra' (Allah will bring about, after hardship, ease). This provides encouragement and reassurance that difficulties are not permanent and that, with faith and righteous conduct, relief and blessings will follow. In essence, the verse encourages responsible and compassionate spending according to one's capacity while assuring people of divine support and the eventual arrival of ease after any hardship. It promotes a balanced approach to both giving and receiving within a framework of faith and reliance on God's provision and wisdom.
orig: لينفق ذو سعة من سعته ومن قدر عليه رزقه فلينفق مما آتاه الله لا يكلف الله نفسا إلا ما آتاها سيجعل الله بعد عسر يسرا

translation: And how many a town rebelled against the command of its Lord and His messengers, so We called it to a severe account and punished it with a terrible punishment.
interpretation:
This verse serves as a stern warning, highlighting the consequences of rejecting divine guidance. It employs the phrase "how many a town" (وكأين من قرية) to emphasize the vast number of communities throughout history that have faced destruction due to their disobedience. The key themes within the verse are: 

1. **Rebellion (عتت):** The term 'atat' (عتت) signifies defiance and stubborn refusal to obey. It's not just simple disobedience, but a deliberate and persistent act of rebellion against God's commands and the messages brought by His messengers.

2. **Accountability (حاسبناها):** The phrase "We called it to a severe account" (فحاسبناها حسابا شديدا) emphasizes divine accountability. No community is exempt from being held responsible for its actions. This accountability is not casual but severe, implying a meticulous reckoning of their deeds.

3. **Terrible Punishment (عذبناها عذابا نكرا):** The final part of the verse describes the consequence of their rebellion: a "terrible punishment" (عذابا نكرا). The word 'nukra' (نكرا) conveys the notion of something unfamiliar, appalling, and extreme. It is a punishment that is not only severe but also unprecedented and horrifying. 

In essence, this verse serves as a reminder that societies are not exempt from divine judgment. When they blatantly reject the truth and choose to follow their own desires over divine guidance, they face dire consequences. The verse encourages reflection on the importance of obedience to God and His messengers and serves as a cautionary tale about the potential societal ruin that can result from unchecked arrogance and disobedience.
orig: وكأين من قرية عتت عن أمر ربها ورسله فحاسبناها حسابا شديدا وعذبناها عذابا نكرا

translation: So she tasted the evil consequences of her deed, and the outcome of her affair was loss.
interpretation: This verse describes the aftermath of a particular action or course of conduct taken by a 'she' (the feminine pronoun here indicating a singular entity, which is not explicitly identified in this verse, it could be an individual or even a community). The verse uses strong imagery: 'tasted the evil consequences' suggests experiencing the bitterness and pain that resulted from her choices, implying a direct and unavoidable negative experience. The use of ' وبال (wabal)' (evil consequences) indicates that the results were not just negative, but perhaps disastrous and weighty. Furthermore, the verse states, 'the outcome of her affair was loss' which emphasizes the finality and overall negative result of her actions. This signifies a total failure and a state of being in deficit or ruin. The verse, therefore, serves as a warning, implying that actions have consequences and engaging in undesirable conduct will inevitably lead to a severe negative outcome, both immediately and in the long run. It highlights the importance of considering the potential ramifications of one's choices and actions. The intended recipient of this cautionary message is likely whoever the original context of this verse refers to, whether individual or a group, but also has a timeless message about the cause and effect of negative conduct.
orig: فذاقت وبال أمرها وكان عاقبة أمرها خسرا

translation: Allah has prepared for them a severe punishment. So fear Allah, O you who possess intellect, you who have believed. Allah has sent down to you a Reminder.
interpretation: This verse carries a strong message combining warning and encouragement directed towards believers. It starts by stating that Allah has prepared a severe punishment for those who disobey Him and go against His commands. The specific group to whom this punishment is directed is not explicitly stated within this verse, but considering the general context of the Qur'an, it implies those who persistently reject faith, engage in wrongdoing, or rebel against God's guidance. Immediately following this warning is a call for piety: "So fear Allah." This call is directed to "those who possess intellect" and "those who have believed," highlighting that understanding and true faith should naturally lead to a profound sense of God-consciousness and fear of His punishment. The phrase "those who possess intellect" emphasizes the importance of reason in recognizing the truth of God's message and the gravity of His warnings. Furthermore, it suggests that true intellect lies in acknowledging and obeying God. The verse concludes with a note of reassurance, that God has sent down a 'Reminder' (dhikra). This reminder can be interpreted as the Qur'an itself, the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) or both. The 'dhikr' serves as a means of guidance, an opportunity to rectify ones actions, a message of hope, and the way to avoid the punishment by fearing Allah. In essence, the verse reminds believers that they have been blessed with faith and the intellect to recognize the truth; they should fear Allah, and use his Guidance in the form of Qur'an or the prophet, to navigate life accordingly and avoid His severe punishment.
orig: أعد الله لهم عذابا شديدا فاتقوا الله يا أولي الألباب الذين آمنوا قد أنزل الله إليكم ذكرا

translation: A messenger reciting to you the clear verses of Allah, to bring out those who believe and do righteous deeds from darknesses into the light. And whoever believes in Allah and does righteousness - He will admit him into gardens beneath which rivers flow, wherein they will abide forever. Allah has indeed provided for him an excellent provision.
interpretation: This verse highlights the core purpose of divine revelation and the path to salvation. It emphasizes the role of the Prophet as a messenger who conveys God's clear signs (ayat) to humanity. These signs serve a crucial purpose: to guide believers away from the 'darknesses' of ignorance, misguidance, and sin, and towards the 'light' of faith, knowledge, and righteousness. The 'darknesses' can refer to various forms of spiritual and moral obscurity, while the 'light' signifies divine guidance and clarity. The verse then connects faith (iman) and righteous deeds (amal al-salih) as inseparable components of salvation. It clearly states that those who believe in Allah and do good works will be rewarded with entry into gardens of paradise, a place of eternal bliss. The phrase 'abide forever' stresses the permanence of this reward. Finally, the verse concludes by stating that Allah has prepared for them an 'excellent provision' (rizqa), underscoring the abundance and perfection of the divine reward. This excellent provision includes both the spiritual bliss of paradise and the tangible provisions that will be enjoyed therein. In summary, the verse underscores the transformative power of faith and righteous action, mediated through divine guidance, leading to eternal salvation and the blessings of paradise.
orig: رسولا يتلو عليكم آيات الله مبينات ليخرج الذين آمنوا وعملوا الصالحات من الظلمات إلى النور ومن يؤمن بالله ويعمل صالحا يدخله جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار خالدين فيها أبدا قد أحسن الله له رزقا

translation: Allah is He who created seven heavens and of the earth, their like. [His] command descends among them so that you may know that Allah has power over all things and that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.
interpretation: This verse highlights the vastness and complexity of Allah's creation, emphasizing His absolute power and encompassing knowledge. The mention of 'seven heavens' and 'of the earth, their like' suggests a symmetry and intricate design within the cosmos, a creation that points to the Creator's majesty and wisdom. The phrase 'His command descends among them' refers to Allah's divine plan and continuous governance of the universe. The purpose of this grand creation, as the verse states, is 'so that you may know that Allah has power over all things and that Allah encompasses all things in knowledge.' This underscores the importance of reflecting upon creation as a pathway to understanding Allah's attributes: His infinite power (Qadir) and His all-encompassing knowledge (Al-'Aleem). The verse calls believers to recognize that nothing exists outside of Allah's control or beyond the scope of His knowledge. It is an invitation to humility and submission to the Creator who possesses all power and knowledge.
orig: الله الذي خلق سبع سماوات ومن الأرض مثلهن يتنزل الأمر بينهن لتعلموا أن الله على كل شيء قدير وأن الله قد أحاط بكل شيء علما

translation: O Prophet, why do you prohibit [for yourself] what Allah has made lawful for you, seeking to please your wives? And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.
interpretation: This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) directly, questioning his act of making something lawful unlawful for himself in order to please his wives. The specific incident leading to this revelation is debated among scholars, but it generally revolves around the Prophet vowing to abstain from something lawful, often related to a food item or conjugal relations, to satisfy the wishes of his wives. The verse serves multiple purposes. Firstly, it emphasizes that only Allah has the authority to declare something lawful or unlawful (halal or haram). The Prophet, while being the Messenger of Allah and a paragon of virtue, is also subject to the divine law and cannot unilaterally alter it. Secondly, it highlights the potential dangers of seeking human approval over divine pleasure. The Prophet’s action, though done with good intentions (to maintain harmony in his household), was a subtle deviation from divine guidance. The verse gently reprimands this action, reminding him and the believers that true satisfaction comes from following Allah’s will. Finally, the verse concludes with Allah's attributes of 'Forgiving' (Ghafur) and 'Merciful' (Rahim), which shows that Allah is willing to forgive and overlook human failings when there is repentance and sincere striving to do what is right. This part indicates a compassionate divine message that the Prophet's action, though not ideal, is still forgivable, and he is not condemned, only corrected. The broader lesson for believers is to always prioritize seeking Allah’s pleasure and adhering to His laws over satisfying personal desires or the expectations of others. It underscores the need for balance and the importance of not making something that is halal haram and it emphasizes that while good intentions are important, following Allah's commands is essential.
orig: يا أيها النبي لم تحرم ما أحل الله لك تبتغي مرضات أزواجك والله غفور رحيم

translation: Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths. And Allah is your protector, and He is the All-Knowing, the Wise.
interpretation: This verse, often cited in the context of oaths and expiation, addresses the human tendency to make vows and sometimes find it difficult to fulfill them. The core message is that Islam, as a merciful and practical religion, provides a path for believers to rectify situations where oaths cannot be upheld. The phrase "Allah has already ordained for you the dissolution of your oaths" (قد فرض الله لكم تحلة أيمانكم) signifies that God, in His wisdom, has legislated a means of expiation (kaffarah) for broken oaths. This demonstrates a divine understanding of human fallibility and a desire to ease believers' burdens, not to trap them in inflexible obligations. The mention that "Allah is your protector" (والله مولاكم) emphasizes that God is the one who supports, guides, and provides for the believers, and they should seek guidance from Him. The final attribute, "He is the All-Knowing, the Wise" (وهو العليم الحكيم), underscores that Allah’s commandments are based on His perfect knowledge of everything, including the human condition, and His wisdom ensures fairness and justice in all His rulings. The verse, therefore, offers a message of both accountability (to oaths) and mercy (through expiation), reminding believers that while commitment is valued, there is also a path to rectification through sincere effort and adherence to God's commands. The specific ways to make expiation for oaths are outlined in other parts of the Qur'an and Sunnah (Prophetic traditions), including feeding the poor, clothing the needy, or freeing a slave. If these are beyond the person's ability, fasting is also an option.
orig: قد فرض الله لكم تحلة أيمانكم والله مولاكم وهو العليم الحكيم

translation: And when the Prophet confided a statement to one of his wives, and then she divulged it, and Allah made it known to him, he informed [her] of a part of it and turned away from a part. And when he informed her of it, she said, “Who told you this?” He said, “The All-Knowing, the All-Aware told me.”
interpretation: This verse describes an incident involving the Prophet Muhammad and one of his wives, although the specific wife is not named. The narrative unfolds in several stages: 1) The Prophet confidentially shared some information (hadith) with a wife. The exact nature of this information is not disclosed in the verse but is understood to be something the Prophet wanted kept private. 2) That wife then divulged this secret, effectively betraying the Prophet’s trust. The verse uses the word 'nabba'at,' which implies both informing and revealing a secret. 3) Allah reveals to the Prophet what happened – that his wife had disclosed the secret. This emphasizes divine knowledge and oversight, that nothing is hidden from Allah. 4) The Prophet confronts his wife about the breach of trust, revealing only 'some' of the knowledge, choosing to overlook other aspects. This is interpreted as a display of the Prophet's compassion and forgiveness. He doesn't reveal all that was disclosed to him by Allah, displaying mercy and not seeking to further humiliate the wife. 5) The wife, surprised that the Prophet knew about her actions, asks him who informed him. This reveals her astonishment at the Prophet’s knowledge that she had disclosed the secret, demonstrating that the knowledge must have come from an external source and not her own observation. 6) The Prophet attributes the knowledge to Allah, using the names 'Al-Aleem' (The All-Knowing) and 'Al-Khabeer' (The All-Aware). This reinforces Allah's all-encompassing knowledge and awareness and further clarifies that the source of this knowledge is beyond any mortal being. The verse illustrates several important themes: the importance of trust and confidentiality in marital relations, the divine knowledge and guidance that is given to Prophets, the Prophet Muhammad’s forbearance and mercy, and the absolute knowledge of Allah. This story also serves as an example of human fallibility and weakness, even within the Prophet's household, reminding people that all are subject to human error, but should always turn to Allah for guidance.
orig: وإذ أسر النبي إلى بعض أزواجه حديثا فلما نبأت به وأظهره الله عليه عرف بعضه وأعرض عن بعض فلما نبأها به قالت من أنبأك هذا قال نبأني العليم الخبير

translation: If you two [wives] repent to Allah, [it is best], for your hearts have certainly inclined [to that]. But if you cooperate against him [the Prophet], then indeed, Allah is his protector, and Gabriel and the righteous of the believers and the angels, moreover, are [his] supporters.
interpretation: This verse addresses two wives of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him), commonly understood to be Hafsa and Aisha. The verse acknowledges that their hearts may have inclined towards something that displeased the Prophet, perhaps involving jealousy or revealing a secret. It encourages them to repent to God for this. The phrase "your hearts have certainly inclined" (صغت قلوبكما) suggests a deviation from what is expected of them as wives of the Prophet. The verse then issues a warning: If they were to collaborate against the Prophet, they are reminded that he is not without divine support. God Himself is the Prophet's protector (مولاه), along with the angel Gabriel, the righteous among believers, and the angels. The purpose is to both encourage repentance and to emphasize the Prophet's special position and divine protection. The verse indirectly underscores the importance of obedience to the Prophet and the serious consequences of going against his wishes, also highlighting that he has a strong support system even in the face of such challenges, both heavenly and earthly. The broader message is one of guidance towards righteousness and warning against actions that could harm the Prophet or undermine his mission.
orig: إن تتوبا إلى الله فقد صغت قلوبكما وإن تظاهرا عليه فإن الله هو مولاه وجبريل وصالح المؤمنين والملائكة بعد ذلك ظهير

translation: It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will give him in exchange wives better than you, submitting [to Allah], believing, devoutly obedient, turning [to Allah] in repentance, worshipping, traveling [for Allah's cause], previously married, and virgins.
interpretation:
This verse (Surah At-Tahrim, 66:5) is addressed to the wives of the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him). It presents a conditional statement: *if* the Prophet were to divorce his wives, Allah has the power to provide him with wives superior in their qualities. This verse highlights several key points:

1. **Conditional Nature:** The verse does not imply that the Prophet would divorce his wives. It sets a hypothetical scenario to illustrate Allah's power and sovereignty. The word 'ʿasā' (عسى) suggests possibility rather than certainty, often translated as 'it may be' or 'it is expected that.'

2. **Superior Qualities:** The subsequent descriptions of the potentially 'better' wives detail a number of virtues:
    *   **Muslimat (مُسْلِمَات):** Submitting to Allah – indicating outward adherence to Islamic teachings and practices.
    *   **Mu'minat (مُؤْمِنَات):** Believing – signifying inward faith and conviction.
    *   **Qanitat (قَانِتَات):** Devoutly obedient – emphasizing piety and dutifulness to Allah.
    *   **Ta'ibat (تَائِبَات):** Turning in repentance – highlighting the importance of seeking forgiveness and returning to Allah.
    *   **Abidat (عَابِدَات):** Worshipping – stressing dedication to the act of worship.
    *   **Saihat (سَائِحَات):** Traveling – this can mean traveling for the sake of Allah, such as in migration or religious pursuits, or it can be interpreted as fasting, as is understood in some classical exegesis.
    *  **Thayibat (ثَيِّبَات):** Previously married – highlighting the diverse marital backgrounds of women.
    *   **Abkara (أَبْكَارًا):** Virgins – highlighting another facet of women. It is noteworthy that the list includes both previously married and virgins, indicating that the perfection in women is not exclusive to either. 

3. **Emphasis on Piety:** The verse emphasizes the importance of piety, obedience to Allah, and submission as the true measures of a person's worth. The Prophet's wives were role models for the community, and this verse served as a reminder that these qualities were paramount.

4.  **Contextual Background:** This verse is revealed in the context of some of the Prophet's wives expressing discomfort about a particular matter (relating to the consumption of honey and the potential issue of marital privacy that ensued as mentioned in other verses of the same surah). While this verse is not a direct threat towards the wives, it does hint at the significance of adhering to the principles of the faith, demonstrating Allah's ability to provide other alternatives for the Prophet if circumstances require it, though this is not His intention. The purpose of this verse is more about emphasizing the ideal characteristics of believers.

5.  **Not a Prediction:** The verse isn't a prediction of the Prophet's future marriages, rather a conditional assertion of Allah's capability to provide for His prophet if needed. It serves as a reminder of divine power and ultimate control.

In summary, the verse is not a criticism of the Prophet's wives but rather a demonstration of Allah’s power and a description of the virtues He desires in believing women, highlighting piety and obedience, while addressing a specific incident and its implications within the Prophet's household.
orig: عسى ربه إن طلقكن أن يبدله أزواجا خيرا منكن مسلمات مؤمنات قانتات تائبات عابدات سائحات ثيبات وأبكارا

translation: O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire whose fuel is people and stones, over which are [appointed] angels, harsh and severe; they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them but do what they are commanded.
interpretation:
This verse is a powerful call to believers to take responsibility for their own salvation and the salvation of their families. It emphasizes the grave consequences of failing to do so, depicting Hellfire with its intense fuel and the powerful, unyielding angels who oversee it. 

The verse conveys several key points:

1. **Responsibility for Self and Family:** The address "O you who have believed" highlights that this is a direct command to those who have accepted the faith. It's not merely a suggestion, but an obligation to protect oneself and one's family from the hellfire. This implies that faith is not just a personal matter; it extends to the well-being of one's loved ones. 

2. **The Terrifying Nature of Hellfire:** The imagery of a fire fueled by "people and stones" emphasizes the sheer intensity and horror of Hell. The stones may be interpreted literally or metaphorically, suggesting that even the most inanimate objects contribute to the inferno. It is not an ordinary fire.

3. **Angels of Punishment:** The mention of "harsh and severe" angels underlines the seriousness of the consequences. These angels are not compassionate; they are resolute in their execution of God's commands. Their obedience and lack of disobedience to Allah emphasize the inescapability of the decree. 

4. **Obedience to Allah:** The phrase "they do not disobey Allah in what He commands them but do what they are commanded" serves as both a description of the angels and an implicit directive for believers. Just as the angels are utterly submissive to God’s will, so should believers strive to follow God’s commandments to protect themselves and their families from eternal punishment. 

In essence, the verse is a strong warning and a call to action. It urges believers to proactively safeguard themselves and their families through righteousness, good deeds, and following the divine guidance provided in the Quran and Sunnah. It is a reminder that salvation requires effort and that the stakes are incredibly high.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا قوا أنفسكم وأهليكم نارا وقودها الناس والحجارة عليها ملائكة غلاظ شداد لا يعصون الله ما أمرهم ويفعلون ما يؤمرون

translation: O you who disbelieved, make no excuses today. You are only being recompensed for what you used to do.
interpretation: This verse is directed towards those who actively rejected faith (disbelievers) on the Day of Judgment. It's a stark declaration that their attempts to offer excuses or justifications for their disbelief and wrongdoings during their earthly life will be futile. The phrase "make no excuses today" emphasizes the finality of the judgment and the futility of any further argument. Their fate is sealed, and they will be recompensed solely based on their actions – "You are only being recompensed for what you used to do." This highlights the principle of accountability in Islam, where individuals are held responsible for their choices and deeds, and their fate in the afterlife is determined by those actions. The verse serves as a warning for those who reject faith and a reminder of the consequences of their choices.
orig: يا أيها الذين كفروا لا تعتذروا اليوم إنما تجزون ما كنتم تعملون

translation: O you who have believed, repent to Allah with sincere repentance. Perhaps your Lord will remove from you your misdeeds and admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow on the Day when Allah will not disgrace the Prophet and those who believed with him. Their light will proceed before them and on their right; they will say, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us. Indeed, You are over all things competent."
interpretation:
This verse from Surah At-Tahrim (66:8) emphasizes the importance of sincere repentance (Tawbah Nasuha) for believers. It highlights several key aspects:

1. **Sincere Repentance (Tawbah Nasuha):** The verse calls upon believers to repent to Allah with a 'sincere repentance.' This signifies a complete turning away from sin, a genuine regret for past wrongdoings, a firm resolve not to repeat them, and seeking forgiveness from Allah. It's not just a verbal expression but a change of heart and action. The term 'Nasuha' itself suggests a form of repentance that is pure and leaves no trace of the sin behind.

2. **Divine Forgiveness and Reward:** The verse then offers hope that by engaging in sincere repentance, believers can anticipate Allah's forgiveness. It uses the term 'perhaps' (عسى) which implies both hope and the need for continuous striving. Specifically, Allah will remove their misdeeds (سيئاتكم) and grant them entrance into Gardens of Paradise (جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار) – a clear reward for their repentance and faith.

3. **The Day of Judgment:** The verse then transitions to the Day of Judgment, emphasizing that it will be a day of honor and distinction for the believers. Allah will not disgrace the Prophet (peace be upon him) and those who believed alongside him. This highlights the Prophet's unique status and the high esteem of the faithful.

4. **Light on the Day of Judgment:** A significant image presented is that of the believers' light (نورهم) proceeding before them and on their right. This light is a symbol of their faith, righteous actions, and the guidance they received in their earthly life. It will be their guide and their distinction on that Day. Some interpretations say that this light comes as a result of their faith and worship in their lives, not just their repentance.

5. **Prayer for Perfection and Forgiveness:** Despite their elevated status, believers still ask for Allah's grace and mercy on that Day, saying, "Our Lord, perfect for us our light and forgive us." This displays their humility and continued need for divine help even after their good deeds and sincere repentance. They recognize that even with divine grace they are still in need of forgiveness and grace. This also highlights that the Day of Judgment is not a place where people can have full confidence of their status, but rather, must pray to God for support and continued blessings.

6. **Allah's Omnipotence:** The verse concludes by affirming Allah's power and competence over all things (إنك على كل شيء قدير), which gives solace and comfort to the believers. It reminds them that forgiveness and reward are completely in the hands of Allah, who is all-powerful, and that they should therefore turn to Him in humility and hope.

In essence, this verse is a powerful encouragement for all believers to constantly evaluate themselves, repent sincerely for their wrongdoings, and strive to live a righteous life. It offers a message of hope, assuring them of Allah's forgiveness and promising them a reward on the Day of Judgment.
orig: يا أيها الذين آمنوا توبوا إلى الله توبة نصوحا عسى ربكم أن يكفر عنكم سيئاتكم ويدخلكم جنات تجري من تحتها الأنهار يوم لا يخزي الله النبي والذين آمنوا معه نورهم يسعى بين أيديهم وبأيمانهم يقولون ربنا أتمم لنا نورنا واغفر لنا إنك على كل شيء قدير

translation: O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and be harsh upon them. And their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.
interpretation:
This verse addresses the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and commands him to engage in 'jihad' (striving) against two specific groups: the 'kuffar' (disbelievers) and the 'munafiqeen' (hypocrites). The striving against them is not limited to physical combat in all situations, as the word 'jahada' implies a broader effort that includes argumentation, persuasion, and defending the truth. 

The verse also instructs the Prophet to be 'ghaleeth' (harsh) upon them. This harshness is not arbitrary cruelty but rather a firm and resolute stance against their disbelief and hypocrisy. It signifies not compromising on the core principles of Islam and not showing leniency where it may encourage further transgression. The context and circumstances would determine the appropriate application of this firmness.

The verse concludes by stating that 'ma'wahum jahannam wa bi'sa al-masir' (their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination). This is a severe warning about the consequences of disbelief and hypocrisy in the afterlife. It serves as a reminder of the gravity of these actions and the ultimate accountability before God. 

It's important to understand this verse within the broader context of the Qur'an, considering other verses that emphasize forgiveness, compassion, and peaceful resolution. The verse emphasizes firmness against those who actively oppose Islam and seek to undermine its principles, while other verses focus on guiding people to the truth through wisdom and kindness. The specific forms of struggle and harshness, according to scholarly interpretation, are often contextual and dependent upon the circumstances at hand, which does not give an unlimited permission to engage in extreme harshness. The overarching goal of these commands is ultimately the establishment of justice, truth, and the worship of the One God. The verse warns against the danger of hypocrisy and unbelief, and the ultimate consequence that awaits them.
orig: يا أيها النبي جاهد الكفار والمنافقين واغلظ عليهم ومأواهم جهنم وبئس المصير

translation: Allah presents an example of those who disbelieved: the wife of Noah and the wife of Lot. They were under two righteous servants of Ours, but they betrayed them, so those two husbands could not avail them anything against Allah. And it was said, "Enter the Fire with those who enter."
interpretation: This verse provides a powerful example to those who disbelieve, emphasizing that familial or marital ties to righteous individuals do not guarantee salvation or prevent divine punishment. The wives of Prophet Noah and Prophet Lot, despite being married to two of God's righteous servants, chose to betray their faith and the messages of their husbands. This betrayal, which could involve disbelief, hypocrisy, or actively opposing the prophets, highlights the individual responsibility of each person for their own actions and beliefs. Their relationship with these prophets didn't shield them from the consequences of their misdeeds. The verse concludes with their being commanded to enter the Fire, demonstrating that personal piety and faith are the only criteria for salvation, not inherited or relational righteousness. The example serves as a stark warning that proximity to faith without sincere adherence is futile and that ultimately, each person is accountable to God for their own choices, irrespective of family connections.
orig: ضرب الله مثلا للذين كفروا امرأت نوح وامرأت لوط كانتا تحت عبدين من عبادنا صالحين فخانتاهما فلم يغنيا عنهما من الله شيئا وقيل ادخلا النار مع الداخلين

translation: And Allah presents an example for those who believed: the wife of Pharaoh, when she said, "My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds and save me from the wrongdoing people."
interpretation: This verse highlights the exemplary faith of Pharaoh's wife, Asiya (though not explicitly named in the Quran), as a model for believers. Despite being married to the most powerful and tyrannical ruler of her time, she remained steadfast in her belief in Allah and rejected her husband's claims of divinity. Her prayer encapsulates several crucial aspects of faith. Firstly, she asks for a "house near You in Paradise," signifying her desire for closeness to God rather than worldly comforts or status. This prioritizes the afterlife and her relationship with God above all else. Secondly, she seeks refuge from the influence and deeds of Pharaoh, demonstrating a complete rejection of evil and oppression. Her request to be saved from the "wrongdoing people" further emphasizes her detachment from the unjust society she was part of. This verse serves as a powerful reminder that true faith can exist even in the most oppressive of environments and that a believer’s priorities should always be the pleasure of God and striving to be free from the influence of evil. It also showcases that a person's true worth and status is not determined by their worldly position or their spouse’s actions, but by their faith and devotion to Allah. Her story is an encouragement to maintain integrity in faith, regardless of surrounding pressures and personal circumstances.
orig: وضرب الله مثلا للذين آمنوا امرأت فرعون إذ قالت رب ابن لي عندك بيتا في الجنة ونجني من فرعون وعمله ونجني من القوم الظالمين

translation: And [mention] Mary, the daughter of Imran, who guarded her chastity, so We breathed into her [womb] through Our spirit. And she testified to the words of her Lord and His scriptures and was of the devoutly obedient.
interpretation:
This verse highlights the exceptional status of Mary, the mother of Jesus, within Islamic theology. It emphasizes several key aspects of her character and divine selection:

1. **"And [mention] Mary, the daughter of Imran"**: This establishes her lineage, connecting her to a respected family. It's a common Qur'anic practice to reference figures within their family context to establish their place within a historical and societal framework.

2. **"who guarded her chastity" (أحصنت فرجها)**: This is a crucial point. The phrase emphasizes her purity and virginity, both of which are considered foundational to the miraculous birth of Jesus. The term used, 'farj', refers specifically to her private parts, underscoring the significance of her chastity. It highlights that her conception was not through normal human means.

3. **"so We breathed into her [womb] through Our spirit" (فنفخنا فيه من روحنا)**: This directly references the miraculous conception of Jesus. The 'spirit' (روحنا) here is understood as a spirit created and belonging to God, not a physical entity. The act of breathing is a metaphor for divine creation, indicating that Jesus's existence is a direct act of God's power and will. It highlights the exceptional nature of his birth.

4. **"And she testified to the words of her Lord and His scriptures" (وصدقت بكلمات ربها وكتبه)**: This points to Mary's profound faith and belief in God's revelations. She is depicted not just as an instrument of divine will but also as a conscious and devoted believer. This emphasizes her active role in her relationship with God, and it is mentioned that she believed in the previous scriptures.

5. **"and was of the devoutly obedient" (وكانت من القانتين)**: The term 'qaniteen' signifies those who are constantly and humbly obedient to God. This is a final endorsement of Mary's character, solidifying her as an exemplary model of piety and submission to God's will. Her obedience extends to all that God has commanded.

In summary, this verse portrays Mary as a woman of exceptional piety, chosen by God for a unique role in history. Her chastity, divine conception of Jesus, unwavering faith, and deep obedience are presented as models for believers. The verse highlights the miraculous and divine aspect of the birth of Jesus while affirming Mary's elevated spiritual status within Islam.
orig: ومريم ابنت عمران التي أحصنت فرجها فنفخنا فيه من روحنا وصدقت بكلمات ربها وكتبه وكانت من القانتين

translation: Blessed is He in whose hand is dominion, and He is over all things competent.
interpretation: This verse, تبارك الذي بيده الملك وهو على كل شيء قدير, is a powerful declaration of God's absolute sovereignty and power. The phrase 'تبارك الذي' (Tabaraka alladhi) signifies that God is 'blessed' in the sense of being exalted, perfect, and overflowing with goodness. It's an affirmation of His transcendence and freedom from any deficiency. 'بيده الملك' (biyadihi al-mulk) which translates to 'in whose hand is dominion', emphasizes that all authority, control, and ownership of the universe are entirely His. This highlights His ultimate power and reign over all creation. The concluding part 'وهو على كل شيء قدير' (wa huwa 'ala kulli shay'in qadeer) – 'and He is over all things competent' – underscores His limitless capacity and ability. There's nothing beyond His power, and He is fully capable of doing whatever He wills. In summary, the verse is a concise and comprehensive statement about God's perfection, absolute authority, and limitless power, emphasizing His unique and unparalleled status as the sole sovereign of the cosmos and the One upon whom all things depend.
orig: تبارك الذي بيده الملك وهو على كل شيء قدير

translation: He who created death and life to test you [as to] which of you is best in deed - and He is the Exalted in Might, the Forgiving.
interpretation: This verse highlights the divine purpose behind the creation of both life and death. It's not a random occurrence but rather a deliberate test (ibtilakum) set by God. The purpose isn't simply to see who performs more actions, but who performs 'ahsan 'amala', which translates to 'best in deed'. 'Ahsan' here implies actions that are not only righteous and good but are also done with sincerity, excellence, and in accordance with God's guidance. It signifies quality over quantity.
